releases:\n\n- **`langchain`** latest release: Jun 22, 2026  \n  https://pypi.org/project/langchain\n- **`langgraph`** latest release: Jun 29, 2026  \n  https://pypi.org/project/langgraph\n- **`langchain-core`** latest release: Jun 18, 2026  \n  https://pypi.org/project/langchain-core\n- **`langchain-classic`** latest release: Jun 10, 2026  \n  https://pypi.org/project/langchain-classic\n\nThe docs position **LangChain v1** as the production-ready base for building agents:\n- LangChain v1 release notes:  \n  https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\n### The modern API: `create_agent`\n\nThe central fact in LangChain 1.x is:\n\n- **`langchain.agents.create_agent` is now the standard API**\n- It **replaces** the older `langgraph.prebuilt.create_react_agent`\n\nOfficial source:\n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\nThe docs state explicitly:\n- \"`create_agent` is the standard way to build agents in LangChain 1.0\"\n- it replaces `langgraph.prebuilt.create_react_agent`\n- middleware is the main customization mechanism\n\n### What replaced legacy patterns\n\nLangChain 1.x deliberately reduced the surface area of the core package.\n\nWhat moved out:\n\n- legacy chains and chain implementations\n- retrievers from the old `langchain.retrievers`\n- indexing API\n- hub module\n- deprecated/community exports\n\nThose now live in:\n- **`langchain-classic`**\n\nOfficial source:\n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1#langchain-classic\n\nSo the architectural reset is:\n\n- **Old world**: chains, retrievers, prebuilt patterns, broad namespace\n- **New world**: agents + middleware + provider-agnostic message/tool/model abstractions\n\n### New extension model: middleware\n\nMiddleware is now the key abstraction for customizing agent behavior.\n\nLangChain docs list built-in middleware such as:\n\n- `PIIMiddleware`\n- `SummarizationMiddleware`\n- `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware`\n\nAnd custom middleware hooks including:\n\n- `before_agent`\n- `before_model`\n- `wrap_model_call`\n- `wrap_tool_call`\n- `after_model`\n- `after_agent`\n\nOfficial source:\n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1#middleware\n\nThis is a major change: instead of stitching together chains or agent executors, you now modify agent behavior through middleware.\n\n### Runtime layer: LangGraph\n\nLangChain\u2019s own docs are explicit:\n\n- **LangChain** = agent framework / abstractions / integrations\n- **LangGraph** = orchestration runtime\n\nLangGraph provides:\n\n- durable execution\n- checkpointing / persistence\n- streaming\n- interrupts / human-in-the-loop\n- time travel\n- memory primitives\n\nSources:\n- LangGraph overview:  \n  https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/overview\n- LangGraph v1 notes:  \n  https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langgraph-v1\n\nLangGraph v1 specifically says:\n- `create_react_agent` is deprecated in favor of LangChain `create_agent`\n- LangGraph remains the underlying runtime\n\n### Practical interpretation for a CTO\n\nUse the stack by abstraction level:\n\n- **LangChain 1.x** when you want portable agent APIs and provider-agnostic tooling\n- **LangGraph** when you need explicit workflow control, durable state, custom graphs, or production-grade long-running orchestration\n- **`langchain-classic`** only for migration or legacy code\n\n### Bottom line on LangChain\n\nLangChain 1.x is no longer a \u201cgrab bag\u201d framework. It is now a narrower agent framework centered on `create_agent`, middleware, and standard content blocks, with LangGraph clearly underneath.\n\n---\n\n## 3) Deep Agents\n\n### Current version\n\nPyPI shows:\n\n- **`deepagents` 0.6.12**\n- released **Jun 25, 2026**\n\nSource:\n- https://pypi.org/project/deepagents\n\n### What Deep Agents is\n\nThe docs define Deep Agents as an **agent harness** built on top of LangChain and LangGraph, with batteries included for:\n\n- planning\n- subagents\n- filesystem access\n- permissions\n- context management\n- human approval\n- long-term memory\n\nSources:\n- Overview: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n- API reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents\n\n### Core API\n\nThe primary constructor is:\n\n- **`create_deep_agent(...)`**\n\nOfficial docs and reference:\n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents\n\nThe quickstart pattern is:\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"openai:gpt-5.5\",\n    tools=[...],\n    system_prompt=\"You are a helpful assistant\",\n)\n```\n\n### Subagents\n\nDeep Agents includes a built-in **`task` tool** for spawning subagents.\n\nCore concepts visible in the docs/reference:\n\n- `SubAgent`\n- `CompiledSubAgent`\n- `SubAgentMiddleware`\n- `create_sub_agent`\n- default `general-purpose` subagent\n- async subagent support:\n  - `AsyncSubAgent`\n  - `AsyncSubAgentMiddleware`\n\nSources:\n- Overview / delegation section:  \n  https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n- Reference:  \n  https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents\n\nThis is one of the main differentiators from vanilla LangChain agents: Deep Agents bakes subagent orchestration into the default harness.\n\n### Filesystem backends\n\nDeep Agents exposes built-in filesystem tools:\n\n- `ls`\n- `read_file`\n- `write_file`\n- `edit_file`\n- `glob`\n- `grep`\n- optionally `execute`\n\nDocs also describe pluggable backends including:\n\n- `StateBackend` \u2014 state-backed, ephemeral\n- `StoreBackend` \u2014 LangGraph store-backed, persistent\n- `FilesystemBackend` \u2014 real filesystem\n- `CompositeBackend` \u2014 path-routed composite\n- `ContextHubBackend`\n- `LocalShellBackend`\n- `LangSmithSandbox`\n\nSources:\n- Overview:  \n  https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n- Reference backend classes:  \n  https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents\n\nThis is notable operationally: Deep Agents treats filesystem access as a first-class substrate, not an add-on tool.\n\n### Human-in-the-loop\n\nDeep Agents supports HITL via `interrupt_on`.\n\nBehavior:\n\n- configure tools that require approval\n- backed by LangGraph interrupts\n- requires a checkpointer to pause/resume safely\n- decisions can include `approve`, `edit`, `reject`, `respond`\n\nOfficial docs:\n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\nThe docs are explicit that:\n- a **checkpointer is required**\n- you resume with the same thread ID\n- filesystem-permission interrupts are also supported\n- conditional interrupts require `langchain>=1.3.3`\n\n### Other core capabilities\n\nThe current Deep Agents stack also includes:\n\n- `write_todos` planning\n- memory via `AGENTS.md`\n- skills via `SKILL.md`\n- summarization middleware\n- prompt caching support on some providers\n- interpreters with QuickJS via `CodeInterpreterMiddleware`\n- dynamic subagents\n- sandbox-backed `execute`\n\nRelevant docs:\n- Overview: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n- Interpreters: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/interpreters\n\n### CTO take\n\nDeep Agents is best understood as:\n- **LangChain `create_agent` + LangGraph runtime + a strongly opinionated default harness**\n\nUse it when you want:\n- fast time-to-agent\n- delegation/subagents\n- filesystem-native behavior\n- long-running task support\n- built-in planning/HITL/context tooling\n\nDo **not** use it when you want minimalism or very custom orchestration; then drop to LangChain or LangGraph directly.\n\n---\n\n## 4) Next.js\n\n### Current major version\n\nThe current major version is:\n\n- **Next.js 16**\n- docs currently show **Latest Version 16.2.9**\n\nSources:\n- Upgrade guide / docs header:  \n  https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n- Next.js 16 announcement:  \n  https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### Runtime requirements\n\nOfficial requirements:\n\n- **Minimum Node.js: 20.9**\n- **Minimum TypeScript: 5.1.0**\n- Supported browsers:\n  - Chrome 111+\n  - Edge 111+\n  - Firefox 111+\n  - Safari 16.4+\n\nSource:\n- Installation docs:  \n  https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/installation\n- Next 16 release notes:  \n  https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### Build tooling: Turbopack is now default\n\nThis is the most important tooling shift:\n\n- **Turbopack is now the default bundler**\n- `next dev` uses Turbopack by default\n- `next build` also uses Turbopack by default\n- You can opt back to webpack with:\n  - `next dev --webpack`\n  - `next build --webpack`\n\nSources:\n- Installation docs:  \n  https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/installation\n- Next 16 announcement:  \n  https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\nThe upgrade guide also says:\n- if you have a **custom webpack config**, `next build` will now fail unless you explicitly deal with the Turbopack transition\n\nSource:\n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n### Key breaking changes\n\n#### 1) `middleware.ts` \u2192 `proxy.ts`\nNext.js 16 introduces `proxy.ts` as the explicit network-boundary file.\n\n- `proxy.ts` replaces `middleware.ts`\n- `proxy.ts` runs on **Node.js runtime**\n- `middleware.ts` remains for Edge use cases but is deprecated\n\nSource:\n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n#### 2) Async request APIs\nSynchronous access has been removed for several APIs.\n\nNow must use async access for:\n- `params`\n- `searchParams`\n- `cookies()`\n- `headers()`\n- `draftMode()`\n\nSource:\n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n#### 3) `next lint` removed\n- `next lint` command removed\n- `next build` no longer runs lint automatically\n- use ESLint CLI or Biome directly\n\nSources:\n- Installation docs:  \n  https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/installation\n- Next 16 release notes:  \n  https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n#### 4) PPR / caching model cleanup\n- `experimental.ppr` removed\n- `experimental.dynamicIO` renamed to `cacheComponents`\n- caching is now centered on:\n  - `cacheComponents`\n  - `\"use cache\"`\n  - new APIs like `updateTag()` / revised `revalidateTag()`\n\nSource:\n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n#### 5) Parallel routes now require explicit `default.js`\nBuilds can fail without them.\n\nSource:\n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n#### 6) Image behavior/security defaults changed\nNotable changes include:\n- `images.minimumCacheTTL` default increased\n- `images.imageSizes` default changed\n- `images.qualities` default changed to `[75]`\n- local `next/image` src with query strings now requires `images.localPatterns`\n- local IP optimization blocked by default\n\nSource:\n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### Other notable platform changes\n\n- **Build Adapters API** introduced in alpha\n- **React Compiler support** is stable\n- **Turbopack filesystem caching** available in beta\n- `create-next-app` now defaults to:\n  - TypeScript\n  - Tailwind\n  - ESLint\n  - App Router\n  - Turbopack\n  - optionally `AGENTS.md`\n\nSources:\n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/installation\n\n### CTO take\n\nNext.js 16 is a meaningful platform consolidation release:\n\n- Turbopack is no longer optional background tech; it is the default build system.\n- The framework is forcing cleanup of old APIs (`next lint`, sync request APIs, deprecated config flags).\n- If you run custom webpack-heavy builds, treat upgrade planning as a real migration project.\n- If you are greenfield, the default stack is now much cleaner and faster than in the 13/14 era.\n\n---\n\n# Strategic recommendations\n\n## If you are standardizing an AI application stack\nUse this layering:\n\n- **Frontend / full-stack web**: Next.js 16\n- **Agent abstraction layer**: LangChain 1.x\n- **Runtime / orchestration / durability**: LangGraph\n- **Batteries-included agent apps**: Deep Agents\n- **Model default**: a GPT-5 mini-class model for cost/performance, with a reasoning model or `reasoning_effort` escalation path\n\n## If you have an existing LangChain codebase\nPriorities:\n\n1. move new agent work to `create_agent`\n2. stop building on deprecated `create_react_agent`\n3. isolate legacy chains/retrievers into `langchain-classic`\n4. adopt LangGraph primitives where persistence/HITL/time-travel matter\n\n## If you have an existing Next.js 14/15 codebase\nCheck for:\n\n- custom webpack config\n- `middleware.ts`\n- sync `params/searchParams`\n- `next lint` in CI\n- old PPR or `experimental.*` caching flags\n- assumptions about image defaults\n\n---\n\n# Source list\n\n## OpenAI / model ecosystem\n- OpenAI community discussion citing official GPT-5 reasoning-effort behavior:  \n The key architectural shift is:\n\n- **`create_agent` is the modern standard**\n- older agent patterns have been replaced by a **middleware-centric agent API**\n- **LangGraph** is the runtime/orchestration layer under LangChain agents\n- legacy 0.x-era functionality has been moved aside into **`langchain-classic`** or archived docs\n\nSources:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/migrate/langchain-v1  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langgraph-v1\n\n### Current versions\nThere are two version signals worth tracking:\n\n#### A. Official LangChain release notes baseline\nThe official Python changelog highlights these milestone versions:\n\n- `langchain v1.3.0` \u2014 May 12, 2026\n- `langgraph v1.2.0` \u2014 May 12, 2026\n- `deepagents v0.6.0` \u2014 May 12, 2026\n\nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/changelog\n\n#### B. Current package index versions\nPyPI now shows newer patch-level package versions beyond those milestone notes:\n\n- `langchain` latest PyPI release: **1.3.11**  \n  https://pypi.org/project/langchain\n- `deepagents` latest PyPI release: **0.6.12**  \n  https://pypi.org/project/deepagents\n\nI could not confirm an exact current PyPI version for `langgraph` from a clean official/package-index result in the same way, so the safest citable runtime milestone remains the official release-note line: **LangGraph v1.2.0**.  \nSources:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/changelog  \n- https://pypi.org/project/langchain  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langgraph-v1\n\n### The modern agent-building API\nThe new standard is **`create_agent`**.\n\nLangChain\u2019s v1 release notes explicitly say `create_agent` replaces `langgraph.prebuilt.create_react_agent`. It is simpler at the top level, but more extensible because it is built around **middleware**.\n\nSources:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/migrate/langchain-v1  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/migrate/langgraph-v1\n\n### What replaced the legacy patterns\nThe important migration story is not just \u201cnew function name.\u201d It is a broader replacement of older agent/chains patterns.\n\n#### Replacements called out in official docs\n\n| Legacy / older pattern | Modern replacement |\n|---|---|\n| `langgraph.prebuilt.create_react_agent` | `langchain.agents.create_agent` |\n| pre-model hooks | middleware `before_model` |\n| post-model hooks | middleware `after_model` |\n| ad hoc tool error handling | middleware `wrap_tool_call` |\n| prompted structured output | `ToolStrategy` / `ProviderStrategy` |\n| older `langchain` broad namespace | streamlined `langchain`; legacy moved to `langchain-classic` |\n\nSources:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/migrate/langchain-v1  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\nLangChain\u2019s own philosophy/release docs also state that the old sprawl of chains/agents was intentionally replaced with a more compact 1.x architecture.  \nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/philosophy\n\n### Middleware is now the control plane\nModern LangChain agents are increasingly configured through middleware rather than one-off wrappers.\n\nExamples called out in official docs include:\n\n- summarization middleware\n- human-in-the-loop middleware\n- retries\n- moderation\n- dynamic model selection\n- tool-call wrapping\n\nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/middleware/overview\n\n### Runtime layer: LangGraph\nThe runtime beneath LangChain agents is **LangGraph**. LangChain\u2019s docs describe the relationship clearly:\n\n- **LangChain** = opinionated agent framework\n- **LangGraph** = lower-level orchestration/runtime layer\n\nLangGraph remains the place to drop down when you need:\n\n- custom state graphs\n- explicit routing/fan-out\n- checkpointing\n- durable execution\n- typed streaming\n- human interrupts\n- advanced orchestration patterns\n\nSources:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langgraph-v1  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/workflows-agents  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/use-graph-api\n\n### Notable runtime advances in the 1.x era\nFrom the official changelog, the runtime story now includes:\n\n- typed `GraphOutput`\n- typed streaming formats (`version=\"v2\"` and later event streaming evolutions)\n- checkpoint/state durability\n- `DeltaChannel` for more efficient state/checkpoint storage\n- node/run timeout controls\n- better event streaming and observability\n\nSources:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/changelog  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/streaming  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/observability\n\n### CTO takeaway\nLangChain 1.x is no longer best understood as \u201ca prompt-chaining library.\u201d It is now:\n\n1. a slimmed-down high-level agent framework (`create_agent`)\n2. powered by middleware as the main extension mechanism\n3. sitting on top of **LangGraph**, which is the real runtime substrate for durable agent systems\n\n---\n\n## 3) `deepagents`: current version and core APIs\n\n### Executive take\n`deepagents` is LangChain\u2019s more opinionated agent harness for long-horizon, tool-using, file-working, subagent-spawning systems. It is positioned above `create_agent`, not below it.\n\nSources:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview  \n- https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents\n\n### Current version\nCurrent PyPI package version:\n\n- **`deepagents 0.6.12`** \u2014 released **June 25, 2026**\n\nSource:  \n- https://pypi.org/project/deepagents\n\nNote: LangChain\u2019s official changelog milestone mentions `deepagents v0.6.0` on May 12, 2026, but PyPI shows later patch releases through `0.6.12`.  \nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/changelog\n\n### Core API: agent creation\nPrimary Python constructor:\n\n- **`create_deep_agent(...)`**\n\nPrimary JS/TS constructor:\n\n- **`createDeepAgent(...)`**\n\nSources:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/javascript/deepagents\n\nThe docs position it as a pre-wired execution graph with:\n\n- tool loop\n- planning/todo support\n- filesystem tools\n- context management\n- subagents\n- skills/memory\n- optional HITL controls\n\nSources:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents\n\n### Built-in tool surface\nThe docs show that deep agents come with a default tool environment including:\n\n- `write_todos`\n- `ls`\n- `read_file`\n- `write_file`\n- `edit_file`\n- `glob`\n- `grep`\n- `task` for subagent delegation\n\nSources:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/javascript/deepagents\n\n### Subagents\nSubagent delegation is a core feature, not an add-on. The official docs describe deep agents as supporting:\n\n- subagent spawning\n- isolated context windows\n- delegation via a `task` tool\n- composition with custom LangGraph subgraphs\n\nA key extensibility point: any LangGraph `CompiledStateGraph` can be used as a subagent.\n\nSources:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n### Filesystem backends\nThe backend model is one of the most important parts of `deepagents`.\n\nCore backend classes documented in the Python reference:\n\n- `StateBackend`\n- `StoreBackend`\n- `FilesystemBackend`\n- `CompositeBackend`\n- `BaseSandbox`\n\nSources:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/backends  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n#### Backend roles\n\n| Backend | Purpose |\n|---|---|\n| `StateBackend` | Ephemeral files stored in agent state |\n| `StoreBackend` | Persistent files in LangGraph `BaseStore` |\n| `FilesystemBackend` | Direct host filesystem access |\n| `CompositeBackend` | Route different paths to different backends |\n| `BaseSandbox` | Sandbox abstraction for execution environments |\n\nSource:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/backends\n\nThis is a strong design choice for enterprise use, because it separates:\n\n- scratch state\n- durable memory/artifacts\n- host-level filesystem access\n- sandboxed execution\n\n### Human-in-the-loop\nThe docs describe human control as a first-class part of the harness through:\n\n- approval workflows\n- interrupts / steering\n- human-in-the-loop middleware concepts\n\nSources:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents\n\n### CTO takeaway\n`deepagents` is effectively LangChain\u2019s \u201copinionated production harness\u201d for:\n- multi-step agent work\n- file-centric workflows\n- subagent decomposition\n- persistent/durable state\n- human checkpoints\n\nIf `create_agent` is the lightweight default, `deepagents` is the bundled higher-level harness for agentic applications that need working memory, planning, and delegation.\n\n---\n\n## 4) Next.js: current major version, runtime requirements, breaking changes, build tooling\n\n### Executive take\nThe current major line is **Next.js 16**. In mid-2026, the safest stable target is the **16.2.x** line, while **16.3** is present as preview/recent release activity depending on channel. The official upgrade docs currently show **\u201cLatest Version 16.2.10\u201d**.\n\nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-2  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog\n\n### Current major version\n- **Major version:** `16`\n- Official upgrade guide shows latest version in docs: **16.2.10**\n\nSource:  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n### Runtime requirements\nNext.js 16 raises the baseline:\n\n- **Node.js 20.9.0+**\n- **Node.js 18 is no longer supported**\n- **TypeScript 5.1+**\n- Browser support baseline:\n  - Chrome 111+\n  - Edge 111+\n  - Firefox 111+\n  - Safari 16.4+\n\nSource:  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n### Key breaking changes\nThe most important migration-impact changes called out by official docs:\n\n#### 1. Async Request APIs are now fully async\nNext.js 15 introduced this direction; Next.js 16 removes the temporary sync compatibility.\n\nAffected APIs include:\n- `cookies`\n- `headers`\n- `draftMode`\n- `params`\n- `searchParams`\n\nSource:  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n#### 2. `middleware` \u2192 `proxy`\nThe older network-boundary convention is deprecated/replaced by `proxy`.\n\nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n#### 3. Stabilized APIs lose `unstable_` prefixes\nThe upgrade guide calls out removal of `unstable_` prefixes for APIs that have stabilized.\n\nSource:  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n#### 4. Partial Prerendering experimental config cleanup\n`experimental_ppr` route segment config was removed from pages/layouts in favor of newer patterns.\n\nSource:  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n#### 5. `next/image` defaults changed\nThe release notes call out image-default changes as part of the major version shift.\n\nSource:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### Build tooling: Turbopack is now the default\nThis is one of the most important ecosystem signals in frontend engineering right now.\n\nNext.js 16 makes **Turbopack stable and default** for:\n\n- `next dev`\n- `next build`\n\nBefore 16, teams had to opt in with `--turbopack` / `--turbo`. package exists on PyPI**\n- **Latest observed core code tag is pre-release `0.7.0a3`**\n- `deepagents` is still **pre-1.0** and should be treated accordingly\n\n## What deepagents is\n\nOfficial docs describe Deep Agents as an **agent harness** built on LangGraph, with built-in support for:\n- planning\n- subagents\n- filesystems\n- context management\n- steering / HITL\n\nOverview:\nhttps://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n## Core APIs and capabilities\n\n## Agent execution\n\nThe quickstart shows a standard invocation model:\n\n- install with `pip install deepagents`\n- run the agent with **`agent.invoke({...})`**\n- pass a chat-style `messages` array\n\nQuickstart:  \nhttps://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/quickstart\n\nExample shape from docs:\n\n```python\nresult = agent.invoke({\n    \"messages\": [{\n        \"role\": \"user\",\n        \"content\": \"What is langgraph?\"\n    }]\n})\n```\n\n## Agent construction / customization\n\nThe public release notes show construction customization such as:\n\n- **`create_deep_agent(..., middleware=[...])`**\n\nGitHub release notes mention middleware replacement behavior, including `SummarizationMiddleware`.  \nhttps://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/releases\n\n## Subagents\n\nSubagents are a first-class part of the design, not a bolt-on. Docs and release notes describe:\n\n- isolated context windows\n- built-in delegation\n- inline subagents\n- async/remote subagents\n\nSources:\n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n- https://www.langchain.com/blog/deep-agents-v0-5\n\n### Inline vs async subagents\n\nThe v0.5 announcement explains two modes:\n\n- **inline subagents**: supervisor waits\n- **async subagents**: returns task ID, work continues remotely\n\nSource:  \nhttps://www.langchain.com/blog/deep-agents-v0-5\n\n## Filesystem backends and file model\n\nDeepagents has a distinctive **filesystem-centric** architecture. Official overview breaks the environment into layers including:\n\n- tools\n- virtual filesystem\n- filesystem permissions\n- code execution\n\nOverview:  \nhttps://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\nThe docs explicitly say the virtual filesystem is backed by **pluggable backends**, but the surfaced docs here do **not** give a clean backend matrix with exact class names for every backend. So the safe statement is:\n\n- deepagents supports **pluggable filesystem backends**\n- file tools like `write_file` and `read_file` are built in\n- exact backend implementation choices should be verified in source/reference before standardizing across the org\n\nSources:\n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/quickstart\n\n## Human-in-the-loop\n\nHITL is a core feature, not an add-on. Official docs mention:\n\n- human-in-the-loop approval\n- interrupts\n- steering\n\nOverview:\nhttps://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\nAnd the managed runtime docs extend this with:\n- durable runs\n- thread state\n- sandboxes\n- traces\n- revisions\n\nManaged Deep Agents:\nhttps://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/managed-deep-agents-overview\n\n## Managed/runtime status\n\nLangChain also offers **Managed Deep Agents**, but the docs say it is in **private beta** and limited to **LangSmith Cloud in the US region**.  \nhttps://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/managed-deep-agents-overview\n\n## CTO take\n\nDeepagents is compelling if you want an opinionated harness for:\n- multi-step agents\n- subagent decomposition\n- file-backed context management\n- HITL controls\n\nBut it is still a **fast-moving pre-1.0 project**. Treat it as:\n- promising\n- powerful\n- not yet as lifecycle-stable as LangChain/LangGraph 1.x\n\n---\n\n# 4) Next.js\n\n## Current major version\n\nThe current major version is **Next.js 16**.  \nhttps://nextjs.org/blog/next-16  \nhttps://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\nThe official docs show **16.2.10** as the current stable docs baseline, while **16.3** is still preview.  \nhttps://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16  \nhttps://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-3-instant-navigations\n\n## Runtime requirements\n\nNext.js 16 requires:\n\n- **Node.js 20.9.0+**\n- **TypeScript 5.1.0+**\n- supported browsers:\n  - Chrome 111+\n  - Edge 111+\n  - Firefox 111+\n  - Safari 16.4+\n\nSource:  \nhttps://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\nThis is a meaningful floor bump. If you still have Node 18 in CI, containers, or internal tooling, you are behind.\n\n## Key breaking changes\n\n## 1. Turbopack is now the default bundler\n\nStarting with Next.js 16:\n- `next dev` uses Turbopack by default\n- `next build` uses Turbopack by default\n\nSources:\n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack\n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\nThis is the biggest practical shift in build tooling.\n\n## 2. `next lint` is removed\n\nThe old framework-level lint command is gone. `next build` also no longer runs linting.\n\nYou now need to run linting explicitly through:\n- ESLint CLI\n- Biome\n- or your own CI command\n\nSource:  \nhttps://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16  \nhttps://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n## 3. Runtime config is removed\n\nRemoved:\n- `serverRuntimeConfig`\n- `publicRuntimeConfig`\n\nUse env vars and modern server/client boundaries instead.  \nhttps://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n## 4. `middleware.ts` is deprecated in favor of `proxy.ts`\n\nThis is a naming and convention shift the docs call out.  \nhttps://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n## 5. Parallel routes are stricter\n\nNext.js 16 requires explicit `default.js` files for parallel route slots; builds fail otherwise.  \nhttps://nextjs.org/blog/next-16  \nhttps://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n## 6. Old config names are removed\n\n- `experimental.turbo` \u2192 replaced by **`turbopack`**\n- older `devIndicators` options removed\n- AMP support removed\n\nSources:\n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopack\n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n## Current build tooling reality\n\n## Turbopack is the strategic default\n\nTurbopack is now:\n- stable\n- default for dev\n- default for build\n\nDocs:\nhttps://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack  \nhttps://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n## But Turbopack is not a perfect webpack clone\n\nImportant caveats in official docs:\n\n- webpack plugins are not supported by Turbopack\n- `webpack()` config is not honored by Turbopack\n- some Sass customizations still require webpack\n- some platforms without native bindings fall back to WASM and lose Turbopack support\n\nSource:  \nhttps://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack\n\n### Native runtime support matters\n\nTurbopack native bindings exist for mainstream:\n- macOS\n- Windows\n- Linux\n- x64 / ARM64\n- glibc / musl variants\n\nOn platforms like FreeBSD/OpenBSD, docs indicate fallback behavior without Turbopack support.  \nhttps://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack\n\n## Point release status\n\nAs of early July 2026:\n- **16.2.x** is the safe stable family\n- **16.3** is preview, not the default enterprise target yet\n\nSources:\n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n- https://nextjs.org/blog\n\n## CTO take\n\nFor production estates, the practical posture is:\n\n- standardize on **Next.js 16.2.x**\n- move infra to **Node 20.9+**\n- assume **Turbopack-first**, not The tournament runs from **11 June to 19 July 2026** and includes **104 matches**. LX** was played on **8 February 2026** at **Levi\u2019s Stadium** in **Santa Clara, California**. The **Seattle Seahawks** defeated the **New England Patriots**, **29-13**, to win the franchise\u2019s **second** Super Bowl title.  \nSources: Levi\u2019s Stadium event page: https://levisstadium.com/event/super-bowl-lx ; NFL coverage: https://www.nfl.com/news/seahawks-patriots-in-super-bowl-lx-what-we-learned-from-seattle-s-29-13-win ; Seahawks team recap: https://www.seahawks.com/video/final-minutes-of-the-super-bowl-lx-victory-vs-the-new-england-patriots-seattle-seahawks\n\n### MVP\n\nThe NFL named **Kenneth Walker III** the **Super Bowl LX MVP** after he totaled **161 scrimmage yards**, including **135 rushing yards on 27 carries** and **two catches for 26 yards**. NFL.com notes that his 135 rushing yards were the most in a Super Bowl since Terrell Davis ran for 157 in Super Bowl XXXII.  \nSource: https://www.nfl.com/news/seahawks-rb-kenneth-walker-iii-named-super-bowl-lx-mvp\n\n### Game shape and notable detail\n\nThe game was controlled largely by Seattle\u2019s defense and kicking game before opening up later. NFL.com says kicker **Jason Myers** made a **Super Bowl-record five field goals** and scored **17 points**, while Seattle\u2019s defense repeatedly disrupted Patriots quarterback **Drake Maye**.  \nSources: https://www.nfl.com/news/seahawks-jason-myers-first-200-point-scorer-record-five-field-goals-super-bowl-lx ; https://www.nfl.com/news/seahawks-cb-devon-witherspoon-shines-brightest-for-seattle-s-defense-in-super-bowl-lx-win-over-patriots\n\n### Significance\n\nFor Seattle, the win delivered the club\u2019s **second Lombardi Trophy** and capped one of the more surprising quarterback redemption arcs in recent years with **Sam Darnold** at the helm.  \nSources: https://www.nfl.com/news/sam-darnold-silences-skeptics-as-seahawks-dominate-patriots-in-super-bowl-lx ; https://www.nfl.com/news/social-media-reacts-to-seahawks-win-over-patriots-in-super-bowl-lx\n\n---\n\n## 3) The 2026 NBA Finals\n\n### Result and core facts\n\nThe **New York Knicks** beat the **San Antonio Spurs** **4-1** in the **2026 NBA Finals**. The series ran from **3 June to 13 June 2026**, and New York clinched the title in **Game 5**, winning **94-90** on the road in San Antonio.  \nSources: NBA Finals page: https://www.nba.com/playoffs/2026/nba-finals ; Game 5 box/recap: https://www.nba.com/game/nyk-vs-sas-0042500405 ; NBA Finals schedule page: https://www.nba.com/news/2026-nba-finals-schedule\n\n### Clinching game\n\nIn the clincher, **Jalen Brunson** scored **45 points** as the Knicks closed out the series. NBA.com says he scored **15 points in the fourth quarter** and led New York to its first championship since 1973.  \nSources: https://www.nba.com/news/live-updates-2026-nba-finals-game-5-knicks-seek-first-title-since-1973 ; https://www.nba.com/news/4-takeaways-knicks-spurs-game-5\n\n### Finals MVP\n\n**Jalen Brunson** won the **Bill Russell NBA Finals MVP Award**. NBA.com called Game 5 one of the strongest closeout performances in recent Finals history.  \nSource: https://www.nba.com/news/jalen-brunson-wins-bill-russell-trophy-as-2026-nba-finals-mvp\n\n### Historical significance\n\nThis Finals carried several layers of historical weight:\n\n- It gave the Knicks their **first championship in 53 years**, and their **first since 1973**.  \n  Sources: https://www.nba.com/news/how-the-knicks-won-the-2026-nba-championship ; https://www.nba.com/news/2026-nba-finals-schedule\n\n- It was the franchise\u2019s **third NBA title** overall.  \n  Source: NBA Finals overview: https://www.nba.com/playoffs/2026/nba-finals\n\n- Game 4 became a signature moment: NBA.com says New York erased a **29-point deficit**, the **largest comeback in NBA Finals history**, on the way to a 107-106 win and a 3-1 series lead.  \n  Sources: https://www.nba.com/watch/list/collection/2026-nba-finals-game-recap-videos ; https://www.nba.com/news/starting-5-finals-game-5-tonight-will-there-be-a-champion-or-a-game-6\n\n- Brunson, **Mikal Bridges**, and **Josh Hart** became the **first trio of teammates to win both an NCAA title and an NBA championship together**, according to NBA.com.  \n  Source: https://www.nba.com/news/nova-knicks-title-new-york\n\nIn newsroom terms, this was one of the year\u2019s cleanest \u201chistory returns\u201d stories: a flagship franchise, a half-century drought, and a star guard delivering the closeout.\n\n---\n\n## 4) The 98th Academy Awards\n\n### Date and host\n\nThe **98th Academy Awards** were held on **Sunday, 15 March 2026**, at the **Dolby Theatre at Ovation Hollywood** in Los Angeles. The ceremony was hosted by **Conan O\u2019Brien**.  \nSources: Oscars main page: https://www.oscars.org/oscars ; Academy press release: http://press.oscars.org/news/98th-oscarsr-production-team-announced\n\n### The film that won the night\n\nThe dominant Best Picture winner was **_One Battle After Another_**, which also won **Best Director** for **Paul Thomas Anderson** and several additional top-line awards. Both ABC\u2019s winners list and the Academy\u2019s 2026 ceremony page identify it as the night\u2019s top film.  \nSources: Academy ceremony page: https://www.oscars.org/oscars/ceremonies/2026 ; ABC News winners list: https://abcnews.com/GMA/Culture/oscars-2026-full-winners-list/story?id=130769299 ; ABC7 winners list: https://abc7.com/post/oscars-2026-winners-list-see-won-best-picture-director-actor-actress-more/18711211\n\n### Major-category winners\n\nAcross the main headline categories, the winners were:\n\n- **Best Picture:** **_One Battle After Another_**  \n- **Best Director:** **Paul Thomas Anderson**, **_One Battle After Another_**  \n- **Best Actor:** **Michael B. Jordan**, **_Sinners_**  \n- **Best Actress:** **Jessie Buckley**, **_Hamnet_**  \n- **Best Supporting Actor:** **Sean Penn**, **_One Battle After Another_**  \n- **Best Supporting Actress:** **Amy Madigan**, **_Weapons_**  \n\nSources:  \nAcademy ceremony page: https://www.oscars.org/oscars/ceremonies/2026  \nABC News full list: https://abcnews.com/GMA/Culture/oscars-2026-full-winners-list/story?id=130769299  \nABC7 full list: https://abc7.com/post/oscars-2026-winners-list-see-won-best-picture-director-actor-actress-more/18711211  \nRotten Tomatoes recap: https://editorial.rottentomatoes.com/article/oscars-2026-full-list-of-nominees-winners\n\n### Films that dominated\n\nTwo films clearly framed the night:\n\n- **_One Battle After Another_** emerged as the top overall winner, taking **Best Picture** and **Best Director**, among other awards.  \n  Sources: https://www.oscars.org/oscars/ceremonies/2026 ; https://abcnews.com/GMA/Culture/oscars-2026-full-winners-list/story?id=130769299\n\n- **_Sinners_** remained a major force. ABC and trade coverage say it entered with a record **16 nominations** and won **four Oscars**, including **Best Actor** for Michael B. Jordan and **Original Screenplay** for Ryan Coogler. NASA says the mission safely ended with splashdown in the **Pacific Ocean** on **10 April 2026 at 8:07 p.m. EDT** off the coast of California, completing an approximately **10-day** lunar flyby mission.  \nSources: Launch day blog: https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/04/01/live-artemis-ii-launch-day-updates ; splashdown live updates: https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/04/10/artemis-ii-flight-day-10-re-entry-live-updates ; Artemis II mission FAQ: https://www.nasa.gov/missions/nasa-answers-your-most-pressing-artemis-ii-questions\n\n### Crew\n\nThe crew was:\n- **Reid Wiseman** (NASA), commander  \n- **Victor Glover** (NASA), pilot  \n- **Christina Koch** (NASA), mission specialist  \n- **Jeremy Hansen** (Canadian Space Agency), mission specialist  \n\nNASA\u2019s official mission and crew pages list all four.  \nSources: https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-ii ; https://www.nasa.gov/feature/our-artemis-crew/\n\n### Records and milestones\n\nArtemis II delivered several firsts and records:\n\n- It was the **first crewed Artemis mission** and the **first human lunar flyby since Apollo 17 in 1972**.  \n  Sources: https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-ii ; https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-welcomes-record-setting-artemis-ii-moonfarers-back-to-earth\n\n- On **6 April 2026**, NASA says the crew **surpassed Apollo 13\u2019s record** for the **farthest human spaceflight from Earth**. NASA\u2019s flight-day updates give the mission\u2019s maximum distance as **252,756 miles from Earth**.  \n  Sources: NASA news release: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-artemis-ii-crew-eclipses-record-for-farthest-human-spaceflight ; flight-day-6 updates: https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/04/06/artemis-ii-flight-day-6-lunar-flyby-updates\n\n- NASA also emphasized the mission\u2019s public reach, saying agency-owned platforms drew **more than 149.4 million views** across launch, flyby, splashdown and continuous streams.  \n  Source: https://www.nasa.gov/general/nasas-artemis-ii-breaks-agency-streaming-record\n\n### Outcome\n\nThe outcome was unambiguously successful: NASA described the astronauts as returning safely after a **record-setting mission**, and agency updates said the flight validated spacecraft systems for future deep-space crewed missions, including later Artemis Moon landings.  \nSources: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-welcomes-record-setting-artemis-ii-moonfarers-back-to-earth ; https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-ii\n\nFor a newsroom, the clean takeaway is that Artemis II turned lunar exploration back into a live human story: first crew around the Moon in more than half a century, new distance record, safe return.\n\n---\n\n## Bottom line for editors\n\nIf you need one-line descriptors for the January\u2013July 2026 almanac:\n\n- **World Cup:** the first **48-team** men\u2019s World Cup, co-hosted by **Canada, Mexico and the U.S.**, has already delivered knockout volatility, including **Paraguay over Germany** and **Morocco over the Netherlands**, with the **round of 16 now underway**.  \n- **NFL:** the **Seahawks beat the Patriots 29-13** in **Super Bowl LX** at **Levi\u2019s Stadium**; \u201cthe easiest way to start building agents and applications powered by LLMs\u201d\n- built on top of LangGraph for \u201cdurable execution, streaming, human-in-the-loop, persistence, and more\u201d  \nSource: https://pypi.org/project/langchain/\n\n## 2.2 What changed in LangChain v1\n\nThe official \u201cWhat\u2019s new in LangChain v1\u201d page says v1 is centered on three changes:\n\n1. **`create_agent`** is the new standard\n2. **Standard content blocks**\n3. **Simplified package/namespace**, with legacy functionality moved to **`langchain-classic`**  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\n## 2.3 The modern agent-building API\n\nThe official recommendation is now explicit:\n\n- **Use `langchain.agents.create_agent`**\n- It replaces **`langgraph.prebuilt.create_react_agent`** as the standard entry point  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\nOfficial wording:\n> \u201c`create_agent` is the standard way to build agents in LangChain 1.0\u201d and provides a simpler interface than `langgraph.prebuilt.create_react_agent` while offering more customization through middleware.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\nThat is the major ecosystem shift: **the new abstraction is no longer \u201cpick a chain/prompt recipe\u201d; it is \u201cbuild an agent with middleware on a runtime.\u201d**\n\n## 2.4 What replaced the legacy patterns\n\n### Replaced\n- `langgraph.prebuilt.create_react_agent` as the default high-level entry point  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\n### Moved out of the core package\nLegacy functionality now lives in **`langchain-classic`**, including:\n- legacy chains and chain implementations\n- retrievers from the old module structure\n- indexing API\n- hub module\n- `langchain-community` exports\n- other deprecated functionality  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\nSo the 2026 message to engineering teams is simple:\n- **Use `langchain` for modern agent apps**\n- **Use `langchain-classic` only if you\u2019re carrying old code forward**  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\n## 2.5 Middleware is now the main extension model\n\nLangChain v1 makes **middleware** the defining extension point for agents. The official docs list built-in middleware such as:\n- `PIIMiddleware`\n- `SummarizationMiddleware`\n- `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware`  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\nThe docs also define middleware hook points:\n- `before_agent`\n- `before_model`\n- `wrap_model_call`\n- `wrap_tool_call`\n- `after_model`\n- `after_agent`  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\nThis is important strategically: LangChain has moved from \u201cchains as composition units\u201d to **middleware + agent loop as composition units**.\n\n## 2.6 Standard content blocks\n\nLangChain v1 introduced a unified `content_blocks` abstraction for:\n- reasoning traces\n- citations\n- tool calls\n- text\n- other provider-native structured content  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\nSupported integrations explicitly listed include:\n- `langchain-anthropic`\n- `langchain-aws`\n- `langchain-openai`\n- `langchain-google-genai`\n- `langchain-ollama`  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\nThe architectural value is high: this is LangChain\u2019s answer to provider fragmentation.\n\n## 2.7 The runtime layer: LangGraph\n\nLangChain\u2019s own docs and site make the layering explicit:\n\n- **LangChain** = high-level framework for building agents quickly\n- **LangGraph** = low-level orchestration framework and runtime for reliable agents  \nSources: https://pypi.org/project/langchain/ , https://www.langchain.com/langgraph\n\nThe official LangGraph site describes it as:\n- an **agent runtime**\n- a **low-level orchestration framework**\n- focused on reliability and low-level control  \nSource: https://www.langchain.com/langgraph\n\nLangChain\u2019s v1 page says that because `create_agent` is built on LangGraph, you automatically get:\n- **Persistence**\n- **Streaming**\n- **Human-in-the-loop**\n- **Time travel**  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1\n\nThis is the runtime story in one sentence:  \n**LangChain is now the ergonomic surface; LangGraph is the durable execution substrate.**\n\n## 2.8 CTO interpretation\n\nLangChain 1.x is no longer best understood as a \u201cbag of prompt/chains utilities.\u201d It is now:\n- a **high-level agent framework**\n- with **middleware-first customization**\n- on top of a **durable runtime** (LangGraph)\n\nFor greenfield work, this is the right mental model:\n- Start with **LangChain `create_agent`**\n- Drop to **LangGraph** when you need custom control flow, deterministic branches, deep state control, or runtime-level observability\n\n---\n\n# 3) deepagents: current version and core APIs\n\n## 3.1 Current version\n\nThe official PyPI page surfaced by search currently shows:\n- **`deepagents` version 1.0.2**  \nSource: https://pypi.org/project/deepagents\n\nThe official docs describe `deepagents` as a standalone library built on top of LangChain and using LangGraph as runtime.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n## 3.2 What deepagents is\n\nThe official overview defines Deep Agents as:\n- \u201cthe easiest way to start building agents and applications that are powered by LLMs\u201d\n- with built-in support for\n  - task planning\n  - file systems for context management\n  - subagent spawning\n  - long-term memory  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\nIt is explicitly called an **\u201cagent harness.\u201d**  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\nThat\u2019s an important distinction:\n- **LangChain** = framework primitives\n- **LangGraph** = runtime\n- **deepagents** = opinionated harness with batteries included\n\n## 3.3 Core construction API\n\nThe central API is:\n- **`create_deep_agent`**  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\nThe docs show examples using models like:\n- `openai:gpt-5.5`\n- `anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6`\n- `google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash`\n- other provider-prefixed model strings  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n## 3.4 Core capabilities / APIs to know\n\nThe official docs group Deep Agents into four major layers:\n\n### A. Execution environment\nIncludes:\n- tools\n- virtual filesystem\n- filesystem permissions\n- code execution  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n#### Filesystem tool surface\nBuilt-in filesystem operations listed:\n- `ls`\n- `read_file`\n- `write_file`\n- `edit_file`\n- `glob`\n- `grep`\n- `execute` (sandbox backends only)  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n#### Backends\nThe virtual filesystem can be backed by:\n- in-memory state\n- local disk\n- LangGraph store\n- composite routing\n- custom backend  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n#### Permissions\nThe docs describe declarative permission rules via `permissions=` with:\n- `operations`\n- `paths`\n- `mode`  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n### B. Context management\nIncludes:\n- skills\n- memory\n- summarization/context offloading\n- prompt caching  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n#### Memory\nMemory uses **`AGENTS.md`** files passed through the `memory` parameter.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n#### Skills\nSkills use the Agent Skills standard and live in directories containing **`SKILL.md`**.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n### C. Delegation\nTwo main built-in APIs:\n- `write_todos` for structured task tracking\n- `task` for ephemeral subagents  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n#### Planning API\n`write_todos` persists task state with statuses:\n- `pending`\n- `in_progress`\n- `completed`  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n#### Subagents API\nThe `task` tool creates subagents with:\n- fresh context\n- autonomous execution\n- single final handoff\n- default `general-purpose` strategy or custom subagents  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n### D. Steering / human-in-the-loop\nHuman control is provided through LangGraph interrupts and enabled using:\n- **`interrupt_on`** in `create_deep_agent`  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\nThe docs give `interrupt_on={\"edit_file\": True}` as an example.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n## 3.5 Runtime layer and observability\n\nThe overview states directly:\n- `deepagents` is built on **LangChain**\n- uses the **LangGraph runtime** for\n  - durable execution\n  - streaming\n  - human-in-the-loop\n  - other runtime features  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\nThe docs also recommend **LangSmith** for tracing, debugging, and production deployment workflows.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n## 3.6 CTO interpretation\n\ndeepagents is the strongest fit when you want:\n- long-running, multi-step, file-aware agents\n- a built-in planner/subagent model\n- controllable approvals\n- less custom orchestration code than raw LangGraph\n\nIt is not the lowest-level system; it is the **opinionated productivity layer** for complex task agents.\n\n---\n\n# 4) Next.js: current major version, runtime requirements, breaking changes, build tooling\n\n## 4.1 Current major version\n\nThe official upgrade docs currently show:\n- **Latest Version: 16.2.10** on the general upgrading page  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/upgrading\n\nThe official v16 upgrade guide snapshot surfaced by search shows:\n- **Latest Version: 16.2.9**  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\nThe discrepancy is minor and likely reflects page update timing. The important point is clear: **Next.js 16 is the current major line.**\n\n## 4.2 Runtime and platform requirements\n\nThe official Next.js 16 release notes list:\n- **Node.js 20.9+**\n- **TypeScript 5.1+**\n- supported browsers: **Chrome 111+, Edge 111+, Firefox 111+, Safari 16.4+**  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\nThis is not a soft recommendation; it is a version-floor change.\n\n## 4.3 The big architectural changes in v16\n\n### A. Turbopack is now the default bundler\nOfficial wording:\n- Turbopack is now the **default bundler**\n- stable for both development and production builds  \nSources: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16 , https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack\n\nThe docs describe Turbopack as:\n- an **incremental bundler**\n- written in **Rust**\n- built into Next.js  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack\n\nIf you need webpack instead:\n- `next dev --webpack`\n- `next build --webpack`  \nSources: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16 , https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack\n\n### B. Cache Components replace implicit App Router caching\nNext.js 16 introduces:\n- `cacheComponents: true`\n- `use cache`\n- `cacheLife`\n- `cacheTag`  \nSources: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16 , https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents\n\nThe official cacheComponents docs say:\n- data fetching is **dynamic by default**\n- you explicitly choose what to cache at the page/component/function level\n- PPR behavior is effectively unified under Cache Components  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents\n\nThis is a major design change: **implicit caching assumptions are gone.**\n\n### C. `proxy.ts` replaces `middleware.ts`\nOfficial release notes:\n- `proxy.ts` replaces `middleware.ts`\n- `proxy.ts` runs on the **Node.js runtime**\n- `middleware.ts` is still available for Edge cases but is deprecated  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\nThis is both a naming and runtime-boundary clarification.\n\n## 4.4 Key breaking changes\n\nFrom the official Next.js 16 release notes and upgrade guide:\n\n### Version requirements\n- Node 18 is no longer supported\n- Node 20.9+ minimum\n- TS 5.1+ minimum  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### Removed / renamed config and features\n- `experimental.dynamicIO` \u2192 **`cacheComponents`**\n- `experimental.ppr` removed\n- `experimental.turbopack` moved to top-level **`turbopack`**\n- `next lint` command removed; linting no longer runs as part of `next build`\n- `serverRuntimeConfig` / `publicRuntimeConfig` removed in favor of env vars\n- AMP support removed  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### Async request APIs\nBreaking changes include async access requirements for:\n- `params`\n- `searchParams`\n- `cookies()`\n- `headers()`\n- `draftMode()`  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### Image behavior changes\nNotable defaults/constraints changed for:\n- `images.minimumCacheTTL`\n- `images.imageSizes`\n- `images.qualities`\n- `images.maximumRedirects`\n- `images.localPatterns` requirement for local src with query strings  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### Parallel route requirement\n- All parallel route slots now require explicit `default.js`, or builds fail  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n## 4.5 Build tooling status\n\n### Turbopack support and constraints\nOfficial docs note:\n- Turbopack is the default\n- Babel is automatically used if a Babel config file is detected in Next.js 16\n- webpack plugins are **not supported** by Turbopack\n- webpack loaders are supported/configurable\n- some Sass features such as `sassOptions.functions` are not supported in Turbopack  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack\n\n### Platform support for Turbopack native bindings\nSupported native bindings:\n- macOS x64 / ARM64\n- Windows x64 / ARM64\n- Linux glibc x64 / ARM64\n- Linux musl x64 / ARM64  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack\n\nOn unsupported platforms, the docs say Next.js falls back to WASM bindings, which **do not support Turbopack**, so you should use webpack instead.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack\n\n### Build adapters API\nNext.js 16 release notes describe a **Build Adapters API (alpha)** for custom deployment integrations.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### create-next-app defaults\nThe official release notes say `create-next-app` now defaults to:\n- App Router\n- TypeScript-first config\n- Tailwind CSS\n- ESLint  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n## 4.6 CTO interpretation\n\nFor engineering orgs, Next.js 16 means:\n\n- **Assume Turbopack first**\n- **Audit custom webpack usage before upgrading**\n- **Treat caching as explicit application design**, not framework magic\n- **Plan a runtime policy** around Node-only `proxy.ts` vs remaining Edge usage\n- **Budget for upgrade work** if you depend on old middleware semantics, old lint/build assumptions, or implicit App Router caching\n\n---\n\n# Strategic conclusions\n\n## What has converged\n\nAcross OpenAI, LangChain/deepagents, and Next.js, the same macro-pattern appears:\n\n1. **Explicit runtime layers**\n   - OpenAI: model/tool/platform pricing is explicit\n   - LangChain: LangGraph is explicit runtime\n   - Next.js: Turbopack/runtime/caching boundaries are explicit\n\n2. **Middleware / orchestration over ad hoc glue**\n   - LangChain middleware\n   - deepagents harness + permissions + interrupts\n   - Next.js `proxy.ts` and cache APIs\n\n3. **Long-running, tool-using systems are the default target**\n   - OpenAI tool billing and reasoning modes\n   - deepagents subagents/filesystem/planning\n   - LangGraph persistence/streaming/human-in-the-loop\n\n4. **Framework \u201cmagic\u201d is being reduced**\n   - Next.js moved away from implicit caching\n   - LangChain moved away from sprawling legacy namespaces/chains\n   - OpenAI pricing makes tradeoffs visible enough that routing is architectural\n\n## What a practical 2026 stack looks like\n\nFor most CTOs, a pragmatic mid-2026 default stack would be:\n\n- **Model platform:** OpenAI GPT-5.x, routed by workload\n  - `gpt-5.5` for premium workflows\n  - `gpt-5.4-mini` for high-volume tool-heavy work\n  - specialized models for codex/research/realtime as needed  \n  Source: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing\n\n- **Agent framework:** LangChain 1.x with `create_agent`\n  - middleware for policy, summarization, approvals\n  - LangGraph when workflow control gets complex  \n  Sources: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langchain-v1 , https://www.langchain.com/langgraph\n\n- **Long-task harness:** deepagents when you need task planning, subagents, filesystem workflows, and HITL out of the box  \n  Source: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n- **Web platform:** Next.js 16 with Turbopack-first assumptions and explicit Cache Components strategy  \n  Sources: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16 , https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack , https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents\n\n## Main risks to watch\n\n- **OpenAI cost sprawl** from tool calls, search, containers, and long-context output\n- **LangChain migration drift** if teams keep mixing `langchain-classic` and v1 patterns\n- **deepagents overuse** where a simple `create_agent` or custom LangGraph workflow would be cheaper/smaller\n- **Next.js 16 surprises** if your app depends on webpack plugins, implicit caching, or old middleware assumptions\n\n---\n\n# Source list\n\n## OpenAI\n- Pricing: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing\n- Models overview: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models\n- Reasoning Internally, Veltrix appears more concentrated around a single AMR family plus fleet software. Based on internal company materials surfaced through research, Veltrix has raised **$142.0 million** across Seed through Series C, most recently an **$85 million Series C in October 2025** at a **$610 million post-money valuation**. These figures indicate reduced near-term financing risk, but they are not independently audited in the available evidence.
