The package is documented in LangChain\u2019s Deep Agents docs and API reference, and is positioned as an opinionated agent harness built on LangGraph with built-in planning, filesystem tools, subagents, and human-in-the-loop support.  \nSources: PyPI https://pypi.org/project/deepagents/ ; package stats mirror https://pypistats.org/packages/deepagents ; overview docs https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\nFor your engineering team, the key implementation recommendation is:\n\n- use **`create_deep_agent(...)`** as the primary construction API;\n- use a **`CompositeBackend`** for production-friendly filesystem routing;\n- define at least one explicit **research subagent** in `subagents=`;\n- enable **human approval** via `interrupt_on=` and a **checkpointer**;\n- treat `deepagents` as the orchestration harness, with LangGraph persistence and LangChain models/tools beneath it.\n\nSources: API reference https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent ; overview https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview ; backends https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends ; human-in-the-loop https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop ; subagents https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents\n\n---\n\n## 1. Version and dependency baseline\n\n### Current package version\n\n- **Package:** `deepagents`\n- **Latest version:** **0.6.12**\n- **Release date on PyPI:** **2026-06-25**\n- **Python versions shown on PyPI:** **3.11** and **3.12**\n\nSource: https://pypi.org/project/deepagents/\n\n### Important version-sensitive notes\n\nSeveral documented behaviors are version-gated:\n\n- `model=None` in `create_deep_agent(...)` is **deprecated since 0.5.3** and will be removed in `deepagents==1.0.0`; engineering should always pass an explicit model.  \n  Source: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\n- `StoreBackend` namespace factories receive a LangGraph **`Runtime`** in **`deepagents>=0.5.2`**; earlier `0.5.x` used `BackendContext`.  \n  Source: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n- Filesystem permission interrupts require **`deepagents>=0.6.8`**.  \n  Source: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n- Conditional HITL interrupts require **`langchain>=1.3.3`**.  \n  Source: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n### Recommended install baseline\n\nAt minimum:\n\n```bash\npip install -U deepagents\n```\n\nThen add a model provider package, for example:\n\n```bash\npip install -U deepagents langchain-openai\n```\n\nor\n\n```bash\npip install -U deepagents langchain-anthropic\n```\n\nThe official docs show provider-specific installs such as `langchain-google-genai`, `langchain-openai`, `langchain-anthropic`, `langchain-openrouter`, `langchain-fireworks`, `langchain-baseten`, and `langchain-ollama`.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n---\n\n## 2. What Deep Agents gives you for a research assistant\n\nDeep Agents is meant for agents that need:\n\n- planning over multi-step work,\n- access to a virtual filesystem,\n- context offloading/summarization,\n- delegation to subagents,\n- runtime human approval.\n\nThe overview states that Deep Agents provides built-in capabilities for:\n\n- task planning,\n- file systems for context management,\n- subagent spawning,\n- long-term memory,\n- human approval,\n- context offloading and summarization.\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\nFor a research assistant, that maps well to this workflow:\n\n1. break a research task into subtasks,\n2. fetch/read/store intermediate findings in files,\n3. delegate deep dives to isolated subagents,\n4. summarize and synthesize final output,\n5. pause for approval before sensitive operations.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Core API: `create_deep_agent(...)`\n\nThe primary constructor is:\n\n**`deepagents.create_deep_agent(...)`**  \nReference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\n### Signature elements that matter most\n\nThe reference documents these parameters:\n\n- `model`\n- `tools`\n- `system_prompt`\n- `middleware`\n- `subagents`\n- `skills`\n- `memory`\n- `permissions`\n- `backend`\n- `interrupt_on`\n- `response_format`\n- `state_schema`\n- `context_schema`\n- `checkpointer`\n- `store`\n- `debug`\n- `name`\n- `cache`\n\nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\n### Return type\n\n`create_deep_agent(...)` returns a **`CompiledStateGraph`**.  \nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\n### Built-in tools automatically included\n\nBy default, the created agent has access to:\n\n- `write_todos`\n- `ls`\n- `read_file`\n- `write_file`\n- `edit_file`\n- `glob`\n- `grep`\n- `execute`\n- `task`\n\nThe docs note that `execute` only works if the backend implements `SandboxBackendProtocol`; otherwise it returns an error.  \nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\n### Minimal example\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\n\ndef web_search(query: str) -> str:\n    \"\"\"Search the web and return concise findings.\"\"\"\n    ...\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"openai:gpt-5.5\",\n    tools=[web_search],\n    system_prompt=\"You are a research assistant. Be precise, source-driven, and explicit about uncertainty.\",\n)\n```\n\nThis pattern is consistent with the official quickstart examples.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n### Invocation pattern\n\nThe docs show calling:\n\n```python\nagent.invoke({\n    \"messages\": [{\"role\": \"user\", \"content\": \"what is the weather in sf\"}]\n})\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\nFor a research assistant, the same input shape applies.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Recommended architecture for your research assistant\n\n### Proposed system role\n\nUse Deep Agents as the orchestration layer for a research workflow with:\n\n- one **supervisor agent** built with `create_deep_agent(...)`,\n- one or more **specialized synchronous subagents** via `subagents=`,\n- a **filesystem backend** for notes, evidence, and drafts,\n- HITL on destructive or externally visible operations.\n\n### Recommended top-level configuration\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\nfrom deepagents.backends import CompositeBackend, StateBackend, FilesystemBackend\n\nbackend = CompositeBackend(\n    default=StateBackend(),\n    routes={\n        \"/workspace/\": FilesystemBackend(\n            root_dir=\"/abs/path/to/research_workspace\",\n            virtual_mode=True,\n        ),\n    },\n)\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"openai:gpt-5.5\",\n    backend=backend,\n    tools=[search_web, fetch_page],\n    system_prompt=(\n        \"You are a research assistant. \"\n        \"Ground claims in sources, keep an evidence trail, and separate findings from conclusions.\"\n    ),\n)\n```\n\nWhy this design:\n\n- `StateBackend()` keeps internal artifacts like `/large_tool_results/` and `/conversation_history/` ephemeral.\n- `FilesystemBackend(...)` gives durable project workspace storage under `/workspace/`.\n- `CompositeBackend(...)` avoids mixing internal harness files with project files on disk.\n\nThese behaviors are explicitly recommended in the backends docs.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n---\n\n## 5. Filesystem backends: what to use and why\n\nDeep Agents exposes filesystem tools through a pluggable backend layer. The official built-in backends documented are:\n\n- `StateBackend`\n- `FilesystemBackend`\n- `StoreBackend`\n- `ContextHubBackend`\n- `LocalShellBackend`\n- `CompositeBackend`\n- sandbox backends\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n## 5.1 `StateBackend`\n\n### What it is\nThread-scoped storage in LangGraph state.\n\n### How to use\nIf you do not specify `backend=`, `create_deep_agent(...)` defaults to `StateBackend()`.\n\n```python\nagent = create_deep_agent(model=\"openai:gpt-5.5\")\n```\n\nEquivalent explicit form:\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents.backends import StateBackend\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"openai:gpt-5.5\",\n    backend=StateBackend(),\n)\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n### Best for\n- scratch work,\n- per-thread notes,\n- temporary offloaded outputs.\n\n### Important behavior\nFiles persist across turns within the same thread via checkpoints, but are **not shared across threads**. The docs also note this backend is shared between supervisor and subagents.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n## 5.2 `FilesystemBackend`\n\n### What it is\nDirect read/write access to a real filesystem rooted at `root_dir`.\n\n### Example\n```python\nfrom deepagents.backends import FilesystemBackend\n\nbackend = FilesystemBackend(root_dir=\".\", virtual_mode=True)\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n### Important parameters\n- `root_dir`\n- `virtual_mode`\n\nThe docs explicitly recommend **`virtual_mode=True`** because `root_dir` alone is not sufficient security; with `virtual_mode=False`, the docs say there is **no security** even if `root_dir` is set.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n### Best for\n- local development,\n- controlled CI sandboxes,\n- project workspaces.\n\n### Recommendation\nUse it **inside `CompositeBackend`**, not alone, so internal agent artifacts do not pollute the working directory.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n## 5.3 `StoreBackend`\n\n### What it is\nCross-thread durable storage backed by LangGraph `BaseStore`.\n\n### Example\n```python\nfrom deepagents.backends import StoreBackend\nfrom langgraph.store.memory import InMemoryStore\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"openai:gpt-5.5\",\n    backend=StoreBackend(\n        namespace=lambda rt: (rt.server_info.user.identity,),\n    ),\n    store=InMemoryStore(),\n)\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n### Important parameters\n- `namespace`\n- runtime-provided `store` passed to `create_deep_agent(..., store=...)`\n\n### Best for\n- persistent user memory,\n- reusable research archives across threads,\n- multi-session assistant state.\n\n### Engineering caution\nFor multi-user systems, the docs say to **always set a namespace factory** for isolation.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n## 5.4 `ContextHubBackend`\n\n### What it is\nDurable storage in a LangSmith Context Hub repo.\n\n### Example\n```python\nfrom deepagents.backends import ContextHubBackend\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"openai:gpt-5.5\",\n    backend=ContextHubBackend(\"my-agent\"),\n)\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n### Best for\n- LangSmith-native persistence,\n- versioned context and reusable skills,\n- teams already standardizing on LangSmith Hub.\n\n### Notes\n- Requires `LANGSMITH_API_KEY`.\n- Accepts a repo identifier in `owner/name` or `name` format.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n## 5.5 `LocalShellBackend`\n\n### What it is\nA filesystem backend plus unrestricted local shell execution.\n\n### Example\n```python\nfrom deepagents.backends import LocalShellBackend\n\nbackend = LocalShellBackend(\n    root_dir=\".\",\n    virtual_mode=True,\n    env={\"PATH\": \"/usr/bin:/bin\"},\n)\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n### Important documented execution options\nThe docs state support for:\n- `timeout` (default 120s)\n- `max_output_bytes` (default 100,000)\n- `env`\n- `inherit_env`\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n### Recommendation\nDo **not** use this for a general research assistant in production. The docs are very explicit that it grants arbitrary shell execution on the host and is appropriate only for controlled development environments.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n## 5.6 `CompositeBackend`\n\n### What it is\nPath-prefix router across multiple backends.\n\n### Example\n```python\nfrom deepagents.backends import CompositeBackend, StateBackend, StoreBackend\nfrom langgraph.store.memory import InMemoryStore\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"openai:gpt-5.5\",\n    backend=CompositeBackend(\n        default=StateBackend(),\n        routes={\n            \"/memories/\": StoreBackend(namespace=lambda _rt: (\"memories\",)),\n        },\n    ),\n    store=InMemoryStore(),\n)\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n### Best for\n- separating ephemeral workspace from durable memory,\n- isolating internal system files from user files,\n- mounting multiple knowledge sources into one virtual FS.\n\n### Recommendation for your team\nUse `CompositeBackend` as the default production pattern.\n\n---\n\n## 6. How to define subagents\n\nSubagents are central to a research assistant because they isolate context-heavy tasks like source discovery, document review, and synthesis.\n\nOfficial subagent docs: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents  \nReference types: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/SubAgent and https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/CompiledSubAgent\n\n## 6.1 What `subagents=` accepts\n\nThe `create_deep_agent(...)` reference says `subagents` can contain:\n\n- `SubAgent`\n- `CompiledSubAgent`\n- `AsyncSubAgent`\n\nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\nFor the scope you asked about, the key patterns are `SubAgent` and `CompiledSubAgent`.\n\n## 6.2 Default general-purpose subagent\n\nDeep Agents automatically adds a synchronous **`general-purpose`** subagent unless you provide one with that name or disable it in the harness profile.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents ; https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\nThis means the built-in `task` tool is available by default as long as at least one synchronous subagent exists.\n\n## 6.3 Dictionary-based `SubAgent`\n\nThe docs define a dictionary-based spec with these fields:\n\n- `name` \u2014 required\n- `description` \u2014 required\n- `system_prompt` \u2014 required\n- `tools` \u2014 optional\n- `model` \u2014 optional\n- `middleware` \u2014 optional\n- `interrupt_on` \u2014 optional\n- `skills` \u2014 optional\n- `permissions` \u2014 optional\n- `response_format` \u2014 optional\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents ; summarized in the `create_deep_agent` reference https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\n### Example: research subagent\n\n```python\nsubagents = [\n    {\n        \"name\": \"source-researcher\",\n        \"description\": \"Finds high-quality primary and secondary sources for a research question.\",\n        \"system_prompt\": (\n            \"You are a focused research subagent. \"\n            \"Search broadly, prefer primary sources, extract key claims, and return a concise evidence report with URLs.\"\n        ),\n        \"tools\": [search_web, fetch_page],\n        \"model\": \"openai:gpt-5.5\",\n    },\n    {\n        \"name\": \"evidence-synthesizer\",\n        \"description\": \"Synthesizes findings from notes and source documents into a structured brief.\",\n        \"system_prompt\": (\n            \"You synthesize notes into a structured report. \"\n            \"Separate factual findings, uncertainty, and recommendations.\"\n        ),\n    },\n]\n```\n\n## 6.4 `CompiledSubAgent`\n\nUse `CompiledSubAgent` when you already have a prebuilt runnable/graph.\n\nThe reference notes:\n\n- `CompiledSubAgent` wraps a precompiled runnable,\n- the runnable\u2019s state schema must include a `messages` key,\n- it does **not** inherit `create_deep_agent(state_schema=...)`.\n\nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/CompiledSubAgent\n\n### Why use it\nUse it when a sub-workflow is custom enough that you want a bespoke LangChain/LangGraph agent rather than the declarative subagent form.\n\n## 6.5 Inheritance and override behavior\n\nThe `create_deep_agent` reference states:\n\n- declarative `SubAgent` specs inherit top-level `interrupt_on` by default;\n- if a declarative subagent has its own `interrupt_on`, it overrides the inherited config;\n- `CompiledSubAgent` does **not** inherit top-level `interrupt_on`;\n- `CompiledSubAgent` also does not automatically inherit custom `state_schema`;\n- subagents inherit parent filesystem `permissions` unless they specify their own.\n\nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\n## 6.6 Practical subagent design for research\n\nRecommended synchronous subagents:\n\n1. **`source-researcher`**  \n   web/source discovery, fast iteration, broad search.\n\n2. **`document-reader`**  \n   reads local documents or fetched text, extracts claims and evidence.\n\n3. **`fact-checker`**  \n   verifies unsupported claims against stored notes and URLs.\n\n4. **`brief-writer`**  \n   converts evidence files into a final memo or answer draft.\n\nThis decomposition aligns with the docs\u2019 reason for subagents: context quarantine and specialization.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents\n\n---\n\n## 7. Human-in-the-loop support\n\nOfficial docs: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\nDeep Agents supports HITL via LangGraph interrupts, configured through `interrupt_on=` in `create_deep_agent(...)`.\n\n## 7.1 Core API\n\n`interrupt_on` is a mapping of tool names to configurations. Each value can be:\n\n- `True`\n- `False`\n- `InterruptOnConfig`\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n### Documented semantics\n\n- `True` = enable interrupts with default allowed decisions\n- `False` = disable interrupts\n- `InterruptOnConfig` = custom config with `allowed_decisions`, and in Python optionally `when`\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n## 7.2 Checkpointer requirement\n\nThe docs explicitly say a **checkpointer is required** for HITL. Example shown:\n\n```python\nfrom langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver\n\ncheckpointer = MemorySaver()\n```\n\nand then:\n\n```python\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    ...,\n    interrupt_on={...},\n    checkpointer=checkpointer,\n)\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n## 7.3 Allowed decision types\n\nThe docs list these supported decision types:\n\n- `approve`\n- `edit`\n- `reject`\n- `respond`\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n## 7.4 Basic configuration example\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\nfrom langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"openai:gpt-5.5\",\n    tools=[send_email, export_report],\n    interrupt_on={\n        \"send_email\": True,\n        \"export_report\": {\"allowed_decisions\": [\"approve\", \"reject\"]},\n    },\n    checkpointer=MemorySaver(),\n)\n```\n\nThis mirrors the official configuration pattern.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n## 7.5 Conditional interrupts with `when`\n\nPython supports conditional interrupts using a `when` predicate on `InterruptOnConfig`. The docs show a predicate that receives `ToolCallRequest`.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\nExample pattern from docs:\n\n```python\nfrom langchain.agents.middleware import ToolCallRequest\n\ndef writes_outside_workspace(request: ToolCallRequest) -> bool:\n    path = request.tool_call[\"args\"].get(\"file_path\", \"\")\n    return not path.startswith(\"/workspace/\")\n```\n\nThis is useful for your research assistant if you want to pause only when:\n- writing outside approved directories,\n- emailing or publishing outputs,\n- updating durable memory.\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n## 7.6 Resuming after interrupt\n\nThe docs show resuming with:\n\n```python\nfrom langgraph.types import Command\n\nresult = agent.invoke(\n    Command(resume={\"decisions\": decisions}),\n    config=config,\n    version=\"v2\",\n)\n```\n\nwith the same `thread_id` config used before interruption.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n## 7.7 Filesystem permission interrupts\n\nAn additional mechanism is to mark a `FilesystemPermission` rule with `mode=\"interrupt\"`. The docs say this requires `deepagents>=0.6.8`.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\nExample pattern:\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import FilesystemPermission, create_deep_agent\nfrom langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"openai:gpt-5.5\",\n    permissions=[\n        FilesystemPermission(\n            operations=[\"write\"],\n            paths=[\"/secrets/**\"],\n            mode=\"interrupt\",\n        )\n    ],\n    checkpointer=MemorySaver(),\n)\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n### Recommendation for your team\nEnable HITL for:\n- outward-facing actions,\n- writes to protected paths,\n- memory updates that persist across users or threads,\n- any external notifications or publication tool.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Recommended engineering blueprint\n\n## 8.1 Target behavior\n\nThe assistant should:\n\n- decompose research requests,\n- gather evidence through custom search/fetch tools,\n- store intermediate notes in `/workspace/`,\n- delegate deep dives to subagents,\n- synthesize results into a final structured response,\n- pause for approval before publication or sensitive writes.\n\n## 8.2 Suggested filesystem layout\n\nUsing `CompositeBackend`, expose:\n\n- `/workspace/` \u2192 `FilesystemBackend(root_dir=..., virtual_mode=True)`\n- `/memories/` \u2192 `StoreBackend(namespace=...)` if persistent research memory is desired\n- default \u2192 `StateBackend()`\n\nThis matches the documented routing model.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n## 8.3 Suggested main-agent construction\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent, FilesystemPermission\nfrom deepagents.backends import CompositeBackend, StateBackend, FilesystemBackend, StoreBackend\nfrom langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver\nfrom langgraph.store.memory import InMemoryStore\n\nbackend = CompositeBackend(\n    default=StateBackend(),\n    routes={\n        \"/workspace/\": FilesystemBackend(\n            root_dir=\"/abs/path/to/research_workspace\",\n            virtual_mode=True,\n        ),\n        \"/memories/\": StoreBackend(\n            namespace=lambda rt: (rt.server_info.user.identity, \"research-memory\"),\n        ),\n    },\n)\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"openai:gpt-5.5\",\n    backend=backend,\n    store=InMemoryStore(),\n    checkpointer=MemorySaver(),\n    tools=[search_web, fetch_page, export_report],\n    subagents=[\n        {\n            \"name\": \"source-researcher\",\n            \"description\": \"Finds and summarizes relevant sources with URLs.\",\n            \"system_prompt\": \"Search broadly, prefer primary sources, and return concise evidence with citations.\",\n            \"tools\": [search_web, fetch_page],\n        },\n        {\n            \"name\": \"brief-writer\",\n            \"description\": \"Writes structured research briefs from notes and sources.\",\n            \"system_prompt\": \"Produce structured, source-grounded briefs and state uncertainty clearly.\",\n        },\n    ],\n    permissions=[\n        FilesystemPermission(\n            operations=[\"write\"],\n            paths=[\"/workspace/**\"],\n            mode=\"allow\",\n        ),\n        FilesystemPermission(\n            operations=[\"write\"],\n            paths=[\"/memories/**\"],\n            mode=\"interrupt\",\n        ),\n    ],\n    interrupt_on={\n        \"export_report\": {\"allowed_decisions\": [\"approve\", \"reject\"]},\n    },\n    system_prompt=(\n        \"You are a research assistant. \"\n        \"Ground every factual claim in sources, preserve URLs, and separate evidence from inference.\"\n    ),\n)\n```\n\nThis is composed entirely from documented APIs and patterns.  \nSources:  \n- `create_deep_agent`: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent  \n- backends: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends  \n- HITL: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop  \n- subagents: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents\n\n---\n\n## 9. Risks and cautions\n\n### 1. Do not rely on implicit defaults\n`model=None` is deprecated. Always provide `model=` explicitly.  \nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\n### 2. Do not use bare `FilesystemBackend` in production APIs\nThe docs recommend `StateBackend`, `StoreBackend`, or sandbox backends instead for safer environments.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n### 3. Do not use `LocalShellBackend` for untrusted workloads\nIt provides arbitrary host shell execution.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n### 4. HITL requires persistence\nIf you enable `interrupt_on`, you need a checkpointer and stable thread IDs on resume.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n### 5. Persistent storage needs explicit namespacing\n`StoreBackend` without proper namespace isolation can leak shared memory across users.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n---\n\n## 10. Implementation checklist\n\n1. Pin `deepagents==0.6.12` initially for predictable rollout.  \n   Source: https://pypi.org/project/deepagents/\n\n2. Choose and pin a supported model provider package.\n\n3. Build the main agent with `create_deep_agent(...)`.\n\n4. Use `CompositeBackend(default=StateBackend(), routes=...)`.\n\n5.         "report": "# Design brief: building a research assistant with `deepagents` (Python)\n\n## 1) Executive summary\n\nThis brief recommends building the research assistant on LangChain\u2019s `deepagents` Python library using its `create_deep_agent` entry point, built-in filesystem tools, subagent delegation via `task`, and human-in-the-loop controls for sensitive actions. As of now, the current PyPI release is **`deepagents 0.6.12`**. The library is positioned as an \u201cagent harness\u201d with built-in planning, filesystem/context management, subagent spawning, and long-term-memory patterns, rather than a bare agent loop.  \nSources:  \n- PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/deepagents  \n- Overview: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview  \n- Python reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents\n\n---\n\n## 2) Recommended target stack\n\n### Package versions\nFor reproducibility, pin at least the main package version explicitly:\n\n```txt\ndeepagents==0.6.12\n```\n\nYou will also need a model provider package depending on the model you choose; the docs show examples with packages such as `langchain-google-genai` and `langchain-anthropic`. The Deep Agents docs do **not** prescribe a single exact companion version on the pages I found, so pin those based on your provider compatibility testing rather than inventing versions.  \nSources:  \n- PyPI current version: https://pypi.org/project/deepagents  \n- Quickstart/overview examples: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview  \n- Quickstart: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/quickstart\n\n### Recommended initial model strategy\nDeep Agents works with any LangChain chat model that supports tool calling. Models can be passed either as:\n- a model string in `provider:model` format, or\n- a preconfigured chat model instance from `init_chat_model(...)`.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/models\n\nExample from docs:\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(model=\"anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6\")\n```\n\nOr with model-specific parameters:\n\n```python\nfrom langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\n\nmodel = init_chat_model(\n    model=\"google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash\",\n    thinking_level=\"medium\",\n)\nagent = create_deep_agent(model=model)\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/models\n\n---\n\n## 3) Core API: creating the agent\n\n## Primary constructor\nThe main API is:\n\n- **`create_deep_agent(...)`**\n\nIt is the official entry point for constructing a fully configured deep agent with planning, filesystem, subagent, and summarization middleware.  \nSources:  \n- Reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent  \n- Graph overview: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph\n\n## Parameters engineering should care about\nFrom the official docs/reference, the most important parameters for this project are:\n\n- **`model`** \u2014 model string or chat model instance  \n- **`tools`** \u2014 custom tools merged with built-in tools  \n- **`system_prompt`** \u2014 top-level instructions  \n- **`subagents`** \u2014 declarative or compiled subagents  \n- **`memory`** \u2014 memory file paths to load  \n- **`skills`** \u2014 skill directories/files  \n- **`backend`** \u2014 filesystem backend  \n- **`interrupt_on`** \u2014 per-tool human approval rules  \n- **`checkpointer`** \u2014 required for HITL flows  \n- **`middleware`** \u2014 advanced customization hook  \n\nSources:  \n- Reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent  \n- Customization: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/customization\n\n## Minimal baseline example\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\n\ndef search_web(query: str) -> str:\n    \"\"\"Search the web and return results.\"\"\"\n    return \"...\"\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6\",\n    tools=[search_web],\n    system_prompt=\"You are a careful research assistant. Cite sources and verify claims.\",\n)\n```\n\nPattern grounded in official examples:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/customization\n\n## Built-in capabilities\nThe reference indicates Deep Agents includes built-in tooling such as:\n- `write_todos`\n- filesystem tools\n- `task` for subagent delegation\n- other harness middleware such as summarization/context management\n\nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\n### Design implication\nFor a research assistant, this means the main engineering work is not \u201cbuild an agent loop,\u201d but:\n1. define high-value research tools,\n2. choose the right backend,\n3. author subagents,\n4. add approval gates for risky actions,\n5. shape prompts and memory.\n\n---\n\n## 4) Filesystem backends\n\nDeep Agents exposes a filesystem surface through tools like:\n- `ls`\n- `read_file`\n- `write_file`\n- `edit_file`\n- `glob`\n- `grep`\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\nThis is central to the research-assistant design, because Deep Agents uses files as context-management infrastructure: large outputs can be externalized and revisited later instead of kept in the active model context.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/context-engineering\n\n## Supported/prebuilt backend options\n\n### A. Default thread-scoped backend\nIf you call `create_deep_agent(...)` without `backend=...`, the default backend is thread-scoped and stored in LangGraph state.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\nExample:\n\n```python\nagent = create_deep_agent(model=\"google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash\")\n```\n\n### B. `FilesystemBackend`\nUse for direct access to a host filesystem directory.\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\nfrom deepagents.backends import FilesystemBackend\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash\",\n    backend=FilesystemBackend(root_dir=\"/path/to/workspace\"),\n)\n```\n\nDocs say `FilesystemBackend` reads/writes files directly from the filesystem and that this backend grants direct filesystem access; the reference notes it is generally expected to be used with HITL.  \nSources:  \n- Backends guide: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends  \n- Reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/backends/filesystem/FilesystemBackend  \n- Module reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/backends/filesystem\n\nImportant documented details:\n- parameter: **`root_dir`**\n- default root is current working directory if omitted\n- path traversal is blocked\n- reference mentions `virtual_mode` behavior as well\n\nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/backends/filesystem/FilesystemBackend\n\n### C. `StoreBackend`\nUse for durable storage via LangGraph store, persisted across threads.\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\nfrom deepagents.backends import StoreBackend\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash\",\n    backend=StoreBackend(),\n)\n```\n\nDocs explicitly say this backend is persisted across threads.  \nSources:  \n- Backends guide: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends  \n- Reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/backends/store/StoreBackend\n\n### D. `ContextHubBackend`\nThe docs list a Context Hub backend that stores files durably in a LangSmith Hub repo, without provisioning a separate LangGraph store.\n\n```python\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash\",\n    backend=ContextHubBackend(\"my-agent\"),\n)\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\nI found this in the official docs page, but not a separate reference page through search results, so engineering should verify import path from the installed package before implementation.\n\n### E. `LocalShellBackend`\nThe docs list a local shell backend with filesystem and host shell execution.\n\n```python\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash\",\n    backend=LocalShellBackend(\n        root_dir=\".\",\n        env={\"PATH\": \"/usr/bin:/bin\"},\n    ),\n)\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\nAs with `ContextHubBackend`, I found the documented class usage in the official docs page, but not a clean separate reference page via search. Verify import path in the installed version before shipping.\n\n## Recommended backend choice for this project\n\n### Recommended for phase 1\n- **Main choice:** `StoreBackend()` for durable research artifacts across threads/users/sessions.\n- **Alternative for local prototyping:** `FilesystemBackend(root_dir=...)`\n- **Avoid in production initially:** `LocalShellBackend` unless you have a strong sandboxing model.\n\n### Why\nA research assistant benefits from persisted artifacts:\n- collected source notes\n- intermediate summaries\n- extracted citations\n- final reports\n\n`StoreBackend` is the best fit when research should survive across sessions. The default state backend is useful for ephemeral experiments, but docs describe it as thread-scoped rather than cross-thread durable.  \nSources:  \n- Backends guide: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends  \n- State backend reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/backends/state/StateBackend  \n- Store backend reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/backends/store/StoreBackend\n\n---\n\n## 5) Filesystem tool surface and context strategy\n\nThe built-in filesystem middleware exposes these tool names:\n- `ls`\n- `read_file`\n- `write_file`\n- `edit_file`\n- `glob`\n- `grep`\n\nThe `FsToolName` reference confirms the built-in tool-name set.  \nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/filesystem/FsToolName\n\n### Design guidance\nUse the filesystem as the assistant\u2019s working memory layer:\n- write raw search results to files\n- write per-source extraction notes\n- keep a rolling `/reports/outline.md`\n- store per-topic synthesis files\n- have the main agent read only the slices it needs with `read_file` or `grep`\n\nThis follows the Deep Agents context-engineering guidance: large outputs and history can be offloaded to files so the active context stays smaller and more controllable.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/context-engineering\n\n### Suggested workspace layout\n\n```txt\n/research/\n  /queries/\n  /sources/\n  /notes/\n  /drafts/\n  /final/\n  /memory/AGENTS.md\n```\n\nThis is a design recommendation, not a documented requirement.\n\n---\n\n## 6) How to define subagents\n\nDeep Agents supports subagent delegation through a `task` tool. The official subagents guide says subagents are useful for:\n- context quarantine\n- specialized instructions\n- keeping the main agent\u2019s context clean when tools return large outputs\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents\n\n## A. Declarative subagents with `SubAgent`\n\nOfficial class:\n- **`SubAgent`**\n\nReference fields include:\n- **`name`**\n- **`description`**\n- **`system_prompt`**\n- **`tools`**\n- **`model`**\n- **`middleware`**\n- **`interrupt_on`**\n- **`skills`**\n- **`permissions`**\n- **`response_format`**\n\nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/SubAgent\n\nExample structure:\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\nfrom deepagents.middleware.subagents import SubAgent\n\nresearcher = SubAgent(\n    name=\"researcher\",\n    description=\"Finds and synthesizes primary and secondary sources.\",\n    system_prompt=(\n        \"You are a research specialist. \"\n        \"Search broadly, verify key claims, and return concise sourced findings.\"\n    ),\n    tools=[search_web, fetch_url],\n    model=\"anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6\",\n)\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6\",\n    tools=[search_web, fetch_url],\n    subagents=[researcher],\n)\n```\n\nGrounded by:\n- subagents guide: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents  \n- `SubAgent` reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/SubAgent\n\n## B. Precompiled subagents with `CompiledSubAgent`\n\nOfficial class:\n- **`CompiledSubAgent`**\n\nDocumented fields:\n- **`name`**\n- **`description`**\n- **`runnable`**\n\nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/CompiledSubAgent\n\nImportant documented constraint:\n- the `runnable`\u2019s state schema must include a **`messages`** key\n\nThe reference also notes how parent/child return values are handled:\n- if `structured_response` is non-`None`, it is JSON-serialized into the returned `ToolMessage`\n- otherwise the last non-empty `AIMessage` text is used\n\nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/CompiledSubAgent\n\nExample:\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\nfrom deepagents.middleware.subagents import CompiledSubAgent\n\ncustom_worker = CompiledSubAgent(\n    name=\"citation_checker\",\n    description=\"Verifies citations against retrieved documents.\",\n    runnable=my_compiled_graph,\n)\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"openai:gpt-5.5\",\n    subagents=[custom_worker],\n)\n```\n\n## Recommended subagent set for the research assistant\n\n### 1. `general-purpose`\nDeep Agents includes a general-purpose subagent pattern by default; docs say it has filesystem tools by default and can be customized with additional tools/middleware.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents\n\n### 2. `source-finder`\nPurpose:\n- run web search\n- collect candidate sources\n- write source manifests to files\n\nSuggested tools:\n- `search_web`\n- `fetch_url`\n\n### 3. `extractor`\nPurpose:\n- read selected sources\n- extract claims, dates, quotes, and URLs\n- normalize citation snippets into files\n\nSuggested tools:\n- `fetch_url`\n- filesystem tools\n\n### 4. `synthesizer`\nPurpose:\n- read notes and source files\n- draft section summaries\n- highlight uncertainty/conflicts\n\nSuggested tools:\n- filesystem tools only\n\n### 5. `citation-checker`\nPurpose:\n- verify that every claim in output is backed by a cited URL\n- reject unsupported sentences\n\nThis can be a declarative `SubAgent` or a stricter `CompiledSubAgent`.\n\n### Why this structure\nThe docs\u2019 reason for subagents is mainly context isolation and specialization. For research workflows, that maps directly to search, extraction, synthesis, and verification stages.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents\n\n---\n\n## 7) Human-in-the-loop support\n\nDeep Agents has first-class human-in-the-loop support through:\n- **`interrupt_on`**\n- **`checkpointer`**\n- LangGraph resume semantics via **`Command(resume=...)`**\n\nSources:  \n- Deep Agents HITL docs: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop  \n- LangGraph interrupts: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts\n\n## Required pieces\n\n### A. `interrupt_on`\nOfficial example:\n\n```python\ninterrupt_on={\n    \"remove_file\": True,\n    \"fetch_file\": False,\n    \"notify_email\": {\"allowed_decisions\": [\"approve\", \"reject\"]},\n}\n```\n\nDocs explain:\n- `True` means interrupt with default allowed decisions\n- `False` means no interrupt\n- dict form allows explicit configuration such as `allowed_decisions`\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n### B. `checkpointer`\nThe docs explicitly state a checkpointer is required for HITL.\n\n```python\nfrom langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver\n\ncheckpointer = MemorySaver()\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n### C. Resume primitive\nLangGraph\u2019s interrupt model resumes execution using:\n\n```python\nfrom langgraph.types import Command\n```\n\nand then:\n\n```python\nagent.invoke(Command(resume=...), config=config)\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts\n\n## Supported decision types\nThe official docs describe these actions:\n- **`approve`**\n- **`edit`**\n- **`reject`**\n- **`respond`**\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n## Recommended HITL policy for this research assistant\n\n### Require approval for:\n- any file deletion\n- any file overwrite in `/final/`\n- any external notification/email/slack tool\n- any shell execution if enabled\n- publishing/export steps\n\n### No approval needed for:\n- web search\n- URL fetching\n- read-only filesystem operations\n- note creation in draft directories\n\n### Example configuration\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\nfrom langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver\n\ncheckpointer = MemorySaver()\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6\",\n    tools=[search_web, fetch_url, notify_email],\n    interrupt_on={\n        \"notify_email\": {\"allowed_decisions\": [\"approve\", \"reject\"]},\n        \"write_file\": True,\n        \"edit_file\": True,\n    },\n    checkpointer=checkpointer,\n)\n```\n\nThis policy is a design recommendation. The underlying mechanics are documented here:  \nhttps://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n---\n\n## 8) Recommended implementation blueprint\n\n## Phase 1 architecture\n\n### Main agent\nResponsibilities:\n- receive the user research request\n- create/update a plan\n- decide which subagent to delegate to\n- maintain the report outline\n- enforce source/citation expectations\n\n### Tools\nAt minimum:\n- `search_web(query: str) -> str`\n- `fetch_url(url: str) -> str`\n\nOptionally:\n- domain-specific retrieval tools\n- internal knowledge base search\n- citation formatter/exporter\n\nDeep Agents docs show standard Python tools passed in `tools=[...]`.  \nSources:  \n- Overview: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview  \n- Customization: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/customization\n\n### Backend\n- production default: `StoreBackend()`\n- local dev: `FilesystemBackend(root_dir=\"./workspace\")`\n\n### Memory\nThe docs support `memory=[...]` and `skills=[...]` inputs.\n\nExample from docs:\n\n```python\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6\",\n    memory=[\"./AGENTS.md\"],\n    skills=[\"./skills/\"],\n)\n```\n\nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/customization\n\n### Suggested `AGENTS.md`\nPut stable operating rules there, for example:\n- always cite URLs\n- distinguish verified facts from tentative claims\n- prefer primary sources when available\n- if sources disagree, report the disagreement\n- do not claim a fact unless a retrieved source supports it\n\nThis use of memory is consistent with Deep Agents memory docs.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/memory\n\n---\n\n## 9) Example starter implementation\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\nfrom deepagents.backends import StoreBackend\nfrom deepagents.middleware.subagents import SubAgent\nfrom langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver\n\ndef search_web(query: str) -> str:\n    \"\"\"Search the web and return candidate results with URLs.\"\"\"\n    return \"...\"\n\ndef fetch_url(url: str) -> str:\n    \"\"\"Fetch a web page and return extracted text.\"\"\"\n    return \"...\"\n\nsource_finder = SubAgent(\n    name=\"source-finder\",\n    description=\"Find candidate sources and write source lists.\",\n    system_prompt=(\n        \"Find relevant sources, prefer official and primary references, \"\n        \"and return a concise sourced summary.\"\n    ),\n    tools=[search_web, fetch_url],\n    model=\"anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6\",\n)\n\nsynthesizer = SubAgent(\n    name=\"synthesizer\",\n    description=\"Read notes and draft report sections with citations.\",\n    system_prompt=(\n        \"Draft clear research sections. Every factual claim must cite a URL. \"\n        \"Call out uncertainty or source disagreement.\"\n    ),\n    tools=[fetch_url],\n    model=\"anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6\",\n)\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6\",\n    tools=[search_web, fetch_url],\n    system_prompt=(\n        \"You are a research assistant. Verify claims, use subagents when useful, \"\n        \"and maintain clean file-based working notes.\"\n    ),\n    backend=StoreBackend(),\n    subagents=[source_finder, synthesizer],\n    memory=[\"./AGENTS.md\"],\n    skills=[\"./skills/\"],\n    interrupt_on={\n        \"write_file\": True,\n        \"edit_file\": True,\n    },\n    checkpointer=MemorySaver(),\n)\n```\n\nThis code is assembled from official API patterns and names documented in:\n- `create_deep_agent`: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n- customization examples: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/customization\n- subagents docs: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents\n- subagent reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/SubAgent\n- backends docs: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n- HITL docs: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n---\n\n## 10) Risks and implementation cautions\n\n### 1. Version sensitivity\nDeep Agents is evolving quickly; the current version is `0.6.12`. Lock the package version and run contract tests around:\n- imports\n- `SubAgent` definitions\n- backend constructors\n- interrupt/resume behavior\n\nSource: https://pypi.org/project/deepagents\n\n### 2. Backend safety\nThe reference explicitly warns by implication that `FilesystemBackend` gives direct filesystem access and is generally expected to be paired with HITL.  \nSource: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/backends/filesystem\n\n### 3. Shell execution risk\nIf you use a shell-capable backend, treat it as privileged execution and gate it behind approval and sandboxing. The docs list `LocalShellBackend` as direct host execution.  \nSource: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n### 4. Citation quality is not automatic\nDeep Agents gives orchestration primitives, not truth guarantees. The same pattern holds for `gpt-5-mini` and `gpt-5-nano`. So if you want to cut spend, reducing long completions often matters more than shaving modest prompt tokens.  \nSources:  \nhttps://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5  \nhttps://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5-mini  \nhttps://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5-nano\n\n## B. Cached input can materially reduce cost\nOfficial cached-input prices:\n\n- `gpt-5-mini`: **$0.025 / 1M**\n- `gpt-5-nano`: **$0.005 / 1M**\n\nIf your system repeatedly sends large stable prefixes\u2014system prompts, tool schemas, policy blocks, shared retrieval framing\u2014prompt caching can meaningfully change unit economics.  \nSources:  \nhttps://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5-mini  \nhttps://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5-nano\n\n## C. Large context windows increase risk of accidental spend\nRetrieved official model pages show very large capacities, including **400,000-token context windows** and **128,000 max output** on GPT-5-family small models. Without hard caps, teams can create surprisingly expensive requests through oversized prompts, verbose outputs, or retry loops.  \nSources:  \nhttps://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5-mini  \nhttps://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5-nano  \nhttps://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5\n\n## D. Tool calls may add separate fees\nOpenAI\u2019s GPT-5 page notes that pricing can also include **other model-specific metrics** and that **tool-specific models may incur a fee per tool call**. React 19 keeps `useFormState` only as deprecated  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-15\n\n## 4) Browser support\nNext.js 16 browser baseline is:\n- Chrome 111+\n- Edge 111+\n- Firefox 111+\n- Safari 16.4+  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n**Action**\n- Reconfirm customer/browser support commitments\n- Re-run browser regression tests, especially if you still support older Safari variants\n\n---\n\n## Build tooling defaults: the biggest operational change\n\n## 1) Turbopack is now the default bundler\nNext.js 16 makes **Turbopack** the default bundler. The release notes say Turbopack reached stability for development and production builds and is the default bundler for new projects.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n**Operational implication**\nIf your app assumes webpack-specific behavior, the upgrade may fail or behave differently even if application code itself compiles.\n\n### If you have a custom webpack config\nThe version-16 upgrade docs explicitly warn:\n\n> If your project has a custom `webpack` configuration and you run `next build` (which now uses Turbopack by default), the build will fail...  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n**Action**\n- Search `next.config.*` for a `webpack(config)` function\n- If present, choose one of these paths:\n\n#### Option A: short-term safety\nForce webpack during migration:\n- `next dev --webpack`\n- `next build --webpack`  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\nThis is the safest first production rollout path.\n\n#### Option B: migrate to Turbopack config\nMove webpack-specific assumptions to supported Turbopack config where possible:\n- top-level `turbopack`\n- `turbopack.ignoreIssue`\n- related Turbopack config APIs  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n### Babel behavior changes under Turbopack\nIn 16, **Turbopack automatically enables Babel if it finds a Babel config**, instead of hard-failing.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n**Action**\n- If you have `.babelrc` / `babel.config.*`, test whether Babel transforms are still intended\n- Measure build performance; unexpected Babel activation can slow builds\n\n---\n\n## 2) Turbopack filesystem caching defaults changed after 16.0\n\n### In 16.0\nFilesystem cache existed, but as beta / separately flagged behavior.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### In 16.1\nTurbopack filesystem caching for **`next dev`** became **stable and on by default**.  \nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-1  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackFileSystemCache\n\nThe config docs record:\n- `v16.1.0`: enabled by default for development\n- build filesystem cache still experimental  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackFileSystemCache\n\n**Action**\n- Expect changed local-dev performance characteristics after upgrading to 16.1+\n- If debugging build-cache issues, inspect `.next` caching behavior\n\n### In 16.2\nNo default change to build cache was documented as stable; build cache remained something you configure/experiment with.  \nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-2  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackFileSystemCache\n\n### In 16.3 preview\nPersistent filesystem cache for **`next build`** appears in preview guidance, but 16.3 was not yet stable in mid-2026.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-3-turbopack\n\n---\n\n## 3) Linting defaults changed\n\n### `next lint` is deprecated in 15.5 and removed in 16\n15.5 introduced deprecation warnings; 16 removes the `next lint` command.  \nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-15-5  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\nThe 16 release notes say:\n- use **ESLint directly** or **Biome**\n- `next build` no longer runs linting\n- codemod available:  \n  `npx @next/codemod@canary next-lint-to-eslint-cli .`  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n**Action**\n- Replace scripts like:\n  - `\"lint\": \"next lint\"`\n- With direct CLI scripts, e.g.:\n  - `\"lint\": \"eslint .\"`\n  - `\"lint:fix\": \"eslint . --fix\"`\n- Move lint execution into CI explicitly\n\n### ESLint config format default changes\n`@next/eslint-plugin-next` defaults to **ESLint Flat Config** in 16.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n**Action**\n- If still on legacy `.eslintrc*`, decide whether to:\n  - keep legacy config temporarily, or\n  - migrate to `eslint.config.mjs`\n\n---\n\n## Breaking changes and removals you must handle\n\n## 1) Async Request APIs: 15 introduced it, 16 finishes the break\n\nThe v15 upgrade guide marks these request-time APIs as asynchronous:\n- `cookies()`\n- `headers()`\n- `draftMode()`\n- `params` in App Router file conventions\n- `searchParams` in `page.js`  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-15\n\nIn v15, temporary synchronous access remained available with warnings/casts. In v16, the 16 release notes list sync access as removed behavior:\n- must use `await cookies()`\n- must use `await headers()`\n- must use `await draftMode()`\n- must use async `params` / `searchParams`  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n**Action**\nAudit for all of the following patterns:\n\n### Before\n```ts\nconst c = cookies()\nconst h = headers()\nconst d = draftMode()\nconst { slug } = params\nconst q = searchParams.query\n```\n\n### After\n```ts\nconst c = await cookies()\nconst h = await headers()\nconst d = await draftMode()\n\nconst { slug } = await params\nconst sp = await searchParams\nconst q = sp.query\n```\n\nIn client components receiving promised props, use `use()` from React if needed, as documented in the v15 guide.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-15\n\n---\n\n## 2) `middleware.ts` -> `proxy.ts`\nNext.js 16 introduces **`proxy.ts`** as the explicit Node.js network boundary file and says it replaces `middleware.ts` conceptually for that role. The release notes say:\n- `proxy.ts` runs on the Node.js runtime\n- `middleware.ts` still exists for Edge runtime use cases\n- `middleware.ts` is deprecated and will be removed in a future version  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n**Action**\n- If your middleware logic is Node-runtime-friendly and not specifically Edge-bound, plan to rename and adapt it to **`proxy.ts`**\n- If you intentionally depend on Edge behavior, keep `middleware.ts` for now but treat it as technical debt\n\n**Important nuance**  \nIn 15.5, **Node.js middleware runtime** became stable inside `middleware.ts` via `runtime: 'nodejs'`. In 16, the framework direction shifts toward **`proxy.ts`** for this boundary.  \nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-15-5  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n---\n\n## 3) Caching model changes and API renames/removals\n\n### `experimental.dynamicIO` -> `cacheComponents`\nNext.js 16 removes `experimental.dynamicIO` and uses top-level **`cacheComponents`** instead.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### `experimental.ppr` removed\nThe older PPR flags/config are removed:\n- `experimental.ppr`\n- route-level `export const experimental_ppr`  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### New caching APIs in 16\nNext.js 16 adds and/or formalizes:\n- `updateTag()`\n- `refresh()`\n- `'use cache'`\n- `cacheComponents`  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### `revalidateTag()` signature change\nIn 16, `revalidateTag()` now expects a second argument for cache-life profile / SWR behavior:\n```ts\nrevalidateTag('blog-posts', 'max')\n```\nSingle-argument form is deprecated.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n**Action**\nSearch for:\n```ts\nrevalidateTag('...')\n```\nand migrate to one of:\n```ts\nrevalidateTag(tag, 'max')\nrevalidateTag(tag, 'hours')\nrevalidateTag(tag, 'days')\nrevalidateTag(tag, { expire: 3600 })\n```\nor use `updateTag(tag)` in Server Actions when you need read-your-writes behavior.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n---\n\n## 4) Fetch and Route Handler caching semantics\nNext.js 15 already changed defaults:\n- `fetch()` requests are **no longer cached by default**\n- `GET` Route Handlers are **no longer cached by default**  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-15\n\nIf your production app upgraded within the 15 line without fully auditing behavior, verify again before 16 because the new cache model (`cacheComponents`, `'use cache'`, `updateTag`, `refresh`) may prompt additional cleanup.\n\n**Action**\nAudit for endpoints/pages that silently relied on old implicit caching and choose explicit behavior:\n- `cache: 'force-cache'`\n- `export const fetchCache = 'default-cache'`\n- route config such as `export const dynamic = 'force-static'`\n- or explicit 16 cache components model  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-15\n\n---\n\n## 5) `next/image` security and default behavior changes\n\nNext.js 16 changes multiple image defaults and restrictions:\n\n- local `src` with query strings now requires **`images.localPatterns`**\n- `images.qualities` default changes from `[1..100]` to `[75]`\n- `quality` gets coerced to nearest allowed configured value\n- `images.minimumCacheTTL` default changes from 60s to 14400s\n- `images.imageSizes` drops `16`\n- `images.maximumRedirects` default becomes `3`\n- `images.dangerouslyAllowLocalIP` becomes a more explicit opt-in security exception\n- `images.domains` is deprecated in favor of `images.remotePatterns`  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n15.5 specifically warned ahead of time about:\n- `images.qualities`\n- `images.localPatterns` for local image query strings  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-15-5\n\n**Action**\nAudit all usages of:\n- `<Image quality={...} />`\n- local image URLs with query params like `/photo.jpg?v=1`\n- `images.domains`\n\n### Example migration\n```ts\nconst nextConfig = {\n  images: {\n    qualities: [75, 100],\n    localPatterns: [\n      { pathname: '/photo.jpg', search: '?v=1' },\n      { pathname: '/assets/**', search: '' },\n    ],\n    remotePatterns: [\n      {\n        protocol: 'https',\n        hostname: 'images.example.com',\n      },\n    ],\n  },\n}\n```\nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-15-5  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n---\n\n## 6) Parallel routes now require explicit `default.js`\nIn Next.js 16:\n- all parallel route slots require explicit **`default.js`**\n- builds fail without them\n- previous implicit behavior must be replaced with `default.js` returning `null` or calling `notFound()`  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n**Action**\nSearch for `@slot` parallel routes in `app/` and ensure every slot has `default.js` / `default.tsx`.\n\n---\n\n## 7) `next/font` package cleanup\nThe v15 guide states the old `@next/font` package was removed in favor of built-in `next/font`.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-15\n\n**Action**\nIf any older modules or page config, treat that as unsupported on 16 and remove it before or during the upgrade.\n\n### Migration action\nSearch for:\n- `amp: true`\n- AMP-specific page config\n- AMP-only rendering paths\n\nIf present, remove or replace them before cutover.\n\n---\n\n## 2.4 `middleware.ts` is renamed to `proxy.ts`\n\nThe Next.js 16 upgrade docs and API docs move this feature under the **`proxy`** file convention.  \nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy\n\nThe `proxy` docs include a **How to Migrate** section and clarify that the file convention is now `proxy.js` / `proxy.ts`.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy\n\n### Practical impact\nIf your app currently uses:\n- `middleware.ts`\n- middleware matchers\n- request rewriting/auth logic in middleware\n\nyou must validate the rename and confirm behavior under the new `proxy` convention.\n\n### Additional caveat\nThe `proxy` docs note that the `runtime` config option is **not available in Proxy files**.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy\n\nThat matters if your current middleware depended on runtime configuration assumptions.\n\n---\n\n## 2.5 Async Request APIs and promise-based params\n\nNext.js 15 already introduced significant migration around async request APIs and React 19-era patterns. The official upgrade guide shows examples where route params become promise-based and are awaited or unwrapped with React\u2019s `use()`.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-15\n\nNext.js 16 continues this direction. The version 16 upgrade guide explicitly notes that, to align with the **Async Request APIs** change, image-generating functions now receive **`params`** and **`id`** as promises.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n### Practical impact\nAudit these APIs:\n- `page.js` / `page.tsx` props\n- `layout.js` / `layout.tsx` props\n- `generateMetadata`\n- image generation functions / Open Graph image handlers\n\nIf your code assumes synchronous `params` or `searchParams`, update signatures and reads to match the versioned docs.\n\n### Example migration pattern from the official 15 guide\nThe 15 guide shows moving from:\n```ts\ntype Params = { slug: string }\n```\nto:\n```ts\ntype Params = Promise<{ slug: string }>\n```\nand then:\n```ts\nconst { slug } = await params\n```\nor using:\n```ts\nimport { use } from 'react'\nconst { slug } = use(params)\n```\nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-15\n\nDo not bulk-apply this blindly; apply it where your code actually matches the affected API surfaces documented for your router mode and file type.\n\n---\n\n## 2.6 Caching behavior changed in 15, and 16 adds new caching APIs\n\n### What changed in 15\nThe Next.js 15 release made caching semantics a breaking change:\n- `fetch` requests are no longer cached by default\n- `GET` Route Handlers are no longer cached by default\n- client router navigations are no longer cached by default  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-15\n\nIf your production app was upgraded to 15 without fully auditing behavior, you may already have latent cache regressions or hidden correctness fixes.\n\n### What changes further in 16\nNext.js 16 introduced **Cache Components** and newer cache APIs:\n- `cacheComponents` config\n- `use cache`\n- `cacheLife`\n- `updateTag()`\n- changed guidance for `revalidateTag()`  \nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag\n\nThe `cacheComponents` docs say this flag enables component- and function-level caching using `use cache`, and explicitly tell upgraders from `experimental.useCache`, `experimental.dynamicIO`, or experimental PPR in 15 to use the version 16 guide.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents\n\nThe `revalidateTag` docs state that calling `revalidateTag` **without** the second argument is now deprecated; the recommended stale-while-revalidate pattern is:\n```ts\nrevalidateTag('tag', 'max')\n```\nor a custom `cacheLife` profile, while `updateTag()` is the alternative when you want immediate consistency behavior.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag\n\n### Practical impact\nAudit:\n- custom ISR/revalidation logic\n- tags used with `revalidateTag`\n- any experimental `dynamicIO`, `useCache`, or PPR flags\n- assumptions that navigations or route handlers are cached by default\n\n---\n\n## 3) Runtime and platform requirements\n\n## 3.1 React version requirements\n\nThe official Next.js 15 upgrade guide says the **minimum versions of `react` and `react-dom` are now 19**.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-15\n\nThe Next.js 16 line continues on React 19;         "report": "**Mission summary: NASA\u2019s Artemis II**\n\nNASA\u2019s Artemis II mission launched on **April 1, 2026**, aboard the **Space Launch System (SLS)** from **Launch Complex 39B at Kennedy Space Center, Florida**, and returned with a **Pacific splashdown off the coast of California on April 10, 2026, at 8:07 p.m. EDT**. NASA describes it as the **first crewed mission of the Artemis program** and the **first crewed lunar flyby in more than 50 years**. NASA\u2019s postflight material describes the flight as a roughly **10-day** mission around the Moon and back.  \nSources:  \n- https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/liftoff-nasa-launches-astronauts-on-historic-artemis-moon-mission  \n- https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/04/10/artemis-ii-flight-day-10-live-re-entry-updates  \n- https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-ii  \n\n## Crew and historic firsts\n\nThe four-person crew was:  \n- **Reid Wiseman** (NASA), commander  \n- **Victor Glover** (NASA), pilot  \n- **Christina Koch** (NASA), mission specialist  \n- **Jeremy Hansen** (Canadian Space Agency), mission specialist  \n\nNASA and CSA identified the crew as historically significant well before launch. **Christina Koch** became the **first woman to fly to the vicinity of the Moon** on Artemis II. **Victor Glover** became the **first person of color to take part in a lunar mission**. **Jeremy Hansen** became the **first Canadian** to fly on a lunar mission; CSA also describes him as the first Canadian to go on a mission around the Moon. NASA\u2019s official **Artemis II Priorities and Objectives** document says the mission\u2019s primary goal was to demonstrate the ability of systems and teams to **sustain a crew in the flight environment and return them safely to Earth**, while also validating key operations such as crew rescue, Earth-departure configuration, service module propulsion upgrades, life-support performance, and post-splashdown recovery.  \nSource:  \n- https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/artemis-ii-mission-prioirities-objectives-.pdf?emrc=9fdebb  \n\nDuring the flight, the crew completed a lunar flyby and operated Orion in deep space, testing the spacecraft in the environment it was designed for. On **April 6, 2026**, NASA announced that the crew had surpassed the previous mark set by **Apollo 13 in 1970**. NASA said Orion reached a **maximum distance from Earth of 252,756 miles**, establishing a new record for the farthest humans have traveled from Earth.  \nSources:  \n- https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-artemis-ii-crew-eclipses-record-for-farthest-human-spaceflight  \n- https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/04/06/artemis-ii-flight-day-6-lunar-flyby-updates  \n\nNASA also highlighted a series of visual and operational milestones during the lunar flyby, including crew observations of **Earthrise**, **Earthset**, and a period of communications blackout while Orion passed behind the Moon, all of which helped validate navigation, communications, and mission operations in cislunar space.  \nSource:  \n- https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/04/06/artemis-ii-flight-day-6-lunar-flyby-updates  \n\n## What Artemis II means for the Artemis program\n\nArtemis II is the program\u2019s critical **bridge from uncrewed testing to crewed lunar operations**.         "report": "# NASA Artemis II mission summary\n\n## Overview\n\nArtemis II was NASA\u2019s first crewed Artemis mission and the first crewed flight of the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket and Orion spacecraft. It sent four astronauts on an approximately 10-day lunar flyby mission to test Orion\u2019s systems with humans aboard in deep space, a step NASA says is meant to \u201clay the groundwork for future crewed Artemis missions.\u201d NASA launched Artemis II from Kennedy Space Center on **April 1, 2026**, and Orion splashed down in the Pacific on **April 10, 2026**.  \nSources: NASA mission overview: https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-ii ; NASA launch coverage: https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/04/01/live-artemis-ii-launch-day-updates ; NASA return coverage: https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/04/10/artemis-ii-flight-day-10-re-entry-live-updates ; NASA mission FAQ: https://www.nasa.gov/missions/nasa-answers-your-most-pressing-artemis-ii-questions ; NASA media advisory: https://www.nasa.gov/missions/artemis/artemis-2/nasa-sets-coverage-for-artemis-ii-moon-mission\n\n## Launch and return\n\nNASA says Artemis II lifted off from **Launch Complex 39B at Kennedy Space Center in Florida at 6:35 p.m. EDT on Wednesday, April 1, 2026**. The mission ended when Orion **landed in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California at 8:07 p.m. EDT on Friday, April 10, 2026**. During the flight, NASA consistently described the mission as an **approximately 10-day** journey around the Moon and back.  \nSources: https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/04/01/live-artemis-ii-launch-day-updates ; https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/04/10/artemis-ii-flight-day-10-re-entry-live-updates ; https://www.nasa.gov/missions/nasa-answers-your-most-pressing-artemis-ii-questions\n\n## Crew and the historic firsts\n\nThe Artemis II crew was:\n\n- **Reid Wiseman** (NASA) \u2014 commander  \n- **Victor Glover** (NASA) \u2014 pilot  \n- **Christina Koch** (NASA) \u2014 mission specialist  \n- **Jeremy Hansen** (Canadian Space Agency) \u2014 mission specialist  \n\nNASA\u2019s crew materials and widely cited institutional summaries identify the mission\u2019s historic firsts as:\n\n- **Christina Koch** became the **first woman to go to the Moon** on a lunar mission.  \n- **Victor Glover** became the **first person of color to go to the Moon** on a lunar mission.  \n- **Jeremy Hansen** became the **first Canadian to go to the Moon**.  \n\nNASA\u2019s Artemis II crew page confirms the crew assignments; a Smithsonian Air and Space summary of NASA\u2019s announcement clearly states the firsts above.  \nSources: NASA mission page: https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-ii ; NASA crew feature: https://www.nasa.gov/feature/our-artemis-crew/ ; NASA special Artemis II page: https://www3.nasa.gov/specials/artemis-ii ; Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum: https://airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/meet-crew-artemis-ii\n\n## What the mission accomplished\n\n### 1) It completed the first crewed test of SLS and Orion\nNASA describes Artemis II as the **first mission with crew aboard** SLS and Orion.
