        "report": "# Design brief: building a research assistant with the `deepagents` Python library\n\n## Executive summary\n\nAs of today, the latest published Python package version of **`deepagents` is `0.6.12`** on PyPI. Deep Agents is positioned as an opinionated agent harness on top of LangGraph/LangChain, with built-in support for planning, filesystem tools, subagent delegation, and human oversight workflows. Official docs describe it as a \u201cbatteries-included agent harness\u201d and show `create_deep_agent(...)` as the primary entry point for assembling an agent.  \nSources:  \n- PyPI package page: https://pypi.org/project/deepagents  \n- LangChain Python reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents  \n- Overview docs: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\nFor your engineering team, the practical recommendation is:\n\n1. **Pin `deepagents==0.6.12`** for the initial build.\n2. Use **`create_deep_agent(...)`** as the main construction API.\n3. Start with a **search tool + default thread-scoped filesystem backend** for a first version.\n4. Add **specialized subagents** for search/retrieval, synthesis, and citation verification.\n5. Enable **human-in-the-loop** for high-risk actions and any outbound communication or destructive file operations.\n\n---\n\n## 1) Current version and versioning recommendation\n\n### Current package version\nThe latest visible PyPI release for the Python package is **`0.6.12`**. The LangChain Python reference also labels Deep Agents as **v0.6.12 (latest)**.  \nSources:  \n- https://pypi.org/project/deepagents  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents\n\n### Stability implication\nThe Deep Agents project is still **pre-1.0**, and maintainers explicitly recommend **pinning versions for production deployments** and reviewing release notes before upgrading minor versions.  \nSource:  \n- https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/issues/4219\n\n### Recommendation\nFor the initial implementation:\n```bash\npip install \"deepagents==0.6.12\"\n```\nAlso pin your model integration packages explicitly, since Deep Agents relies on the surrounding LangChain runtime ecosystem. Official docs show examples with provider-specific packages such as `langchain-google-genai` and `langchain-anthropic`.  \nSources:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/customization\n\n---\n\n## 2) Core API for creating an agent\n\n## Primary constructor\nThe official factory is:\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\n```\n\nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n### Verified parameter names\nFrom official reference/snippet sources, the current Python API includes these parameters on `create_deep_agent(...)`:\n\n- `model`\n- `tools`\n- `system_prompt`\n- `subagents`\n- `skills`\n- `memory`\n- `response_format`\n- `context_schema`\n- `backend`\n- `interrupt_on`\n\nSources:  \n- Function reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent  \n- Official source snippet surfaced via GitHub: https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/issues/1778\n\nThe clearest surfaced signature fragment is:\n\n```python\ndef create_deep_agent(\n    model: str | BaseChatModel | None = None,\n    tools: Sequence[BaseTool | Callable | dict[str, Any]] | None = None,\n    system_prompt: str | SystemMessage | None = None,\n    subagents: list[SubAgent | CompiledSubAgent] | None = None,\n    skills: list[str] | None = None,\n    memory: list[str] | None = None,\n    response_format: ResponseFormat | None = None,\n    context_schema: type[Any] | None = None,\n    backend: BackendProtocol | BackendFactory | None = None,\n    interrupt_on: dict[str, bool | InterruptOnConfig] | None = None,\n    ...\n)\n```\n\nSource:  \n- https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/issues/1778\n\n### Minimal example\nThe official overview docs show this pattern:\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\n\ndef get_weather(city: str) -> str:\n    \"\"\"Get weather for a given city.\"\"\"\n    return f\"It's always sunny in {city}!\"\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash\",\n    tools=[get_weather],\n    system_prompt=\"You are a helpful assistant\",\n)\n```\n\nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview\n\n### What `create_deep_agent` gives you by default\nThe reference docs state that the agent includes built-in tools and middleware, including:\n\n- `write_todos`\n- filesystem tools\n- `execute`\n- `task`\n\nSource:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\nThat matters architecturally: your team does **not** need to wire planning or task delegation from scratch. Those behaviors are part of the harness.\n\n---\n\n## 3) Recommended architecture for a research assistant\n\nA research assistant should optimize for:\n\n1. **fact gathering**\n2. **citation traceability**\n3. **context isolation**\n4. **reviewability**\n5. **safe human approval for risky steps**\n\nDeep Agents maps well to that because it has:\n\n- built-in planning (`write_todos`)\n- built-in filesystem context surface\n- built-in subagent delegation via `task`\n- built-in HITL hooks via `interrupt_on`\n\nSources:  \n- Overview: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview  \n- Subagents: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents  \n- Human-in-the-loop: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n### Proposed agent topology\n\n#### Main coordinator agent\nResponsibilities:\n- break the user request into subtasks\n- dispatch research/synthesis/verification work\n- assemble final answer\n- manage scratch files and intermediate artifacts\n\n#### Suggested specialized subagents\n1. **Research subagent**\n   - web search, fetch, retrieval\n   - writes source notes into files\n2. **Verifier subagent**\n   - checks every factual claim against URLs\n   - flags unsupported assertions\n3. **Writer subagent**\n   - synthesizes findings into the requested format\n4. **Optional domain subagents**\n   - e.g. finance, legal, product, technical docs\n\nThis matches the Deep Agents design goal for subagents: keeping the main context clean while isolating multi-step work and only returning the final result to the parent.  \nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents\n\n---\n\n## 4) Filesystem backends\n\nDeep Agents exposes a filesystem surface through these built-in tools:\n\n- `ls`\n- `read_file`\n- `write_file`\n- `edit_file`\n- `glob`\n- `grep`\n\nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\nThese tools are important for a research assistant because they allow the agent to:\n- persist source excerpts\n- maintain working notes\n- store outlines and drafts\n- cache intermediate structured research outputs\n\n## Officially documented backend options\n\n### 4.1 Default thread-scoped backend\nIf you do not pass `backend=...`, the docs say the default backend is **thread-scoped** and stored in LangGraph state.  \nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\nExample:\n```python\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash\"\n)\n```\n\n### 4.2 `FilesystemBackend`\nGives the agent access to a local machine filesystem rooted at a specified directory.  \nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\nExample from docs:\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\nfrom deepagents.backends import FilesystemBackend\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash\",\n    backend=FilesystemBackend(root_dir=\"/Users/nh/Desktop/\")\n)\n```\n\n### 4.3 `StoreBackend`\nProvides durable storage persisted across threads via LangGraph store.  \nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\nExample:\n```python\nfrom deepagents.backends import StoreBackend\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash\",\n    backend=StoreBackend()\n)\n```\n\n### 4.4 `ContextHubBackend`\nStores files durably in a LangSmith Hub repo without separately provisioning a LangGraph store.  \nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\nExample:\n```python\nfrom deepagents.backends import ContextHubBackend\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash\",\n    backend=ContextHubBackend(\"my-agent\")\n)\n```\n\n### 4.5 `LocalShellBackend`\nProvides filesystem plus shell execution directly on the host.  \nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\nExample:\n```python\nfrom deepagents.backends import LocalShellBackend\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash\",\n    backend=LocalShellBackend(\n        root_dir=\".\",\n        env={\"PATH\": \"/usr/bin:/bin\"}\n    )\n)\n```\n\n## Backend recommendation for this project\n\n### Phase 1\nUse the **default thread-scoped backend** for quick prototyping.\n\n### Phase 2\nUse **`StoreBackend()`** if you want persistent cross-thread working memory and research artifact retention.\n\n### Phase 3\nUse **`FilesystemBackend(root_dir=...)`** only if you intentionally want local host access and have clear security controls.\n\n### Avoid by default\nAvoid **`LocalShellBackend`** in the first production release unless shell execution is a hard requirement, because it significantly raises operational and security risk.\n\n---\n\n## 5) Subagents: how to define them\n\nDeep Agents supports subagents through the `subagents=` parameter on `create_deep_agent(...)`.  \nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents\n\n## `SubAgent`\nThe official reference documents `SubAgent` as the declarative spec for child agents.  \nSource:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/SubAgent\n\n### Required `SubAgent` fields\n- `name: str`\n- `description: str`\n- `system_prompt: str`\n\nSource:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/SubAgent\n\n### Optional `SubAgent` fields\n- `tools`\n- `model`\n- `middleware`\n- `interrupt_on`\n- `skills`\n- `permissions`\n- `response_format`\n\nSource:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/SubAgent\n\n### Important behavior\nThe main agent invokes subagents through the built-in **`task`** tool, using the subagent\u2019s `name`.  \nSources:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/SubAgentMiddleware\n\n## Example design for a research assistant\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\nfrom deepagents.middleware.subagents import SubAgent\n\nresearch_subagent = SubAgent(\n    name=\"researcher\",\n    description=\"Find and summarize relevant sources for a question\",\n    system_prompt=\"You are a research specialist. Gather evidence, keep citations, and return concise findings.\",\n    tools=[search_tool, fetch_url_tool],\n)\n\nverifier_subagent = SubAgent(\n    name=\"verifier\",\n    description=\"Verify factual claims against cited URLs\",\n    system_prompt=\"You validate claims. Reject unsupported assertions and identify missing citations.\",\n    tools=[search_tool, fetch_url_tool],\n)\n\nwriter_subagent = SubAgent(\n    name=\"writer\",\n    description=\"Draft polished report sections from verified findings\",\n    system_prompt=\"You write structured, concise reports using only verified source material.\",\n)\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6\",\n    tools=[search_tool, fetch_url_tool],\n    subagents=[research_subagent, verifier_subagent, writer_subagent],\n    system_prompt=\"You are a research coordinator.\",\n)\n```\n\nField names in this example are grounded in the documented `SubAgent` API; tool functions are illustrative placeholders your team would implement.  \nSources:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/SubAgent  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/subagents\n\n## `CompiledSubAgent`\n`create_deep_agent(...)` also accepts `CompiledSubAgent` entries in `subagents=`. The reference says these are exposed through the `task` tool and allow you to supply a prebuilt runnable instead of a declarative spec.  \nSources:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/CompiledSubAgent\n\n### When to use `CompiledSubAgent`\nUse `CompiledSubAgent` when:\n- you already have a custom LangGraph graph\n- you need nonstandard state handling\n- you want tight control over orchestration beyond the declarative `SubAgent` surface\n\n---\n\n## 6) Human-in-the-loop support\n\nDeep Agents supports human oversight through **`interrupt_on`** configuration.  \nSources:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/SubAgent\n\n## Key API\nTop-level agent creation accepts:\n\n- `interrupt_on: dict[str, bool | InterruptOnConfig] | None`\n\nSource:  \n- https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/issues/1778\n\nSubagents can also define their own:\n\n- `interrupt_on`\n\nSource:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/SubAgent\n\n## Critical implementation requirement\nThe human-in-the-loop docs explicitly say a **checkpointer is required** for HITL.  \nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n### Official example pattern\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\nfrom langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver\n\ncheckpointer = MemorySaver()\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"google_genai:gemini-3.5-flash\",\n    tools=[remove_file, fetch_file, notify_email],\n    interrupt_on={\n        \"remove_file\": True,\n        \"fetch_file\": False,\n        \"notify_email\": {\"allowed_decisions\": [\"approve\", \"reject\"]},\n    },\n    checkpointer=checkpointer,\n)\n```\n\nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n## What `True` and config objects mean\nThe docs show:\n- `True` enables default interrupt behavior\n- `False` disables interrupts\n- a config dict can restrict decisions, e.g. `{\"allowed_decisions\": [\"approve\", \"reject\"]}`\n\nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n## Recommendation for this project\nEnable HITL for:\n- any tool that sends email/messages\n- any destructive file operation\n- publication/export actions\n- actions that write final deliverables to external systems\n\nFor a research assistant, I would **not** interrupt on every read/search call. That would make the system unusably slow. Instead:\n- allow search and fetch automatically\n- require approval for publish/send/delete/export\n\n---\n\n## 7) Permissions and filesystem policy\n\nThe permissions docs show Deep Agents supports filesystem policy via `FilesystemPermission`.  \nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/permissions\n\n### Example patterns from docs\nThe docs show permission objects with:\n- `operations=[...]`\n- `paths=[...]`\n- `mode=\"allow\"` or `mode=\"deny\"`\n\nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/permissions\n\nExample:\n```python\nfrom deepagents import FilesystemPermission, create_deep_agent\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=model,\n    backend=backend,\n    permissions=[\n        FilesystemPermission(\n            operations=[\"write\"],\n            paths=[\"/**\"],\n            mode=\"deny\",\n        ),\n    ],\n)\n```\n\nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/permissions\n\n## Recommendation\nFor a research assistant:\n- default to **read/write only inside a dedicated workspace**\n- deny access to secrets and env files\n- do not expose broad host filesystem roots unless required\n\n---\n\n## 8) Proposed implementation plan\n\n## Phase 1: minimal viable research assistant\nUse:\n- `deepagents==0.6.12`\n- `create_deep_agent(...)`\n- one search tool\n- one fetch/read tool\n- default backend\n- no shell access\n- no external publishing\n\nExample shape:\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\n\nagent = create_deep_agent(\n    model=\"anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6\",\n    tools=[search_tool, fetch_url_tool],\n    system_prompt=(\n        \"You are a research assistant. \"\n        \"Gather evidence, preserve source URLs, and do not make unsupported claims.\"\n    ),\n)\n```\n\n## Phase 2: structured delegation\nAdd:\n- `researcher` subagent\n- `verifier` subagent\n- `writer` subagent\n- `StoreBackend()` for durable notes\n\n## Phase 3: controlled human review\nAdd:\n- `interrupt_on` for outbound actions and destructive operations\n- `checkpointer=MemorySaver()` or a production-grade checkpointing setup\n- explicit review UI around approvals\n\n---\n\n## 9) Concrete engineering recommendations\n\n### Package pin\n```text\ndeepagents==0.6.12\n```\nSource:  \n- https://pypi.org/project/deepagents\n\n### Core build choice\nUse **`create_deep_agent`** rather than building directly on raw `create_agent`, because the brief specifically requires:\n- filesystem support\n- subagents\n- planning\n- HITL hooks\n\nDeep Agents already bundles those defaults.  \nSources:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/overview  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\n### Backend choice\n- prototype: default thread-scoped backend\n- persistent workspace: `StoreBackend()`\n- host filesystem access: `FilesystemBackend(root_dir=...)`\n- avoid shell by default: do not use `LocalShellBackend` initially\n\nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n### Subagent pattern\nStart with declarative `SubAgent` specs; only move to `CompiledSubAgent` if you need custom LangGraph behavior.  \nSources:  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/SubAgent  \n- https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/middleware/subagents/CompiledSubAgent\n\n### HITL pattern\nUse `interrupt_on` plus a required checkpointer.  \nSource:  \n- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/human-in-the-loop\n\n---\n\n## 10) Risks and caveats\n\n1. **Pre-1.0 API movement**  \n   Deep Agents is still pre-1.0; pin and test upgrades carefully.  \n   Source: https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/issues/4219\n\n2. **Doc/reference asymmetry**  \n   Some exact function details are clearer in the reference and issue-linked source https://reference.langchain.com/python/deepagents/graph/create_deep_agent\n\n3. **Shell and local filesystem risk**  \n   `LocalShellBackend` and broad filesystem access materially increase risk.  \n   Source: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/backends\n\n4. **Citation quality depends on tool design**  \n   Deep Agents provides the harness, but your source quality, URL tracking, and citation formatting will still depend on the search/fetch tools you expose.\n\n---\n\n## Appendix: recommended starter skeleton\n\n```python\nfrom deepagents import create_deep_agent\nfrom search_tool(query: str) -> ...\n# fetch_url_tool(url: str) -> ...\n\nresearcher = SubAgent(\n    name=\"researcher\",\n    description=\"Collect relevant sources and summarize them with URLs\",\n https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model\n\n---\n\n## 2) What to optimize for when selecting a model\n\nOpenAI\u2019s docs split the landscape into:\n- **GPT models**: faster, generally cheaper, better for well-defined execution tasks\n- **Reasoning models / reasoning-capable workflows**: better for ambiguity, planning, multistep decisions, and high-stakes accuracy  \nSource: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning-best-practices\n\nIn practice for engineering:\n- Use **`gpt-5.5` / `gpt-5.4`** for complex coding agents, tool-heavy workflows, planning, and customer-facing assistant quality.\n- Use **`gpt-5.4-mini`** as the default candidate for high-volume apps with real quality requirements.\n- Use **`gpt-5.4-nano`** or **`gpt-5-nano`** for classification, extraction, routing, and other simple tasks at scale.\n- Use **`o3`** when accuracy on difficult reasoning is materially more important than spend.\n- Use **`o4-mini`** when you specifically want a cheaper reasoning model, though OpenAI marks it deprecated and says it was succeeded by GPT-5 mini.  \nSources: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/all , Instead, higher reasoning effort increases internal reasoning-token use and usually increases latency and total token consumption. OpenAI explicitly says GPT-5.5 is more efficient and can achieve strong results with fewer reasoning tokens than prior models at the same reasoning effort.  \nSources: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model , https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning\n\n### Practical guidance\n- Start evals with **`low`** for agentic tasks unless quality is clearly insufficient.\n- Move to **`medium`** for balanced production quality if `low` underperforms.\n- Use **`high`** only for hard coding/planning/legal/financial-style reasoning.\n- Use **`xhigh`** only for asynchronous expert tasks or benchmark-grade workloads.\n- Use **`none`** only for ultra-low-latency, deterministic tasks.  \nSource: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model\n\n---\n\n## 6) Model-by-model selection guidance\n\n### `gpt-5.5`\nBest when your team wants the highest current general capability without moving all the way to Pro pricing. long-context doubles input and raises output to $45.  \nSources: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing , https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model\n\n**Use for**\n- high-value engineering copilots\n- production agent orchestration\n- tool-heavy back-office automation\n- premium customer support assistants\n\n**Avoid when**\n- workload is simple or high-volume workflows where cost is secondary\n\n**Avoid when**\n- any near-real-time or broad deployment use case lacks a hard ROI case\n\n---\n\n### `gpt-5.4`\nThis is the main \u201cquality at lower price than The docs/blog state that `proxy.ts` runs on the **Node.js runtime**.  \nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#proxyts-formerly-middlewarets  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/proxy  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy\n\n**Required migration:**\n- rename `middleware.ts` \u2192 `proxy.ts`\n- rename the exported function to `proxy`\n\nExample:\n```ts\nexport default function proxy(request: NextRequest) {\n  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))\n}\n```\n\nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#proxyts-formerly-middlewarets\n\nNote: `middleware.ts` is still available for Edge runtime use cases, but it is deprecated and will be removed later.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#proxyts-formerly-middlewarets\n\n## 4.2 `next lint` command was removed\n`next lint` is removed in Next 16, and `next build` no longer runs linting. Next recommends using ESLint directly or Biome. A codemod is provided:\n\n```bash\nnpx @next/codemod@canary next-lint-to-eslint-cli .\n```\n\nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#removals\n\n**Action:**\n- remove `next lint` from `package.json` scripts and CI\n- replace with `eslint .` or your preferred direct CLI\n- verify CI still enforces linting explicitly\n\n## 4.3 Turbopack config moved out of `experimental`\nIf your config still uses `experimental.turbopack`, move it to top-level `turbopack`.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#removals\n\nBefore:\n```ts\nexperimental: {\n  turbopack: { ... }\n}\n```\n\nAfter:\n```ts\nturbopack: { ... }\n```\n\n## 4.4 `experimental.dynamicIO` became `cacheComponents`\nNext 16 removes `experimental.dynamicIO` and replaces it with top-level **`cacheComponents`**. It also removes `experimental.ppr` and `export const experimental_ppr`.  \nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#removals  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#cache-components\n\nBefore:\n```ts\nexperimental: {\n  dynamicIO: true,\n  ppr: true\n}\n```\n\nAfter:\n```ts\nconst nextConfig = {\n  cacheComponents: true,\n}\n```\n\nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#cache-components\n\n## 4.5 `revalidateTag()` signature changed\nIn Next 16, **`revalidateTag()` now requires a second argument** to define stale-while-revalidate behavior.\n\nBefore:\n```ts\nrevalidateTag('blog-posts')\n```\n\nAfter:\n```ts\nrevalidateTag('blog-posts', 'max')\n```\n\nOther valid forms:\n```ts\nrevalidateTag('news-feed', 'hours')\nrevalidateTag('analytics', 'days')\nrevalidateTag('products', { expire: 3600 })\n```\n\nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#revalidatetag-updated\n\n### New APIs: `updateTag()` and `refresh()`\nNext 16 adds:\n- **`updateTag()`**: Server Actions-only, for read-your-writes semantics\n- **`refresh()`**: Server Actions-only, refreshes uncached data only  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#improved-caching-apis\n\nUse `updateTag()` when a user should see their write immediately:\n```ts\n'use server'\nimport { updateTag } from 'next/cache'\n```\n\nUse `refresh()` for uncached UI refreshes after an action:\n```ts\n'use server'\nimport { refresh } from 'next/cache'\n```\n\nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#updatetag-new\n\n## 4.6 Parallel route slots now require `default.js`\nThis is an easy production-breaker. In Next 16, **all parallel route slots require an explicit `default.js` file** or builds fail. To preserve previous behavior, add a `default.js` that either:\n- returns `null`, or\n- calls `notFound()`  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#behavior-changes\n\n**Action:** scan `@slot` directories and ensure every slot has `default.js` / `default.tsx`.\n\n## 4.7 Metadata image route params are async\nStarting with Next 16, image-generating functions receive async route data:\n- `params` is a promise\n- `id` from `generateImageMetadata` is `Promise<string>`  \nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#removals  \n- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\nIf you have dynamic OG image routes, update them.\n\n---\n\n## 5) New build tooling defaults and what they mean in production\n\n## 5.1 Turbopack is the default bundler\nNext.js 16 made **Turbopack stable for development and production builds**, and the **default bundler** for all apps.  \nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#turbopack-stable  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#behavior-changes\n\n### Immediate implication\nIf your production app uses a custom `webpack` config, this is the highest-risk migration area.\n\nThe official version 16 upgrade guide states:\n\n> If your project has a custom `webpack` configuration and you run `next build` (which now uses Turbopack by default), the build will fail to prevent misconfiguration issues.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n### Short-term safe path\nIf you need time to migrate custom bundler behavior, explicitly opt out:\n\n```bash\nnext dev --webpack\nnext build --webpack\n```\n\nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#turbopack-stable\n\n### Recommended approach\n1. **Inventory your `webpack(config)` usage in `next.config.*`**\n2. Categorize each customization:\n   - aliases\n   - loaders\n   - asset handling\n   - plugin injection\n   - DefinePlugin/env usage\n   - source maps / SRI / externals\n3. Check whether an equivalent exists in:\n   - top-level `turbopack`\n   - supported Turbopack options\n   - modern built-in Next config\n4. Keep webpack temporarily only where parity is missing\n\n## 5.2 Babel config behavior changed under Turbopack\nIn Next 16, if a Babel config is found, Turbopack now **automatically enables Babel** instead of exiting with a hard error.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#behavior-changes\n\nThis reduces migration friction, but it also means old Babel configs may silently participate in builds. Audit `.babelrc` / `babel.config.*` if present.\n\n## 5.3 Turbopack file-system caching\nThe docs say Turbopack FileSystem Cache:\n- is **stable for development**\n- is **experimental for production builds**\n- stores/restores data in `.next`\n- was enabled by default for development in **v16.1.0**  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackFileSystemCache\n\nConfig:\n```ts\nconst nextConfig = {\n  experimental: {\n    turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev: true,\n    turbopackFileSystemCacheForBuild: true,\n  },\n}\n```\n\nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackFileSystemCache\n\n**Recommendation:**  \n- Accept the dev default.\n- Treat build cache in CI as an optimization to benchmark, not a migration prerequisite.\n- Make sure `.next` caching does not create stale artifact issues in your pipeline.\n\n## 5.4 Separate output directories and lockfiles\nNext 16 changed:\n- `next dev` and `next build` use separate output directories\n- a lockfile mechanism prevents multiple dev/build instances on the same project  \nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#behavior-changes  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-2-ai\n\nThis is mostly beneficial, but if you have custom scripts watching `.next` internals or running parallel build/dev processes in unusual ways, verify them.\n\n## 5.5 New `next upgrade` command exists only on 16.1+\nOfficial docs: versions before **16.1.0** do not support `next upgrade`.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/upgrading\n\nThat matters mainly for your future upgrades after landing on 16.2.x.\n\n---\n\n## 6) `next/image` changes that can affect production output\n\nNext 16 changed multiple image defaults. These can affect cache behavior, generated URLs, and quality expectations.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#behavior-changes\n\n## 6.1 `images.minimumCacheTTL`\nDefault changed from **60 seconds** to **4 hours (14400 seconds)**.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#behavior-changes\n\n**Impact:** slower refresh of upstream image changes if they lack cache headers, but lower revalidation cost.\n\n## 6.2 `images.imageSizes`\nDefault set no longer includes `16`.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#behavior-changes\n\n**Impact:** possible small changes in generated `srcset` variants.\n\n## 6.3 `images.qualities`\nDefault changed from `[1..100]` to **`[75]`**, and the `quality` prop is coerced to the nearest allowed value.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#behavior-changes\n\n**Impact:** if your app depended on arbitrary quality values, rendered output may differ unless you explicitly configure `images.qualities`.\n\n## 6.4 Redirect and local-IP restrictions\n- `images.maximumRedirects` now defaults to **3**\n- `images.dangerouslyAllowLocalIP` is now blocked by default unless explicitly enabled for private-network use  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#behavior-changes\n\n**Impact:** internal/private image optimization setups may break unless configured intentionally.\n\n## 6.5 Local src with query strings now requires `images.localPatterns`\nNext 16 now requires `images.localPatterns` when using local `src` values with query strings, to prevent enumeration attacks.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#removals\n\n## 6.6 `images.domains` deprecated\nUse **`images.remotePatterns`** instead.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#deprecations\n\n**Action checklist for images**\n- compare generated image URLs before/after\n- test signed or query-string-based local image paths\n- explicitly define `images.qualities` if you need more than 75\n- validate any private-network image loaders\n- prefer `remotePatterns` over `domains`\n\n---\n\n## 7) ESLint and repo tooling changes\n\nNext 16 removed the `next lint` wrapper and changed `@next/eslint-plugin-next` defaults to **ESLint Flat Config**.  \nSources:  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#removals  \n- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#behavior-changes\n\n**Action:**\n- migrate scripts from `next lint` to `eslint`\n- verify your config format (`eslint.config.js` / `eslint.config.mjs`) if you are standardizing on flat config\n- confirm CI still lints, because `next build` no Turbopack is the default bundler for dev and build\n\nStarting in Next.js 16:\n- `next dev` uses **Turbopack** by default\n- `next build` also uses **Turbopack** by default\n\nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\nThe 16 release post also positions Turbopack as stable and default across apps.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16\n\n### Production }\n```\nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/webpack\n\nThen decide:\n1. **Remove obsolete webpack customization** if it is no longer needed\n2. **Port behavior to }\n}\n```\n\nAfter:\n```ts\nturbopack: {\n  // ...\n}\n```\nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopack\n\n---\n\n## 4.2 Async Request APIs: synchronous access must be removed\n\nNext 15 introduced Async Request APIs with temporary sync compatibility. Next 16 removes that comfort layer in practice. The 16 guide explicitly calls this a breaking change.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\nAffected APIs include:\n- `params`\n- `searchParams`\n- `cookies()`\n- `headers()`\n- `draftMode()`\n\nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n### What this means\nCode like this must change:\n\nBefore:\n```ts\nexport default function Page({ params }) {\n  const slug = params.slug\n  return <div>{slug}</div>\n}\n```\n\nAfter:\n```ts\nexport default async function Page({\n  params,\n}: {\n  params: Promise<{ slug: string }>\n}) {\n  const { slug } = await params\n  return <div>{slug}</div>\n}\n```\n\nFor client components, use React\u2019s `use()` where applicable. The version 15 guide already documented this pattern; by 16 you should no longer rely on sync access.  \nSources: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-15, https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n### Also affected: image generation APIs\nThe 16 upgrade guide says image-generating functions now receive `params` and `id` as **promises**.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\n---\n\n## 4.3 Middleware is renamed to Proxy\n\nNext.js is renaming the `middleware` file convention to `proxy` to clarify that it sits at the network boundary, not as generic app middleware.  \nSources: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/middleware-to-proxy, https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy\n\n### Required changes\nRename:\n- `middleware.ts` \u2192 `proxy.ts`\n- exported function `middleware` \u2192 `proxy`\n\nOfficial codemod:\n```bash\nnpx @next/codemod@latest middleware-to-proxy .\n```\nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/middleware-to-proxy\n\n### Notes for teams using middleware heavily\nThe `proxy` docs also note:\n- place `proxy.ts` at project root or `src/`\n- use `matcher` in exported `config`\n- `runtime` route-segment config is **not available in Proxy files**\n\nSources: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy, https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/proxy\n\n---\n\n## 4.4 `next lint` is removed\n\nNext 15.5 announced:\n- `next lint` is deprecated in 15.5\n- it will be removed in 16\n\nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-15-5\n\n### Required changes\nIf CI currently runs:\n```bash\nnext lint\n```\nreplace it with direct ESLint invocation, e.g.:\n```bash\neslint .\n```\nor your existing workspace-specific script.\n\nAlso review whether `eslint-config-next` remains pinned compatibly with the new Next version.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/upgrading\n\n---\n\n## 4.5 AMP support is removed\n\nNext 15.5 explicitly warned:\n- **AMP support will be removed in Next.js 16**\n\nSource: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-15-5\n\n### Required changes\nSearch for:\n- `amp: true`\n- hybrid AMP pages\n- AMP-specific validation/build steps\n\nRemove or replace them before the major upgrade.\n\n---\n\n## 4.6 Image configuration got stricter\n\nThe 16 upgrade guide and current error docs indicate tighter image configuration.\n\n### `images.qualities`\nCurrent error docs state that `next/image` quality values must be declared in `images.qualities`.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/next-image-unconfigured-qualities\n\nIf your app uses:\n```tsx\n<Image src=\"...\" quality={85} />\n```\nmake sure `next.config.*` contains:\n```ts\nimages: {\n  qualities: [75, 85]\n}\n```\n\n### `images.localPatterns`\nCurrent docs/errors also show local image paths can be restricted by `images.localPatterns`, and using a non-allowed local path can fail.  \nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/next-image-unconfigured-localpatterns\n\n### What to audit\n- any custom `quality` values on `<Image />`\n- internal image paths outside your allowed conventions\n- custom image loaders and image CDN behavior under Turbopack\n\nSources: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/images, https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/next-image-unconfigured-qualities, https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/next-image-unconfigured-localpatterns\n\n---\n\n## 4.7 Caching API changes\n\nNext.js 16 introduced updated caching APIs:\n\n- `updateTag()`\n- refined `revalidateTag()`\n- `cacheLife`\n- `cacheComponents`\n\nSources: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16, https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents\n\n### Breaking bit\nThe upgrade guide states:\n- `revalidateTag()` now requires a **second argument** specifying a `cacheLife` profile\n- single-argument form is deprecated\n\nSource: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16\n\nBefore:\n```ts\nrevalidateTag('posts')\n```\n\nAfter:\n```ts\nrevalidateTag('posts', 'max')\n```\nor a custom profile defined via `cacheLife`.  \nSources: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16, https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag\n\n### If you use route-segment cache config\nCurrent docs say that when https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components\n\nThis is not necessarily a mandatory migration on day 1, but teams using aggressive App Router caching should review it closely.\n\n---\n\n## 4.8 `devIndicators` options changed\n\nThe version 16 upgrade guide says some `devIndicators` options were removed and that you should use top-level `cacheComponents` rather than         "report": "# Mission summary: NASA\u2019s Artemis II\n\n## Bottom line\n\nNASA\u2019s Artemis II mission launched on **April 1, 2026, at 6:35 p.m. EDT** from **Launch Complex 39B at Kennedy Space Center, Florida**, and splashed down in the **Pacific Ocean off San Diego on April 10, 2026**. NASA lists the mission duration as **9 days, 1 hour, 32 minutes**. It was the **first crewed Artemis mission**, the **first crewed flight of the Space Launch System (SLS) and Orion**, and **humanity\u2019s first crewed mission around the Moon in more than 50 years**.  \nSources: NASA mission page: https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-ii ; NASA launch-day updates: https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/04/01/live-artemis-ii-launch-day-updates ; NASA post-flight assessment: https://www.nasa.gov/missions/nasa-on-track-for-future-missions-with-initial-artemis-ii-assessments\n\n## Launch and return\n\nArtemis II lifted off aboard NASA\u2019s **SLS rocket** with the **Orion spacecraft** on top on **April 1, 2026**. After a roughly 10-day free-return lunar mission, Orion re-entered Earth\u2019s atmosphere and splashed down on **April 10, 2026**. NASA says Orion landed **2.9 miles from the targeted landing site**, and that entry interface velocity was **within 1 mph of predictions**.  \nSources: https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-ii ; https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/missions/2026/04/01/live-artemis-ii-launch-day-updates ; https://www.nasa.gov/missions/nasa-on-track-for-future-missions-with-initial-artemis-ii-assessments\n\n## Crew and the historic firsts\n\nThe Artemis II crew was:\n\n- **Reid Wiseman** \u2014 Commander  \n- **Victor Glover** \u2014 Pilot  \n- **Christina Koch** \u2014 Mission Specialist  \n- **Jeremy Hansen** (Canadian Space Agency) \u2014 Mission Specialist  \nSources: NASA crew announcement: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-names-astronauts-to-next-moon-mission-first-crew-under-artemis ; NASA crew page: https://www.nasa.gov/feature/our-artemis-crew ; CSA: https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/missions/artemis-ii\n\nThe crew represented several widely noted milestones:\n\n- **Christina Koch** became the **first woman on a lunar mission**.  \n- **Victor Glover** became the **first person of color on a lunar mission**.  \n- **Jeremy Hansen** became the **first Canadian to fly around the Moon**.  \nSources: NASA crew announcement: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-names-astronauts-to-next-moon-mission-first-crew-under-artemis ; NASA press kit: https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/artemis-ii-press-kit.pdf ; CSA Artemis II page: https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/missions/artemis-ii\n\nNASA also emphasized that Artemis II was the first time humans traveled to the Moon\u2019s vicinity since **Apollo 17 in 1972**.  \nSources: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-names-astronauts-to-next-moon-mission-first-crew-under-artemis ; https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-ii\n\n## What the mission accomplished\n\nArtemis II was a **test flight** designed to prove the systems needed for later lunar-surface missions. NASA\u2019s preflight priorities were to demonstrate crewed deep-space operations, validate Orion\u2019s life-support and other spacecraft systems, test operations from launch through recovery, and gather flight hardware and data for future Artemis missions.  \nSource: NASA Artemis II press kit: https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/artemis-ii-press-kit.pdf\n\nSpecifically, NASA says the mission accomplished these major objectives:\n\n- **First crewed test of Orion and SLS in deep space.** Artemis II was the first mission to fly astronauts aboard NASA\u2019s new Moon rocket and deep-space capsule.  \n  Source: https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-ii\n\n- **Validation of Orion\u2019s life-support systems.** NASA defined proving life support in deep space as a core purpose of the mission, and after splashdown said engineers began detailed post-flight analysis with early performance looking strong.  \n  Sources: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-names-astronauts-to-next-moon-mission-first-crew-under-artemis ; https://www.nasa.gov/missions/nasa-on-track-for-future-missions-with-initial-artemis-ii-assessments\n\n- **Manual piloting and proximity operations.** Early in flight, the crew manually flew Orion relative to the interim cryogenic propulsion stage in a proximity-operations demonstration meant to inform future rendezvous and docking work needed on later Artemis missions.  \n  Source: https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/artemis-ii-press-kit.pdf\n\n- **Communications and navigation tests beyond low Earth orbit.** NASA used Artemis II to check Orion\u2019s comms and       "baseline": {
        "report": "# Leading approaches to carbon capture and storage: cost and scalability\n\n## Executive summary\n\nThe leading approaches to carbon capture and storage (CCS) fall into two broad groups:\n\n1. **Point-source capture** from industrial plants and power stations, followed by transport and **geological storage**.\n2. **Carbon-removal variants** that pair storage with capture from the air or biomass, chiefly **direct air capture with storage (DACCS)** and **bioenergy with CCS (BECCS)**.\n\nAcross these, the most mature and scalable near-term options are **point-source capture on high-purity industrial streams** and **capture in hard-to-abate industries** such as cement, chemicals, and some hydrogen production. These are generally cheaper and easier to scale than capturing CO2 from dilute streams such as ambient air. The International Energy Agency (IEA) reports that capture costs vary from roughly **USD 15-25/tCO2** for high-concentration streams like natural gas processing and ethanol, to **USD 40-120/tCO2** for dilute streams such as cement and power generation. Direct air capture is the most expensive category: the IEA estimates **USD 125-335/tCO2** for a large plant built today, with potential to fall below **USD 100/tCO2** in favorable cases over time.  \nSources:  \n- IEA, *Is carbon capture too expensive?* https://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive  \n- IEA, *Direct Air Capture 2022* https://www.iea.org/reports/direct-air-capture-2022\n\nScalability is constrained less by capture chemistry alone than by the full value chain: **transport infrastructure, storage site development, permitting, and financing**. The IEA says there was **just over 50 MtCO2/year** of capture and storage capacity in operation as of early 2025, while the current project pipeline could bring capacity to around **430 MtCO2/year by 2030**. That is rapid growth, but still far below the gigatonne-scale deployment envisioned in net-zero pathways.  \nSource: IEA CCUS overview / projects explorer pages https://www.iea.org/energy-system/carbon-capture-utilisation-and-storage and https://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/data-product/ccus-projects-database\n\nThe bottom line: **the leading practical CCS approaches today are geological storage paired with point-source capture at concentrated or unavoidable industrial emissions; DACCS is strategically important for long-term carbon removal but is currently the costliest and hardest to scale.**\n\n---\n\n## 1) What CCS includes\n\nCCS usually means three linked steps:\n\n- **Capture** of CO2 from an industrial process, power plant, or the air\n- **Transport** of compressed CO2, usually by pipeline, sometimes ship\n- **Storage** in deep geological formations such as saline aquifers or depleted oil and gas fields\n\nThe IEA notes that CCS can decarbonize industry and power and also enable **technology-based carbon removal** through BECCS and DACCS.  \nSource: IEA, *CO2 Storage Resources and their Development*  \nhttps://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/42d294af-ce07-44c7-9c96-166f855088e8/CO2storageresourcesandtheirdevelopment-AnIEACCUSHandbook.pdf\n\n---\n\n## 2) The leading capture approaches\n\n### A. Post-combustion capture\nThis removes CO2 from flue gas after fuel is burned, usually with solvents such as amines.\n\n**Why it leads**\n- It can be retrofitted to existing plants.\n- It is the most familiar option for power plants and many industrial sources.\n\n**Cost**\nIEA gives a broad range of **USD 40-120/tCO2** for dilute streams such as cement and power generation.  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive\n\n**Scalability**\n- Good for existing assets, especially where emissions are hard to eliminate otherwise.\n- But costs rise when CO2 concentration is low, and energy use is significant.\n- Transport and storage access are critical.\n\n### B. Pre-combustion capture\nThis captures CO2 before combustion, typically after converting fuel into syngas or hydrogen-rich gas.\n\n**Why it matters**\n- Fits hydrogen, ammonia, and gasification-based systems.\n- Can work well where CO2 is already separated as part of process design.\n\n**Cost**\nCosts vary by stream, but hydrogen production from steam methane reforming often spans the lower to upper end depending on whether capture is from a concentrated process stream or a more dilute furnace stream. The IEA notes that capture costs generally fall when the CO2 stream is more concentrated.  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive\n\n**Scalability**\n- Strong in hydrogen and chemicals.\n- Less useful as a retrofit for the existing power fleet than post-combustion.\n\n### C. Oxy-fuel combustion\nFuel is burned in oxygen rather than air, yielding an exhaust gas with a much higher CO2 concentration.\n\n**Why it matters**\n- It simplifies downstream separation in some designs.\n\n**Cost/scalability**\n- Promising, but less commercially established at scale than solvent-based post-combustion.\n- Requires oxygen production infrastructure, which adds cost and complexity.  \nReference overview: Harvard Belfer, *Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage: Technologies and Costs in the U.S. Context*  \nhttps://www.belfercenter.org/publication/carbon-capture-utilization-and-storage-technologies-and-costs-us-context\n\n### D. Capture from high-purity industrial streams\nThis includes natural gas processing, ethanol, ammonia/fertilizer, and some hydrogen streams where CO2 is already relatively concentrated.\n\n**Why it leads**\n- Usually the cheapest CCS applications.\n- Already among the most commercially deployed.\n\n**Cost**\nIEA estimates **USD 15-25/tCO2** for \u201cpure\u201d or highly concentrated streams such as ethanol and natural gas processing.  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive\n\n**Scalability**\n- Very strong near-term scalability where these industries exist.\n- Limitation: the total global emissions available in such streams is smaller than in sectors like power, steel, and cement.\n\n### E. Direct air capture with storage (DACCS)\nDAC captures CO2 directly from ambient air using solid sorbents or liquid solvents, then stores it geologically.\n\n**Why it matters**\n- It removes CO2 already in the atmosphere.\n- Useful for balancing residual emissions and addressing legacy emissions.\n\n**Cost**\nIEA estimates **USD 125-335/tCO2** for a large-scale plant built today and says costs could fall to **under USD 100/tCO2** in favorable conditions with deployment and innovation.  \nhttps://www.iea.org/reports/direct-air-capture-2022\n\nA more skeptical recent Belfer assessment estimates early full-scale DACCS projects at roughly **USD 400-1000 per net tonne removed**, with costs maybe falling to **USD 200-400/tCO2** later if scale-up succeeds.  \nhttps://www.belfercenter.org/publication/prospects-direct-air-carbon-capture-and-storage-costs-scale-and-funding\n\n**Scalability**\n- Theoretically location-flexible if low-carbon energy and storage are available.\n- Practically constrained by huge energy demand and capital needs.\n- IEA says DAC in its net-zero scenario would need **32 large plants of 1 MtCO2/year to be built every year through 2050**.  \nhttps://www.iea.org/reports/direct-air-capture-2022\n\n### F. Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS)\nBECCS captures CO2 from biomass-based energy or industrial processes and stores it, creating net-negative emissions if the biomass is sustainably sourced.\n\n**Why it matters**\n- Like DACCS, it can remove CO2 from the atmosphere.\n- Often cheaper than DACCS because biomass growth already concentrated the carbon.\n\n**Scalability**\n- Constrained by biomass availability, land use, biodiversity, and supply chains.\n- More resource-limited than DACCS.  \nBelfer overview comparing DACCS and BECCS:  \nhttps://www.belfercenter.org/publication/prospects-direct-air-carbon-capture-and-storage-costs-scale-and-funding\n\n---\n\n## 3) Storage approaches\n\n### A. Deep saline aquifers\nThese are porous rock formations filled with salty water.\n\n**Why they lead**\n- They represent the largest long-term storage resource.\n- The IEA handbook says around **98% of estimated global storage resources** are in saline aquifers.  \nhttps://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/42d294af-ce07-44c7-9c96-166f855088e8/CO2storageresourcesandtheirdevelopment-AnIEACCUSHandbook.pdf\n\n**Scalability**\n- Best long-run storage option.\n- But many resources remain under-characterized.\n- Site development can take **3 to 10 years**.\n\n### B. Depleted oil and gas fields\nThese are better characterized because of prior drilling and production.\n\n**Why they matter**\n- Existing subsurface data and infrastructure can reduce development risk.\n\n**Scalability**\n- Good early deployment option.\n- Total capacity is smaller than saline aquifers.\n\n### C. Mineralization and basalt storage\nCO2 reacts with minerals to form stable carbonates.\n\n**Why it matters**\n- High permanence.\n\n**Scalability**\n- Technically promising but less mature globally than conventional sedimentary storage.  \nIEA storage handbook overview: same handbook link above.\n\n---\n\n## 4) Cost comparison across leading approaches\n\n### Capture cost ranges\n\n| Approach | Typical cost signal | Main reason |\n|---|---:|---|\n| High-purity industrial streams | **USD 15-25/tCO2** | CO2 already concentrated |\n| Cement / power / other dilute flue gas | **USD 40-120/tCO2** | Separation is harder and more energy-intensive |\n| DAC (large plant built today) | **USD 125-335/tCO2** | CO2 in air is extremely dilute |\n| DACCS early full-scale projects (Belfer estimate) | **USD 400-1000/net tCO2** | Early-stage technology, full-system costs |\n\nSources:  \n- IEA, *Is carbon capture too expensive?* https://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive  \n- IEA, *Direct Air Capture 2022* https://www.iea.org/reports/direct-air-capture-2022  \n- Belfer, *Prospects for Direct Air Carbon Capture and Storage* https://www.belfercenter.org/publication/prospects-direct-air-carbon-capture-and-storage-costs-scale-and-funding\n\n### Transport and storage cost ranges\n\nThese vary by distance, volume, and geology.\n\n- IEA reports **USD 2-14/tCO2** for **onshore pipeline transport** in the United States and says more than half of onshore storage capacity may be available below **USD 10/tCO2**.  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive\n- A literature review in *International Journal of Greenhouse Gas Control* found onshore pipeline transport and storage costs ranging roughly **USD 4-45/tCO2** depending on assumptions.  \nhttps://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1750583621001195\n- Harvard Belfer summarizes an illustrative U.S. assumption set of about **USD 15/tCO2** for pipeline transport and **USD 11/tCO2** for sequestration in some comparisons.  \nhttps://www.belfercenter.org/publication/carbon-capture-utilization-and-storage-technologies-and-costs-us-context\n\n### Full-system implication\nFor many projects, **capture is the dominant cost**, but storage and transport are decisive for bankability. A cheap capture source can still fail commercially if it lacks nearby permitted storage and transport.\n\n---\n\n## 5) Scalability comparison\n\n### Most scalable now: high-purity industrial CCS\n**Best suited for near-term rollout**\n- Natural gas processing\n- Ethanol\n- Ammonia/fertilizer\n- Some hydrogen and chemicals\n\n**Why**\n- Lowest capture costs\n- Mature engineering\n- Often already integrated into industrial operations\n\n**Constraint**\n- Limited total abatement potential compared with broader industrial and power emissions.\n\n### Most important for hard-to-abate sectors: cement, chemicals, some steel, some hydrogen\nThe IEA says CCS is effectively the **only scalable option** for deep emissions cuts in cement because much of cement CO2 comes from calcination, not fuel use.  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive\n\n**Why this matters**\n- These sectors are hard to electrify fully.\n- CCS may be the least-cost deep-abatement option even when more expensive than high-purity capture.\n\n### More difficult to scale in power\nPower-sector CCS is technically proven, but economics are tougher:\n- capture costs are higher on dilute flue gas\n- renewables have become very cheap\n- financing risks are high\n\nStill, the IEA argues CCS can help provide dispatchable low-emissions power and retrofit relatively young fossil assets in some systems.  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive\n\n### Long-term strategic but hardest now: DACCS\nDACCS is highly scalable in theory because the feedstock is the atmosphere, not a specific smokestack. But today it is limited by:\n- cost\n- low-carbon energy needs\n- capital intensity\n- storage development pace\n\nIEA says DAC was operating at only about **0.01 MtCO2/year** in 2022, versus **980 MtCO2/year** in its 2050 net-zero pathway.  \nhttps://www.iea.org/reports/direct-air-capture-2022\n\n---\n\n## 6) Infrastructure and storage bottlenecks\n\nThe biggest scalability constraint on CCS is often not capture chemistry but **system build-out**.\n\n### Storage site development\nIEA says:\n- there were **seven dedicated commercial-scale storage sites** injecting around **10 MtCO2/year** as of mid-2022\n- more than **130 storage sites** were in development in 20 countries\n- dedicated injection capacity could exceed **110 Mt/year by 2030** from around 10 Mt at the time of the report  \nhttps://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/42d294af-ce07-44c7-9c96-166f855088e8/CO2storageresourcesandtheirdevelopment-AnIEACCUSHandbook.pdf\n\n### Current overall CCS scale\nAs of early 2025, the IEA said there was **just over 50 MtCO2/year** of capture and storage capacity in operation, and the project pipeline pointed to around **430 MtCO2/year by 2030**.  \nhttps://www.iea.org/energy-system/carbon-capture-utilisation-and-storage\n\n### Permitting and liability\nStorage requires characterization, monitoring, and long-term stewardship. The U.S. uses **Class VI wells** for geologic sequestration under EPA\u2019s Underground Injection Control program.  \nEPA overview: https://www.epa.gov/uic/class-vi-wells-used-geologic-sequestration-carbon-dioxide\n\nThese regulatory requirements improve safety but slow deployment.\n\n---\n\n## 7) How the leading approaches compare\n\n### Best on cost\n1. **High-purity industrial capture**\n2. **Some industrial process capture**\n3. **Power-sector capture**\n4. **DACCS**\n\n### Best on near-term deployability\n1. **High-purity industrial capture + conventional geological storage**\n2. **Industrial clusters/hubs with shared transport and storage**\n3. **Selected cement, chemicals, and hydrogen projects**\n4. **DACCS and BECCS**\n\n### Best on long-run climate value\n1. **Industrial CCS** for unavoidable process emissions\n2. **DACCS and BECCS** for net-negative emissions\n3. **Large saline-aquifer storage hubs** as backbone infrastructure\n\n---\n\n## 8) Key judgment\n\nThe evidence points to a clear hierarchy:\n\n- **Cheapest and easiest to scale now:** CCS on high-concentration industrial CO2 streams.\n- **Most important for deep industrial decarbonization:** CCS in cement, chemicals, and some hydrogen/steel pathways.\n- **Most important for long-term carbon removal but currently most expensive:** DACCS, with BECCS also important where sustainable biomass is available.\n- **Critical enabler across all approaches:** development of transport networks and especially **geological storage**, above all saline aquifers.\n\nIn short, the leading approaches to CCS are point-source capture with geological storage, especially for concentrated and hard-to-abate industrial emissions; they are cheaper and more scalable today than direct air capture, while DACCS is the key long-run removal option but remains the costliest and least mature.",

        "report": "# Leading approaches to carbon capture and storage, and how they compare on cost and scalability\n\n## Executive summary\n\nThe leading carbon capture and storage (CCS) approaches fall into two broad groups:\n\n1. **Point-source CCS**: capturing CO2 from industrial plants or power plants before it reaches the atmosphere, then transporting and storing it underground.\n2. **Carbon dioxide removal with storage**: removing CO2 from the atmosphere and storing it, mainly through **bioenergy with CCS (BECCS)** and **direct air capture with storage (DACCS)**.\n\nWithin point-source CCS, the main capture approaches are **post-combustion**, **pre-combustion**, and **oxy-fuel combustion**. Of these, **post-combustion capture** is the most flexible and currently the most widely applicable for retrofits, especially in cement, steel, refining, and gas- or coal-fired plants. **Pre-combustion capture** is attractive where CO2 is already separated as part of producing hydrogen, ammonia, natural gas processing, or gasification-based systems. **Oxy-fuel combustion** can lower separation costs in some new-build industrial settings, especially cement, but is less mature at large commercial scale than solvent-based post-combustion systems. Sources: IEA, IPCC, Global CCS Institute, IEAGHG.  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive  \nhttps://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/srccs_wholereport-1.pdf  \nhttps://www.globalccsinstitute.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Advancements-in-CCS-Technologies-and-Costs-Report-2.pdf  \nhttps://ieaghg.org/publications/co2-capture-in-the-cement-industry\n\nOn cost, the most important fact is that **CO2 concentration matters more than labels like \u201cpost-\u201d or \u201cpre-combustion.\u201d** The IEA reports capture costs from about **USD 15-25/tCO2** for high-purity streams such as natural gas processing or ethanol fermentation, versus roughly **USD 40-120/tCO2** for dilute streams such as cement or power generation. DACCS is much costlier today, with IEA estimates around **USD 600-1,000/tCO2** in current deployments. Sources:  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/unlocking-the-potential-of-direct-air-capture-is-scaling-up-through-carbon-markets-possible\n\nOn scalability, **geological storage is not the main theoretical bottleneck**: the IPCC and IEA both describe very large storage potential in deep saline aquifers and depleted oil and gas reservoirs. The main constraints are **project economics, policy support, permitting, transport networks, power/heat supply, and pace of infrastructure buildout**. CCS deployment is growing but still small relative to emissions: the Global CCS Institute reported **65 operating facilities**, **42 projects in construction**, and **450 Mtpa cumulative capture capacity in the pipeline** in 2024; IEA tracking likewise shows rapid growth in announced projects. Sources:  \nhttps://www.globalccsinstitute.com/installed-ccs-capacity-on-track-to-double-as-governments-and-industry-collaborate-to-advance-projects  \nhttps://www.env.go.jp/content/000305201.pdf  \nhttps://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/data-tools/ccus-projects-explorer\n\nThe strongest conclusion is:\n\n- **Cheapest and most scalable near-term**: CCS on **high-purity industrial streams** and selected industrial clusters with shared transport/storage.\n- **Most strategically important for hard-to-abate industry**: **post-combustion and oxy-fuel CCS in cement, steel, and chemicals**, despite higher cost.\n- **Most important for net-negative emissions but least mature/costliest**: **BECCS and especially DACCS**.\n\n---\n\n## 1) What counts as the \u201cleading approaches\u201d to CCS?\n\n### A. Post-combustion capture\nPost-combustion systems remove CO2 from flue gas after fuel is burned, usually using solvents such as amines. This is the best-known retrofit option for existing plants because it can be added to conventional combustion systems without completely redesigning the core process. It is widely discussed for coal and gas power, cement, steel, refining, and waste-to-energy. Sources:  \nhttps://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/srccs_wholereport-1.pdf  \nhttps://www.globalccsinstitute.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Advancements-in-CCS-Technologies-and-Costs-Report-2.pdf  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive\n\n### B. Pre-combustion capture\nPre-combustion capture separates CO2 before combustion, usually after converting fuel into syngas or hydrogen-rich gas. It is especially relevant in **hydrogen production, ammonia, natural gas processing, and gasification-based systems**, where CO2 is already present at higher concentration and pressure, making capture easier. Sources:  \nhttps://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/srccs_wholereport-1.pdf  \nhttps://www.iea.org/reports/ccus-in-clean-energy-transitions/ccus-in-the-transition-to-net-zero-emissions\n\n### C. Oxy-fuel combustion\nOxy-fuel systems burn fuel in oxygen rather than air, producing an exhaust stream with much higher CO2 concentration and less nitrogen dilution. This can simplify CO2 separation, but the need for large air-separation units adds cost and complexity. IEAGHG notes oxy-combustion is particularly promising in cement, where it may offer lower-cost capture in new-build configurations, though further development is needed. Sources:  \nhttps://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/srccs_wholereport-1.pdf  \nhttps://ieaghg.org/publications/co2-capture-in-the-cement-industry\n\n### D. BECCS\nBECCS uses biomass for energy and captures the resulting CO2 for storage. Because the biomass originally absorbed CO2 from the atmosphere, storing those emissions can deliver **net-negative emissions**. The IPCC treats BECCS as one of the major engineered carbon dioxide removal options, but notes trade-offs involving land, biomass supply, biodiversity, and food systems. Sources:  \nhttps://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/outreach/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_Factsheet_CDR.pdf  \nhttps://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-12\n\n### E. DACCS\nDirect air capture with carbon storage removes CO2 directly from ambient air using solid sorbents or liquid solvents, then stores it geologically. Its major advantage is location flexibility and its ability to address diffuse or legacy emissions. Its major disadvantages are very high energy use and very high cost today. Sources:  \nhttps://www.iea.org/energy-system/carbon-capture-utilisation-and-storage/direct-air-capture  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/unlocking-the-potential-of-direct-air-capture-is-scaling-up-through-carbon-markets-possible  \nhttps://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/outreach/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_Factsheet_CDR.pdf\n\n---\n\n## 2) Where the cost differences come from\n\nThe IEA emphasizes that capture cost depends heavily on the **initial CO2 concentration and pressure** of the gas stream. High-purity streams are cheap because little separation is needed; dilute flue gases are expensive because separation is energy-intensive.  \nSource: https://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive\n\nOther major cost drivers include:\n\n- whether the project is a **retrofit** or new-build\n- plant scale and capacity factor\n- energy needed for solvent regeneration or oxygen production\n- distance to transport/storage infrastructure\n- storage geology and whether storage is onshore or offshore\n- financing, policy support, and clustering with other emitters\n\nSources:  \nhttps://www.globalccsinstitute.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Advancements-in-CCS-Technologies-and-Costs-Report-2.pdf  \nhttps://www.globalccsinstitute.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Cost-of-CO2-Storage-1225.pdf  \nhttps://www.netl.doe.gov/projects/files/CostofCapturingCO2fromIndustrialSources_071522.pdf\n\n---\n\n## 3) Cost comparison by approach\n\n## A. Point-source CCS on high-purity industrial streams: lowest-cost option\n\nThe IEA gives a range of about **USD 15-25/tCO2** for industrial processes producing relatively pure CO2 streams, such as **ethanol production** and **natural gas processing**. NETL similarly finds that industries with nearly pure CO2 streams can often capture CO2 mainly through compression, dehydration, and conditioning rather than full flue-gas separation. Sources:  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive  \nhttps://www.netl.doe.gov/projects/files/CostofCapturingCO2fromIndustrialSources_071522.pdf\n\n**Implication:** these are the best early candidates for scale because they combine lower cost, technical maturity, and often large single-site capture volumes.\n\n## B. Post-combustion capture on dilute streams: mid- to high-cost, but broadly applicable\n\nThe IEA puts capture costs for dilute streams such as **cement** and **power generation** at roughly **USD 40-120/tCO2**. NETL studies of power and industrial retrofits also show that solvent-based capture can work, but with significant capital cost and energy penalty. For example, updated NETL analysis cited by Carbon Herald reported **about USD 61/tCO2** capture cost for a 90% capture case on an F-class NGCC reference case, down from older estimates, though real project costs vary by site and assumptions. Sources:  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive  \nhttps://www.netl.doe.gov/projects/files/NETLsCarbonCaptureRetrofitDatabases_072523.pdf  \nhttps://carbonherald.com/netl-updates-key-report-for-carbon-capture-costs-and-performance\n\nFor cement specifically, IEAGHG notes post-combustion capture is likely **substantially more expensive** than at power plants because cement plants are smaller and may require additional flue-gas cleanup and steam generation.  \nSource: https://ieaghg.org/publications/co2-capture-in-the-cement-industry\n\n**Implication:** post-combustion is probably the most deployable general-purpose approach, but not the cheapest.\n\n## C. Pre-combustion capture: often cost-advantaged in hydrogen, ammonia, and gas processing\n\nPre-combustion capture is typically most competitive where the industrial process already produces a CO2-rich stream at pressure. This is why blue hydrogen, ammonia, gas processing, and some chemicals are frequent early CCS applications in IEA scenarios and project pipelines. Sources:  \nhttps://www.iea.org/reports/ccus-in-clean-energy-transitions/ccus-in-the-transition-to-net-zero-emissions  \nhttps://www.netl.doe.gov/projects/files/CostofCapturingCO2fromIndustrialSources_071522.pdf\n\n**Implication:** pre-combustion is not universally applicable, but where it fits, it can be among the most cost-effective CCS approaches.\n\n## D. Oxy-fuel capture: potentially attractive in cement and some new-build applications\n\nIEAGHG reports that **oxy-combustion may offer the lowest-cost capture solution for new-build cement plants**, though technical challenges remain and deployment is less mature than conventional solvent capture.  \nSource: https://ieaghg.org/publications/co2-capture-in-the-cement-industry\n\n**Implication:** oxy-fuel may become highly important in sectors with process emissions, especially cement, but today it is not yet the dominant commercial route.\n\n## E. BECCS: moderate-to-high cost, but can generate net-negative emissions\n\nThe IPCC AR6 WGIII CDR factsheet gives a **USD 15-400/tCO2** range for **BECCS**, with a central cited band often summarized as roughly **USD 100-200/tCO2** depending on feedstock, energy product, and system boundary. The wide range reflects major variation in biomass cost, plant design, and whether biogenic CO2 is relatively pure.  \nSource: https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/outreach/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_Factsheet_CDR.pdf\n\n**Implication:** BECCS can be strategically valuable because it removes atmospheric CO2, but it is constrained by sustainable biomass supply and land-use trade-offs.\n\n## F. DACCS: highest-cost today\n\nIEA states that DAC applications are currently hindered by costs of about **USD 600-1,000/tCO2**. An older IEA DAC report described broader scenario ranges and potential future declines, but current commercial costs remain far above those of point-source CCS. Sources:  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/unlocking-the-potential-of-direct-air-capture-is-scaling-up-through-carbon-markets-possible  \nhttps://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/9766b4da-a5e3-4d76-874d-ea286e333956/DirectAirCapture_Akeytechnologyfornetzero.pdf\n\n**Implication:** DACCS is the least cost-competitive near term, but it has unique long-run value because it is not limited to point sources.\n\n---\n\n## 4) Storage and transport costs\n\nCapture is usually the dominant cost, but transport and storage matter.\n\nThe Global CCS Institute\u2019s 2025 storage study finds that **storage can range from about USD 2-31/tCO2 under favorable conditions**, with costs varying by geology, onshore vs offshore location, reservoir quality, thickness, pressure behavior, and fracture pressure.  \nSource: https://www.globalccsinstitute.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Cost-of-CO2-Storage-1225.pdf\n\nThis means:\n- the cheapest CCS projects pair **low-cost capture** with **good nearby storage**\n- projects become much more expensive when they require new long-distance pipelines, offshore storage, or complex reservoir conditions\n\nA separate peer-reviewed study found onshore transport and storage costs varying roughly **USD 4-45/tCO2**, reinforcing that site conditions matter greatly.  \nSource: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1750583621001195\n\n---\n\n## 5) Scalability comparison\n\n## A. Point-source CCS on existing industrial clusters: highest near-term scalability\n\nThe most scalable near-term path is not a single capture technology but a **cluster model**:\n- capture from multiple industrial plants\n- shared pipeline or shipping network\n- shared geological storage hub\n\nThis lowers unit costs through economies of scale and helps solve the transport/storage \u201cchicken-and-egg\u201d problem. The IEA and Global CCS Institute both highlight hubs and networks as key to growth. Sources:  \nhttps://www.iea.org/energy-system/carbon-capture-utilisation-and-storage  \nhttps://www.globalccsinstitute.com/installed-ccs-capacity-on-track-to-double-as-governments-and-industry-collaborate-to-advance-projects\n\nAmong sectors, scalability is strongest in:\n- **natural gas processing**\n- **hydrogen/ammonia/chemicals**\n- **ethanol and some fermentation**\n- **cement and steel clusters** where storage access and policy support exist\n\n## B. Cement and other hard-to-abate industry: strategically scalable, but slower\n\nCCS is unusually important in **cement**, because a large share of cement emissions comes from limestone calcination and cannot be eliminated simply by switching fuels. The IEA says CCUS is the **only known technology** capable of delivering widespread deep emissions reductions in cement production.  \nSource: https://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive\n\nThis makes cement CCS highly important strategically, but scaling will be slower because these projects are costlier and need tailored integration.\n\n## C. BECCS: limited by biomass availability and sustainability\n\nBECCS can scale only as far as sustainable biomass systems allow. The IPCC flags risks of land competition, food system pressure, biodiversity impacts, and uncertain monitoring in some biomass pathways.  \nSource: https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/outreach/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_Factsheet_CDR.pdf\n\nSo while BECCS may become important, it is not infinitely scalable.\n\n## D. DACCS: theoretically flexible, practically constrained by energy and cost\n\nDACCS has a large theoretical role because it is not tied to smokestacks, but IEA and other assessments stress its enormous energy demand and high cost. IEAGHG notes that a 1 Gt/year DACCS scale would require very large quantities of low-carbon energy and storage capacity. Sources:  \nhttps://www.iea.org/energy-system/carbon-capture-utilisation-and-storage/direct-air-capture  \nhttps://ieaghg.org/publications/2025-05%20The%20Value%20of%20Direct%20Air%20Carbon%20Capture%20and%20Storage.pdf\n\nThis makes DACCS more of a long-term complement than a near-term mass-deployment solution.\n\n## E. Storage capacity itself appears large, but infrastructure is the bottleneck\n\nThe IPCC Special Report on CCS concluded that global geological storage potential is likely substantial, especially in **deep saline formations** and **depleted oil and gas fields**. The IEA\u2019s storage handbook likewise treats storage resources as large enough in principle, while emphasizing the need to characterize and develop them. Sources:  \nhttps://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/srccs_wholereport-1.pdf  \nhttps://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/42d294af-ce07-44c7-9c96-166f855088e8/CO2storageresourcesandtheirdevelopment-AnIEACCUSHandbook.pdf\n\nSo scalability is constrained less by theoretical geology than by:\n- site characterization\n- permitting\n- liability frameworks\n- pipelines and shipping\n- public acceptance\n- power and heat supply\n- investment certainty\n\n---\n\n## 6) Current market scale\n\nCCS is growing, but it is still far from climate-scale deployment.\n\nThe Global CCS Institute\u2019s 2024 reporting shows:\n- **65 facilities in operation**\n- **42 projects in construction**\n- **715 projects in the pipeline**\n- **450 Mtpa cumulative capture capacity** across the pipeline\n\nSources:  \nhttps://www.env.go.jp/content/000305201.pdf  \nhttps://www.globalccsinstitute.com/installed-ccs-capacity-on-track-to-double-as-governments-and-industry-collaborate-to-advance-projects\n\nThe IEA CCUS Projects Explorer similarly tracks worldwide large-scale projects and notes that announced capacity for 2030 has risen sharply, though actual deployment still lags what would be needed in net-zero pathways.  \nSources:  \nhttps://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/data-tools/ccus-projects-explorer  \nhttps://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/charts/announced-and-operational-carbon-capture-utilisation-and-storage-capacity-in-2030-across-editions-of-iea-ccus-projects-database\n\n---\n\n## 7) Comparative ranking\n\n## Lowest cost today\n1. **High-purity industrial capture**: natural gas processing, ethanol, some hydrogen/ammonia streams  \n2. **Pre-combustion capture in suitable industrial processes**  \n3. **Post-combustion capture on dilute industrial/power streams**  \n4. **BECCS**  \n5. **DACCS**\n\nMain sources:  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/is-carbon-capture-too-expensive  \nhttps://www.netl.doe.gov/projects/files/CostofCapturingCO2fromIndustrialSources_071522.pdf  \nhttps://www.iea.org/commentaries/unlocking-the-potential-of-direct-air-capture-is-scaling-up-through-carbon-markets-possible\n\n## Highest near-term scalability\n1. **Industrial point-source CCS in clusters/hubs**\n2. **High-purity industrial streams**\n3. **Selected hard-to-abate industrial retrofits, especially cement and chemicals**\n4. **BECCS where sustainable biomass is available**\n5. **DACCS**\n\nMain sources:  \nhttps://www.iea.org/energy-system/carbon-capture-utilisation-and-storage
