        "report": "# AI Governance in the US and EU: How regulators are approaching it, and how the frameworks differ\n\n## Executive summary\n\nThe EU has adopted a **binding, horizontal AI law**: the **AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)**. It regulates AI across sectors using a **risk-based model**, with outright bans for certain practices, extensive obligations for **high-risk AI systems**, transparency rules for specific uses such as chatbots and deepfakes, and direct obligations for **general-purpose AI (GPAI) models** and some systemic-risk models. It is enforced through a mix of EU-level coordination and national authorities.  \nSource: EU AI Act text: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng ; European Commission overview: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai\n\nThe US has **not** enacted a single federal AI law comparable to the EU AI Act. Instead, US regulators are using a combination of:\n- **existing laws** enforced by sector regulators,\n- **executive branch management and procurement rules** for federal agencies,\n- **voluntary technical standards**, especially the **NIST AI Risk Management Framework**,\n- and an emerging patchwork of **state AI laws**.  \nSources: AI.gov: https://www.ai.gov/ ; OMB memoranda index: https://www.whitehouse.gov/omb/memoranda/ ; NIST AI RMF: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework\n\nIn short: **the EU uses a centralized, ex ante, risk-classified regulatory regime; the US uses a decentralized, sector-specific, and often ex post enforcement model.**\n\n---\n\n## 1. The EU approach: a single, binding, risk-based AI regime\n\n### 1.1 The AI Act is the center of EU AI governance\n\nThe EU\u2019s main instrument is the **AI Act**, a regulation that applies across the Union without needing national transposition in the way directives do, though Member States still must designate enforcement authorities. The Commission describes it as a comprehensive legal framework for AI.  \nSources:  \n- AI Act: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng  \n- Commission overview: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai\n\n### 1.2 The AI Act uses explicit risk categories\n\nThe Act does not treat all AI systems alike. Instead, it organizes obligations by risk level:\n\n- **Unacceptable risk**: certain AI practices are prohibited.\n- **High-risk AI systems**: allowed only if strict requirements are met.\n- **Limited-risk uses**: subject mainly to transparency obligations.\n- **Minimal-risk uses**: generally not subject to AI-Act-specific mandatory obligations.  \nSource: AI Act: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng\n\n### 1.3 The EU bans some AI practices outright\n\nThe AI Act prohibits certain practices, including specified manipulative systems, some social scoring practices, certain biometric uses, and some emotion-recognition uses in schools and workplaces, among others.  \nSource: AI Act, Article 5: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng\n\n### 1.4 High-risk AI systems face detailed ex ante and lifecycle duties\n\nFor **high-risk** systems, the AI Act requires providers to implement:\n- risk management,\n- data and data governance measures,\n- technical documentation,\n- logging,\n- transparency and instructions for use,\n- human oversight,\n- accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity measures,\n- quality management,\n- post-market monitoring,\n- and incident reporting.\n\nProviders also must go through **conformity assessment**, issue an EU declaration of conformity, and in many cases affix **CE marking**.  \nSource: AI Act: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng\n\nThis is one of the clearest differences from the US: the EU imposes **pre-market and ongoing legal compliance duties** for defined AI categories.\n\n### 1.5 The EU also regulates general-purpose AI models\n\nThe AI Act imposes obligations on **general-purpose AI model providers**, including documentation, information-sharing with downstream providers, certain copyright-related duties, and a public summary of training data content. It adds stronger obligations for GPAI models with **systemic risk**, including model evaluation, risk mitigation, cybersecurity, and incident reporting.  \nSource: AI Act: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng\n\nThis is especially significant because the EU directly regulates upstream model providers, while the US still lacks a comparable binding federal regime for frontier or general-purpose models.\n\n### 1.6 EU enforcement is coordinated and backed by large fines\n\nThe EU has created an **AI Office** within the European Commission to support implementation, particularly for GPAI issues, alongside national competent authorities and market surveillance authorities.  \nSource: AI Office overview: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-office\n\nThe AI Act allows for substantial administrative fines, with the top tier reaching **up to \u20ac35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover**, depending on the violation.  \nSource: AI Act: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng\n\n---\n\n## 2. The broader EU legal environment: GDPR and the Digital Services Act\n\n### 2.1 The AI Act sits alongside the GDPR\n\nThe AI Act does not replace EU data protection law. Where AI involves personal data, organizations still must comply with the **GDPR**, including rules on lawful basis, purpose limitation, data minimization, and data subject rights.  \nSources:  \n- AI Act: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng  \n- GDPR: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng\n\nSo an AI system may comply with the AI Act\u2019s governance requirements and still violate the GDPR if its data processing is unlawful.\n\n### 2.2 The Digital Services Act matters for AI used by platforms\n\nThe **Digital Services Act (DSA)** is not an AI law, but it is highly relevant where AI powers recommender systems, content moderation, search, or ad targeting on online platforms. It imposes systemic-risk, transparency, and audit obligations on very large platforms and search engines.  \nSources:  \n- DSA text: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj  \n- Commission overview: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/digital-services-act-package\n\nThis means EU AI governance is not just the AI Act; it is a layered system combining AI law, privacy law, and platform regulation.\n\n---\n\n## 3. The US approach: fragmented, sectoral, and enforcement-driven\n\n### 3.1 No single federal AI statute\n\nThe US does not currently have an EU-style omnibus federal AI law. Instead, AI governance is spread across:\n- White House and OMB directives,\n- voluntary NIST standards,\n- sector-specific agency enforcement,\n- and state legislation.  \nSources:  \n- AI.gov: https://www.ai.gov/  \n- OMB memoranda: https://www.whitehouse.gov/omb/memoranda/\n\n### 3.2 Federal policy emphasizes governance of government use of AI\n\nA major part of current US federal activity focuses on **how federal agencies themselves use and buy AI**. OMB guidance addresses agency governance, inventories, internal controls, and procurement-related safeguards.  \nSource: OMB memoranda index: https://www.whitehouse.gov/omb/memoranda/\n\nThat is a narrower approach than the EU\u2019s, which directly regulates the private market through a binding statute.\n\n### 3.3 NIST provides the main cross-sector governance framework, but it is voluntary\n\nThe **NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)** is the closest thing the US has to a common AI governance backbone. It is built around four functions:\n- **Govern**\n- **Map**\n- **Measure**\n- **Manage**  \nSource: NIST AI RMF: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework\n\nNIST has also issued supporting resources for generative AI and secure development practices.  \nSources:  \n- Generative AI Profile: https://www.nist.gov/publications/artificial-intelligence-risk-management-framework-generative-artificial-intelligence  \n- Secure development practices for generative AI: https://www.nist.gov/publications/secure-software-development-practices-generative-ai-and-dual-use-foundation-models\n\nBut unlike the EU AI Act, the NIST framework is **not legally binding** on the private sector by itself.\n\n---\n\n## 4. US agencies are regulating AI through existing law\n\nThe US model is built on the principle that AI does **not** create an exemption from existing legal duties.\n\n### 4.1 FTC: unfairness and deception still apply\n\nThe **Federal Trade Commission** has repeatedly warned companies not to exaggerate AI capabilities and not to make unsubstantiated claims about fairness, accuracy, or bias reduction. The FTC has said firms remain subject to unfairness and deception rules when they use AI.  \nSources:  \n- FTC on AI claims: https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/blog/2023/02/keep-your-ai-claims-check  \n- FTC on truth, fairness, and equity in AI: https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/blog/2021/04/aiming-truth-fairness-equity-your-companys-use-ai\n\nThis is a classic **ex post** regulatory posture: the FTC acts when conduct is unfair or deceptive, rather than classifying systems upfront the way the EU does.\n\n### 4.2 EEOC and DOJ: employment AI must comply with civil-rights law\n\nThe **EEOC** has said that employers using algorithmic or AI tools remain responsible for discrimination under **Title VII** and the **ADA**, including adverse impact and disability discrimination.  \nSources:  \n- EEOC adverse impact guidance: https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/assessing-adverse-impact-software-algorithms-and-artificial-intelligence-used  \n- EEOC ADA guidance: https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/americans-disabilities-act-and-use-software-algorithms-and-artificial-intelligence\n\nThe **DOJ** has likewise warned that employers and others cannot avoid ADA obligations by outsourcing decisions to AI vendors.  \nSource: https://www.ada.gov/resources/ai-guidance/\n\nThe EU reaches similar use cases through the AI Act\u2019s **high-risk** category for employment systems, but the US reaches them through **civil-rights statutes**, not a dedicated AI law.\n\n### 4.3 CFPB: complex algorithms do not excuse weak explanations\n\nThe **Consumer Financial Protection Bureau** has stated that creditors using complex algorithms still must provide legally sufficient **adverse action notices** under consumer finance law.  \nSource: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/compliance/circulars/consumer-financial-protection-circular-2022-03-adverse-action-notification-requirements-in-connection-with-credit-decisions-based-on-complex-algorithms/\n\nThis creates a functional transparency obligation, but again it comes from **credit law**, not AI law.\n\n### 4.4 HHS and FDA: healthcare AI is regulated through sector law\n\nIn healthcare, **HHS** has tied AI-related decision support to nondiscrimination duties under Section 1557.  \nSource: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/05/06/2024-08711/nondiscrimination-in-health-programs-and-activities\n\nThe **FDA** regulates AI/ML-enabled medical devices through existing medical-device authorities, focusing on safety and effectiveness rather than a general AI statute.  \nSource: https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/software-medical-device-samd/artificial-intelligence-and-machine-learning-aiml-enabled-medical-devices\n\nThis resembles the EU\u2019s sectoral/product-safety thinking in part, but only in specific domains.\n\n---\n\n## 5. State law is making US AI governance more concrete\n\n### 5.1 Colorado is the clearest US move toward a risk-based AI law\n\nColorado\u2019s **SB24-205** creates obligations for developers and deployers of certain **high-risk AI systems** used in consequential decisions. It requires risk management, impact assessments, notices, and measures to address algorithmic discrimination.  \nSource: https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb24-205\n\nThis is one of the closest US analogues to the EU model, but it is still:\n- a **state** law, not a federal one,\n- narrower in scope,\n- and lacks the EU\u2019s broader conformity-assessment and market-wide institutional architecture.\n\n### 5.2 California has focused more on targeted harms\n\nCalifornia has passed measures focused on **deepfakes**, especially in election and sexually explicit content contexts.  \nSources:  \n- AB 2355: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB2355  \n- AB 2655: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB2655  \n- AB 2839: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB2839  \n- AB 602: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB602\n\nThis shows another feature of the US model: state law is often **targeted and issue-specific**, rather than comprehensive.\n\n---\n\n## 6. The main differences between the US and EU frameworks\n\n### 6.1 Horizontal law vs. fragmented governance\n\n**EU:** one binding cross-sector framework, the AI Act.  \n**US:** no single federal AI law; oversight is fragmented across agencies, statutes, and states.  \nSources:  \n- EU AI Act: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng  \n- AI.gov: https://www.ai.gov/\n\n### 6.2 Ex ante compliance vs. ex post enforcement\n\n**EU:** many obligations apply before market entry or deployment, especially for high-risk systems, via conformity assessment, documentation, and CE-marking-related processes.  \n**US:** much regulation happens after the fact through enforcement under consumer protection, civil-rights, finance, health, and product laws.  \nSources:  \n- EU AI Act: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng  \n- FTC AI guidance: https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/blog/2021/04/aiming-truth-fairness-equity-your-companys-use-ai\n\n### 6.3 Binding categories vs. voluntary frameworks\n\n**EU:** legal categories such as prohibited, high-risk, and transparency-triggering uses are written into law.  \n**US:** NIST offers a common governance framework, but it is voluntary; legal exposure depends on context-specific statutes and enforcement.  \nSources:  \n- EU AI Act: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng  \n- NIST AI RMF: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework\n\n### 6.4 Rights-centered model vs. sector-law model\n\nThe EU framework is explicitly tied to **fundamental rights**, including privacy, non-discrimination, and human dignity.  \nSources:  \n- EU Charter: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:12012P/TXT  \n- AI Act: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng\n\nThe US protects similar interests, but mostly through separate legal domains like discrimination law, consumer protection law, and privacy-related rules rather than a single rights-based AI code.  \nSources:  \n- EEOC guidance: https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/assessing-adverse-impact-software-algorithms-and-artificial-intelligence-used  \n- FTC guidance: https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/blog/2021/04/aiming-truth-fairness-equity-your-companys-use-ai\n\n### 6.5 Direct regulation of general-purpose models\n\n**EU:** GPAI model providers have direct obligations under the AI Act.  \n**US:** no comparable binding federal regime applies horizontally to GPAI model providers.  \nSource: EU AI Act: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng\n\n### 6.6 Uniformity vs. federal-state patchwork\n\n**EU:** a single regulation applies across the internal market.  \n**US:** companies must navigate federal agency expectations plus increasingly important state laws.  \nSources:  \n- EU AI Act: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng  \n- Colorado SB24-205: https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb24-205\n\n---\n\n## 7. Where the two systems are converging\n\nDespite major structural differences, the US and EU are converging on some substantive themes:\n\n- **risk management**\n- **documentation**\n- **testing**\n- **human oversight**\n- **transparency**\n- **monitoring after deployment**\n\nIn the EU, these themes are codified in binding law. In the US, they often appear through NIST guidance, procurement rules, or agency expectations under existing law.  \nSources:  \n- NIST AI RMF: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework  \n- EU AI Act: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng\n\n---\n\n## Conclusion\n\nThe EU is building AI governance as a **single legal framework** with explicit risk categories, enforceable obligations, and direct regulation of both downstream AI systems and some upstream general-purpose models. The US is building AI governance through a **distributed regulatory ecosystem**: executive governance for federal agencies, voluntary standards, sectoral enforcement, and state legislation.\n\nThat means the EU offers more **legal uniformity and upfront compliance structure**, while the US offers more **flexibility but less centralization and predictability**. For companies operating in both jurisdictions, the practical result is that the EU requires a **formal AI compliance program**, while the US requires a **sector-by-sector and state-by-state legal mapping exercise**.\n\nShort answer: **The EU uses a binding, risk-based AI law with ex ante obligations; the US relies on fragmented agency enforcement, voluntary standards, and state laws, with fewer cross-sector federal rules.**",

        "report": "# Report: The current state of mRNA vaccine technology beyond COVID-19, and the most promising applications\n\n## Executive summary\n\nmRNA vaccine technology has moved beyond being a COVID-19-only platform. The strongest evidence now supports **three conclusions**:\n\n1. **mRNA vaccines are already clinically validated beyond COVID-19 for RSV.** Moderna\u2019s RSV vaccine **mRESVIA (mRNA-1345)** was approved by the U.S. FDA in 2024, making it the first non-COVID mRNA vaccine to reach market. Its pivotal trial showed strong protection against RSV lower respiratory tract disease in older adults.  \n   Sources: FDA approval documents and label information:  \n   - https://www.fda.gov/media/179634/download  \n   - https://www.fda.gov/vaccines-blood-biologics/vaccines/mresvia  \n   - NEJM trial: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2307079  \n   - PubMed summary: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38091530/\n\n2. **The near-term pipeline is led by respiratory and congenital/latent viral targets**, especially **influenza** and **cytomegalovirus (CMV)**. Seasonal flu has now produced phase 3 efficacy and immunogenicity data for investigational mRNA vaccines, while CMV has advanced into phase 3 and is one of the clearest unmet-need targets because no licensed CMV vaccine exists.  \n   Sources:  \n   - Influenza phase 3 efficacy: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41259756/  \n   - Influenza phase 3 immunogenicity/safety: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39919447/  \n   - CMV phase 3 trial: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05683457  \n   - CMV phase 2/extension data: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42188814/\n\n3. **The most scientifically exciting, but still less proven, frontier is personalized cancer vaccination.** The most advanced programs\u2014individualized neoantigen mRNA vaccines in melanoma and pancreatic cancer\u2014have shown encouraging signals for recurrence reduction and durable T-cell responses, but they remain investigational and operationally more complex than infectious-disease vaccines.  \n   Sources:  \n   - Melanoma phase 2b KEYNOTE-942: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38246194/  \n   - Pancreatic cancer phase 1 Nature paper: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06063-y  \n   - Longer-term pancreatic follow-up: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08508-4\n\nOverall, the **current state** of mRNA vaccines beyond COVID-19 is best described as **transitioning from platform proof to portfolio proof**: one approved product (RSV), several late-stage infectious-disease candidates, and an oncology pipeline with real biological and early clinical promise but higher execution risk.\n\n---\n\n## 1) Why mRNA remains attractive beyond COVID-19\n\nThe WHO Science Council concluded that mRNA technology has meaningful potential beyond COVID-19, while emphasizing that its value depends on the disease target, product profile, delivery, and manufacturing context\u2014not on the platform alone. WHO also stressed remaining limits, including cold-chain burdens, reactogenicity, and access inequities.  \nSources:  \n- WHO news summary: https://www.who.int/news/item/13-12-2023-who-s-science-council-issues-report-on-mrna-vaccine-technology  \n- WHO Science Council report (draft publicly posted): https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/research-for-health/23-04-01-mrna-draft-report_for-public-consultation.pdf?sfvrsn=c10572d2_6\n\nKey platform advantages repeatedly cited in the literature and by WHO are:\n- **speed of antigen redesign and manufacture**\n- **ability to encode complex or multiple antigens**\n- **strong humoral and cellular immune responses**\n- **fit for personalized or rapidly updated products**, especially where protein manufacturing is slow or individualized production is needed  \nSources:  \n- WHO report: https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/research-for-health/23-04-01-mrna-draft-report_for-public-consultation.pdf?sfvrsn=c10572d2_6  \n- Review of infectious disease progress: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12204004/\n\nThe most important post-COVID question is no longer whether mRNA can work at all. It is **where it is better than existing platforms**.\n\n---\n\n## 2) The clearest commercial and clinical success so far: RSV\n\n### What happened\nIn 2024, the FDA approved **mRESVIA (mRNA-1345)** for prevention of RSV lower respiratory tract disease in older adults. FDA documents identify it as an mRNA RSV vaccine and detail the approval basis.  \nSources:  \n- FDA summary basis: https://www.fda.gov/media/179634/download  \n- FDA product page: https://www.fda.gov/vaccines-blood-biologics/vaccines/mresvia  \n- EMA product page: https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/mresvia  \n- EMA assessment report: https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/assessment-report/mresvia-epar-public-assessment-report_en.pdf\n\n### Why it matters\nThis approval is important because it shows that the mRNA platform can support a **non-COVID, mainstream adult vaccine** that regulators accept on conventional efficacy and safety grounds.\n\n### Evidence\nIn the pivotal phase 2/3 trial published in the *New England Journal of Medicine*, vaccine efficacy was:\n- **83.7%** against RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease with at least two signs or symptoms\n- **82.4%** against disease with at least three signs or symptoms  \nSource:  \n- NEJM: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2307079  \n- PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38091530/\n\n### Interpretation\nRSV is currently the **best proof that mRNA can compete in the established adult respiratory vaccine market**. However, RSV is also a case where mRNA is competing against already approved protein-based alternatives, so its long-term advantage will depend on comparative durability, manufacturing flexibility, combination products, and cost\u2014not just first efficacy.\n\n---\n\n## 3) Influenza: probably the largest near-term opportunity\n\n### Current state\nSeasonal influenza is one of the most promising non-COVID mRNA applications because the market is large, recurrent, and already structured around regular strain updates. That plays directly to mRNA\u2019s strengths.\n\nRecent published phase 3 data show that investigational mRNA flu vaccines have moved into serious late-stage development:\n\n- A phase 3 study reported that a modified mRNA influenza vaccine met criteria for **noninferiority and superiority** versus a licensed inactivated quadrivalent vaccine for influenza-like illness in adults 18\u201364 years old; relative efficacy was **34.5%** in that trial.  \n  Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41259756/\n\n- A separate phase 3 trial of **mRNA-1010** reported safety and immunogenicity findings in adults, comparing the candidate with standard-dose and high-dose licensed quadrivalent influenza vaccines.  \n  Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39919447/\n\n### Why influenza is promising\nInfluenza is promising for mRNA for four reasons:\n\n1. **Update speed** matters every season.\n2. **Multivalency** is intrinsic to the product category.\n3. **Immune breadth optimization** may be easier with sequence design changes than with conventional egg-based production.\n4. Influenza is a natural platform for **combination vaccines**, especially with COVID-19 and RSV.\n\n### Limits\nFlu also shows the key challenge: **being \u201cmRNA\u201d is not enough**. To displace entrenched flu products, mRNA vaccines must show either clearly better effectiveness, faster adaptation, or a compelling role in combo vaccines.\n\n---\n\n## 4) CMV: the most promising unmet-need infectious-disease target\n\n### Current state\n**Cytomegalovirus (CMV)** is one of the strongest mRNA opportunities because it is a high-burden congenital infection target with **no licensed vaccine**.\n\nModerna\u2019s **mRNA-1647** is in phase 3. ClinicalTrials.gov lists a pivotal study evaluating efficacy and safety for prevention of primary CMV infection in healthy participants.  \nSource:  \n- Phase 3 trial: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05683457\n\nPhase 2 and extension data have also been published.  \nSource:  \n- PubMed phase 2/extension: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42188814/\n\nEarlier first-in-human results reported acceptable safety and induction of humoral and cellular immune responses.  \nSource:  \n- Phase 1 PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38478705/\n\n### Why CMV is especially attractive for mRNA\nCMV is a good fit for the platform because protection may require responses against **multiple antigens**, including glycoprotein B and the pentameric complex. mRNA is well-suited to expressing multicomponent antigen sets without the manufacturing complexity of purifying several separate recombinant proteins.\n\n### Interpretation\nAmong infectious-disease programs not yet approved, **CMV may be the single most promising mRNA vaccine application** because:\n- unmet need is high,\n- no approved vaccine exists,\n- the antigenic design benefits from multivalent encoding,\n- and the lead program is already in phase 3.  \nSource for trial status: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05683457\n\n---\n\n## 5) Oncology: high upside, high complexity\n\nCancer vaccines are the area where mRNA is most conceptually differentiated from traditional vaccine platforms. Instead of preventing infection, these vaccines aim to induce T-cell responses against tumor antigens, often personalized to each patient\u2019s tumor mutations.\n\n### 5.1 Personalized melanoma vaccine (mRNA-4157 / V940)\nThe randomized phase 2b **KEYNOTE-942** trial tested individualized neoantigen therapy **mRNA-4157 (V940)** plus pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab alone in resected melanoma. Published results showed improved recurrence-free survival with the combination.  \nSource:  \n- PubMed/Lancet: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38246194/\n\nThis is one of the strongest clinical signals yet for a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine.\n\n### 5.2 Pancreatic cancer (autogene cevumeran)\nA phase 1 *Nature* study of **autogene cevumeran**, an individualized mRNA neoantigen vaccine, in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma showed that:\n- vaccine production was achieved in clinically relevant time,\n- the vaccine induced de novo, high-magnitude neoantigen-specific T-cell responses in **8 of 16 patients**,\n- and responders had longer recurrence-free survival than non-responders at median 18-month follow-up.  \nSource:  \n- Nature 2023: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06063-y\n\nLonger follow-up published in *Nature* reported that vaccine-induced T-cell clones persisted and were associated with prolonged recurrence-free survival in responders.  \nSource:  \n- Nature 2024: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08508-4\n\n### 5.3 Broader oncology pipeline\nBioNTech has also reported positive topline phase 2 results for **BNT111** in advanced melanoma, though company press releases are weaker evidence than peer-reviewed reports.  \nSource:  \n- BioNTech press release: https://www.biontech.com/int/en/home/mediaroom/news/press-releases/2024/07/biontech-announces-positive-topline-phase-2-results-mrna.html\n\n### Why oncology is promising\nmRNA is unusually well matched to oncology because it can:\n- encode **patient-specific neoantigens**\n- support rapid individualized manufacturing\n- induce T-cell responses\n- combine naturally with checkpoint inhibitors\n\n### Why oncology is not yet the most mature application\nThe constraints are substantial:\n- bespoke manufacturing logistics\n- turnaround time requirements\n- biomarker and patient-selection complexity\n- higher cost of goods and operational coordination than standard vaccines\n\n### Interpretation\n**Personalized cancer vaccines are among the most promising long-term mRNA applications scientifically**, but they are still behind RSV, influenza, and CMV in regulatory maturity.\n\n---\n\n## 6) Other infectious-disease areas: active, but earlier or less de-risked\n\n### Zika\nPhase 1 studies of two mRNA Zika vaccine candidates (**mRNA-1325** and **mRNA-1893**) found them safe and immunogenic in adults.  \nSource:  \n- PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36682364/\n\nZika remains scientifically suitable for mRNA, but commercial and development momentum is constrained by fluctuating outbreak dynamics.\n\n### Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)\nAn EBV mRNA vaccine trial is listed on ClinicalTrials.gov (**NCT05831111**), indicating continued platform expansion into latent-virus targets.  \nSource:  \n- ClinicalTrials.gov: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05831111\n\nEBV is attractive because of links to infectious mononucleosis and some malignancies, but it remains early.\n\n### Norovirus\nA norovirus mRNA trial is also listed on ClinicalTrials.gov (**NCT05992935**).  \nSource:  \n- ClinicalTrials.gov: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05992935\n\nThis is promising because norovirus lacks a licensed vaccine and causes major disease burden, but the field is still early.\n\n### HIV\nPreclinical work in nonhuman primates has shown that lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated nucleoside-modified mRNA HIV-1 vaccines can elicit polyfunctional antibodies comparable to protein approaches.  \nSource:  \n- PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33837212/\n\nThis is important scientifically, but HIV remains a very difficult vaccine target, so it is not yet among the most near-term promising applications.\n\n### Malaria, TB, mpox\nWHO materials show active interest and early R&D activity for mRNA approaches to malaria, tuberculosis, and mpox, including within the mRNA technology transfer ecosystem. But these programs are still at an early stage relative to RSV, flu, CMV, or oncology.  \nSources:  \n- WHO malaria intervention prospects: https://www.who.int/campaigns/world-malaria-day/2022/prospects-for-new-interventions  \n- WHO mRNA technology transfer programme: https://www.who.int/initiatives/mrna-technology-transfer-(mrna-tt)-programme  \n- WHO TB vaccine challenge: https://iris.who.int/bitstreams/bd141d40-0a84-4559-9071-c6a61d316640/download  \n- WHO variola/mpox research materials: https://iris.who.int/bitstreams/c0069b7e-3854-4f07-947f-3c159fa8a17c/download\n\n---\n\n## 7) Platform evolution: not just \u201cmRNA,\u201d but better mRNA\n\nThe field is no longer static. Important technical directions include:\n\n### Self-amplifying RNA (saRNA)\nSelf-amplifying RNA aims to reduce dose requirements by enabling intracellular RNA replication. Review articles and preclinical influenza work suggest saRNA can achieve similar protection at much lower doses in some settings.  \nSources:  \n- Review: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10266560/  \n- Influenza preclinical study: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5835025/\n\nThis could matter for cost, scale, and reactogenicity, although broad non-COVID product validation is still limited.\n\n### Better stability and formulation\nLyophilization and improved LNP design are active areas of work intended to improve storage, transport, and tolerability.  \nSources:  \n- Lyophilized LNP-mRNA stability: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35131437/  \n- LNP component review: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35787388/\n\n### Regional manufacturing\nWHO and the Medicines Patent Pool continue to expand the **mRNA Technology Transfer Programme**, aiming to build sustainable production capacity beyond high-income countries.  \nSource:  \n- https://www.who.int/initiatives/mrna-technology-transfer-(mrna-tt)-programme\n\nThis matters because the platform\u2019s future is not just about immunology; it is also about whether manufacturing can become cheaper, more distributed, and less geopolitically concentrated.\n\n---\n\n## 8) What is most promising, ranked\n\n### Tier 1: Most promising now\n#### 1.         "report": "# What is the current state of mRNA vaccine technology beyond COVID-19, and which applications are most promising?\n\n## Executive summary\n\nmRNA vaccine technology is no longer just a COVID-19 story. Beyond COVID-19, the field has now reached three distinct stages at once:\n\n1. **Commercial reality in respiratory infectious disease**: mRNA has already expanded beyond COVID-19 into **RSV**, with Moderna\u2019s mRESVIA approved by the U.S. FDA in 2024 for older adults, later expanded to certain younger at-risk adults. This is the clearest proof that the platform works outside SARS-CoV-2.  \n   Sources: FDA roundup; FDA package insert; NEJM RSV trial  \n   https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-roundup-may-31-2024  \n   https://www.fda.gov/files/vaccines%2C%20blood%20%26%20biologics/published/Package-Insert-MRESVIA_1.pdf  \n   https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2307079\n\n2. **Late-stage pipeline in seasonal and pandemic flu**: influenza is the next most mature non-COVID use. Moderna\u2019s phase 3 seasonal flu program reported superior relative vaccine efficacy versus a licensed standard-dose flu vaccine in adults 50+, and the company has regulatory filings underway or planned in multiple jurisdictions. Pandemic-flu mRNA programs, including H5 candidates, are also advancing.  \n   Sources: phase 3 results; Moderna trial pages; NIHR/CIDRAP on H5 trial launch  \n   https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11970786  \n   https://trials.modernatx.com/study?id=mRNA-1010-P304  \n   https://www.nihr.ac.uk/news/bird-flu-vaccine-trial-launches-prepare-potential-pandemic  \n   https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/avian-influenza-bird-flu/hhs-awards-590-million-moderna-develop-mrna-vaccines-against-pandemic-flu\n\n3. **Fast-moving oncology platform, especially personalized cancer vaccines**: the strongest \u201ctransformational\u201d promise is in cancer, where mRNA\u2019s speed and programmability fit individualized neoantigen vaccines unusually well. The most advanced evidence is the melanoma program mRNA-4157/V940 plus pembrolizumab, which improved recurrence-free outcomes in phase 2b; pancreatic cancer studies also showed vaccine-induced T cell responses associated with delayed recurrence.  \n   Sources: Lancet melanoma phase 2b; Nature pancreatic study  \n   https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(23)02268-7/abstract  \n   https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06063-y\n\nAt the same time, the field is **not uniformly succeeding**. Some highly anticipated programs have stumbled; most notably, Moderna\u2019s phase 3 **CMV** vaccine did **not** meet its primary efficacy endpoint, showing that strong immunogenicity does not guarantee clinical protection.  \nSources: Moderna statement; trial listing  \nhttps://www.modernatx.com/media-center/all-media/blogs/phase-3-cmv-vaccine-readout-reflections  \nhttps://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05085366\n\n**Bottom line:** the most promising applications today are:\n- **Seasonal/pandemic respiratory vaccines**, especially **influenza** and combination respiratory vaccines;\n- **Personalized cancer vaccines**, especially in adjuvant settings and in combination with checkpoint inhibitors;\n- **Selected outbreak or hard-target infectious diseases** where rapid design matters, such as H5 influenza, Zika, chikungunya, and HIV germline-targeting concepts.\n\nThe less mature but intriguing frontier is **tolerizing mRNA for autoimmune disease** and broader **self-amplifying mRNA** platforms, which could reduce dose and improve durability, but these remain earlier-stage than flu/RSV/cancer.  \nSources: Science autoimmune model; Nature Medicine sa-mRNA booster study  \nhttps://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33414215  \nhttps://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-024-02955-2\n\n---\n\n## 1) Where mRNA stands today beyond COVID-19\n\n### 1.1 From emergency platform to general vaccine modality\n\nA major 2024 Lancet review described mRNA therapeutics as moving beyond COVID into vaccines, immunotherapeutics, protein replacement, and genome-editing applications. The broader field review literature now consistently describes hundreds of active trials across infectious disease, oncology, and other indications.  \nSources: Lancet review; global development landscape review  \nhttps://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(23)02444-3/fulltext  \nhttps://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12962614  \nhttps://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12197385\n\n### 1.2 The technology stack is more mature than in 2020\n\nThe current state is not just \u201csame mRNA, new target.\u201d The platform has improved across:\n- **nucleoside modification** to tune innate sensing and translation,\n- **lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery**,\n- **antigen design**,\n- **manufacturing speed and modularity**,\n- and emerging **self-amplifying mRNA (sa-mRNA)** approaches that aim to use lower doses and extend antigen expression.  \nSources: Lancet review; toxicity review; sa-mRNA phase 2/3/3 literature  \nhttps://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(23)02444-3/fulltext  \nhttps://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-023-00859-3  \nhttps://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-024-02955-2  \nhttps://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12396474\n\n### 1.3 But the field still faces real constraints\n\nThe strongest recurring limitations in the literature are:\n- **reactogenicity and toxicity risk** tied to RNA chemistry, dose, and LNP biodistribution;\n- **delivery targeting** beyond muscle and liver;\n- **durability and booster strategy**;\n- **cold chain / thermostability**;\n- and the fact that immunogenicity readouts do not always predict real-world efficacy.  \nSource: Nature Reviews Drug Discovery toxicity review  \nhttps://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-023-00859-3\n\nThat last point matters because several mRNA vaccines look good immunologically in early trials but fail to achieve decisive clinical benefit later.\n\n---\n\n## 2) What has already been achieved commercially?\n\n### 2.1 RSV: the first non-COVID commercial breakthrough\n\nModerna\u2019s **mRESVIA (mRNA-1345)** became the first FDA-approved mRNA vaccine for a non-COVID infectious disease in May 2024. FDA materials show it is indicated to prevent RSV lower respiratory tract disease, first in adults 60+ and later expanded to adults 18-59 at increased risk.  \nSources: FDA roundup; package insert; approval letter summary  \nhttps://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-roundup-may-31-2024  \nhttps://www.fda.gov/files/vaccines%2C%20blood%20%26%20biologics/published/Package-Insert-MRESVIA_1.pdf  \nhttps://www.fda.gov/media/179015/download\n\nThe pivotal NEJM paper reported that a single dose reduced RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease in adults 60+ with no evident major safety signal in the trial.  \nSource: NEJM  \nhttps://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2307079\n\n**Why this matters:** RSV establishes that mRNA is now a validated commercial vaccine platform for respiratory disease beyond SARS-CoV-2.\n\n---\n\n## 3) Which applications are most promising?\n\n## 3.1 Seasonal influenza: probably the strongest near-term opportunity\n\nInfluenza is arguably the **most promising near-term expansion area** after RSV.\n\n### Evidence\nA phase 3 analysis of Moderna\u2019s **mRNA-1010** found that, in adults, the vaccine showed:\n- strong immunogenicity,\n- acceptable safety,\n- and in a major efficacy study, **superior relative vaccine efficacy** versus a licensed standard-dose seasonal flu vaccine in adults 50+.  \nSources: phase 3 publication and trial pages  \nhttps://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11970786  \nhttps://trials.modernatx.com/study?id=mRNA-1010-P304  \nhttps://trials.modernatx.com/study?id=mRNA-1010-P303\n\n### Why flu fits mRNA unusually well\nInfluenza changes constantly, so rapid redesign and manufacturing matter more than with many other pathogens. mRNA also makes multivalent designs straightforward, and preclinical work suggests it may broaden antibody repertoires in useful ways.  \nSources: H10N8/H7N9 phase 1 trial; multivalent universal-preclinical work; WashU report on broader responses  \nhttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.vaccine.2019.04.074  \nhttps://doi.org/10.1126/science.abm0271  \nhttps://medicine.washu.edu/news/mrna-flu-vaccine-offers-immune-protection-against-wide-array-of-influenza-virus-strains\n\n### Why it ranks highly\n- enormous annual disease burden,\n- established vaccination markets,\n- rapid strain update advantages,\n- and now late-stage efficacy data.\n\n**Assessment:** among non-COVID uses, **seasonal influenza is probably the most commercially promising next step**.\n\n---\n\n## 3.2 Pandemic influenza and outbreak response: a strategic strength of the platform\n\nmRNA\u2019s defining advantage is speed. That makes it especially attractive for **pandemic-preparedness vaccines**, including H5 avian influenza and other emergent strains.\n\n### Evidence\n- Moderna launched clinical development of an H5 pandemic flu candidate (**mRNA-1018**) and related programs.  \n- Public health agencies and research groups are explicitly treating mRNA as a pandemic-preparedness platform.  \nSources: NIHR; Moderna trial page; CIDRAP  \nhttps://www.nihr.ac.uk/news/bird-flu-vaccine-trial-launches-prepare-potential-pandemic  \nhttps://trials.modernatx.com/study?id=mRNA-1018-P301  \nhttps://www.cidrap.umn.edu/avian-influenza-bird-flu/hhs-awards-590-million-moderna-develop-mrna-vaccines-against-pandemic-flu\n\nPreclinical H5 mRNA data in ferrets also support this direction, showing strong antibody responses and protection.  \nSource: NIH/PMC preclinical study  \nhttps://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12728207\n\n### Why it ranks highly\nThis is less about immediate annual revenue than about **public-health utility**. For pathogens with unpredictable emergence, mRNA may be the best vaccine modality for first-wave response.\n\n**Assessment:** **pandemic influenza preparedness is one of mRNA\u2019s most strategically important applications**.\n\n---\n\n## 3.3 Personalized cancer vaccines: the most transformative long-term application\n\nIf flu is the strongest near-term commercial opportunity, **personalized cancer vaccination** is the strongest long-term scientific opportunity.\n\n### Melanoma: the clearest clinical signal so far\nIn the phase 2b **KEYNOTE-942** study, adjuvant **mRNA-4157 (V940) + pembrolizumab** improved recurrence-free survival versus pembrolizumab alone in high-risk resected melanoma. The Lancet abstract reports:\n- hazard ratio for recurrence or death: **0.561**\n- 18-month recurrence-free survival: **79% vs 62%**  \nSource: Lancet  \nhttps://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(23)02268-7/abstract\n\nA Nature Reviews Clinical Oncology summary described the vaccine as mitigating melanoma recurrence, reflecting the field\u2019s view that this is a landmark signal for individualized neoantigen mRNA.  \nSource: Nature Reviews Clinical Oncology  \nhttps://www.nature.com/articles/s41571-024-00867-1\n\n### Pancreatic cancer: encouraging mechanistic signal\nIn a Nature study of **autogene cevumeran** in resected pancreatic cancer, investigators showed that personalized mRNA vaccination induced de novo high-magnitude neoantigen-specific T cells in half the evaluable patients, and those responders had longer recurrence-free survival.  \nSources: Nature article; BioNTech follow-up  \nhttps://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06063-y  \nhttps://www.biontech.com/int/en/home/mediaroom/news/press-releases/2024/04/three-year-phase-1-follow-data-mrna-based-individualized.html\n\n### Why cancer is such a good fit for mRNA\nmRNA can encode:\n- multiple neoantigens on one construct,\n- patient-specific sequences,\n- and rapidly manufactured individualized products.\n\nThat is much harder with traditional vaccine technologies.  \nSources: Nature Reviews Cancer; BioNTech mRNA oncology platform page  \nhttps://doi.org/10.1038/s41568-023-00586-2  \nhttps://www.biontech.com/us/en/home/pipeline-and-products/platforms/mrna-platforms.html\n\n### Caveat\nThis is still a **harder commercialization path** than flu or RSV:\n- individualized manufacturing is complex,\n- endpoints take longer,\n- efficacy may depend on combinations with checkpoint blockade,\n- and tumor biology is heterogeneous.\n\n**Assessment:** **personalized cancer vaccines are the most transformative and arguably the most scientifically promising mRNA application, but not the most mature commercially.**\n\n---\n\n## 3.4 Combination respiratory vaccines: highly plausible, commercially attractive\n\nBecause mRNA is modular, combining multiple antigens in one shot is straightforward in principle. That makes **flu + COVID** or broader respiratory combinations attractive.\n\n### Evidence\nModerna\u2019s pipeline includes combination respiratory programs, and European regulatory review has considered mRNA-based combo vaccines.  \nSources: Moderna pipeline; EMA-related reporting context  \nhttps://www.modernatx.com/research/product-pipeline  \nhttps://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/after-fda-recently-declines-review-ema-backs-first-ever-2026a10006r9\n\n### Why it matters\nFor adult vaccination, convenience and uptake often matter as much as pure immunology. If mRNA can deliver high-performing combined respiratory vaccines without compromising efficacy or tolerability, the commercial upside is obvious.\n\n**Assessment:** **combination respiratory vaccines are one of the most plausible medium-term winners**, especially if flu approval lands.\n\n---\n\n## 3.5 HIV: scientifically important, but still high-risk\n\nHIV has always been a difficult vaccine target. mRNA is promising here not because it magically solves HIV, but because it enables highly engineered sequential immunogens for **germline targeting** and antibody maturation strategies.\n\n### Evidence\nIAVI and Moderna launched phase 1 clinical trials of mRNA HIV vaccine antigens, including **mRNA-1644**, in U.S. and African sites. These studies test whether priming/boosting schemes can initiate the B-cell pathways needed for broadly neutralizing antibodies.  \nSources: IAVI press releases; Moderna HIV program summary  \nhttps://www.iavi.org/press-release/iavi-and-moderna-launch-trial-of-hiv-vaccine-antigens-delivered-through-mrna-technology  \nhttps://www.iavi.org/press-release/iavi-and-moderna-launch-first-in-africa-clinical-trial-of-mrna-hiv-vaccine-development-program  \nhttps://www.modernatx.com/research/product-pipeline\n\n### Assessment\nThis is a **high-value but high-risk** application. The scientific logic is strong, but no one should mistake early proof-of-concept immunology for imminent vaccine success.\n\n**Assessment:** promising, but **not near-term**.\n\n---\n\n## 3.6 Zika, chikungunya, rabies, and other emerging infections: useful proving grounds\n\nSeveral non-COVID infectious disease programs have already produced human data:\n\n- **Zika**: two phase 1 trials of mRNA candidates reported safety and immunogenicity in healthy adults.  \n  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36682364  \n  https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(22)00764-2/abstract\n\n- **Chikungunya**: phase 1 data for **mRNA-1388** found it was well tolerated and immunogenic.  \n  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37210308\n\n- **Rabies**: early human studies showed proof of concept for mRNA rabies vaccination, though not yet market-defining efficacy.  \n  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33487468  \n  https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0140673617316653\n\nThese programs matter because they show the platform is portable across pathogens. But most remain early-stage or niche compared with flu/RSV.\n\n**Assessment:** useful and promising, especially for outbreak response, but **second-tier in maturity and impact** compared with flu and cancer.\n\n---\n\n## 3.7 Autoimmune disease: conceptually exciting, but still early\n\nOne of the most intriguing directions is not classic vaccination at all, but **tolerizing mRNA**: using mRNA to teach the immune system not to attack self-antigens.\n\n### Evidence\nA 2021 Science paper from BioNTech researchers showed that a **noninflammatory mRNA vaccine** could suppress disease in mouse models of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, a model used for multiple sclerosis research.  \nSources: Science/PubMed; BioNTech press release  \nhttps://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33414215  \nhttps://www.biontech.com/us/en/home/mediaroom/news/press-releases/2021/01/biontech-publishes-data-novel-mrna-vaccine-approach-treat.html\n\n### Why this matters\nIf this approach translates to humans, it could open a new class of antigen-specific immune tolerance therapies with less generalized immunosuppression.\n\n### Caveat\nThis remains **preclinical/early translational**. There is a large gap between success in autoimmune mouse models and approved human therapies.\n\n**Assessment:** among the most interesting long-range applications, but **far less mature** than cancer or respiratory infection.\n\n---\n\n## 4) Where the field has disappointed or become more cautious\n\n## 4.1 CMV: a major reminder that late-stage success is hard\n\nCytomegalovirus looked like one of the best non-COVID mRNA vaccine opportunities because:\n- there is no licensed CMV vaccine,\n- the disease burden is meaningful,\n- and earlier studies were immunologically promising.\n\nBut Moderna announced that phase 3 **mRNA-1647** did **not** meet its primary endpoint in the congenital CMV prevention setting and said it would discontinue that program for congenital CMV.  \nSources: Moderna statement; ClinicalTrials.gov  \nhttps://www.modernatx.com/media-center/all-media/blogs/phase-3-cmv-vaccine-readout-reflections  \nhttps://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05085366\n\n**Why this matters:** it is a strong warning against assuming that every antigen can be \u201csolved\u201d by plugging it into an mRNA/LNP system.\n\n---\n\n## 5) Why some applications look more promising than others\n\nThe strongest current mRNA opportunities share several traits:\n\n### 5.1 They benefit from rapid redesign\nThis favors:\n- flu,\n- pandemic preparedness,\n- outbreak pathogens.\n\n### 5.2 They benefit from multivalency or personalization\nThis favors:\n- flu,\n- combination respiratory vaccines,\n- neoantigen cancer vaccines.\n\n### 5.3 They need strong T-cell as well as antibody responses\nThis favors:\n- cancer,\n- some chronic infections,\n- perhaps certain intracellular pathogens.\n\n### 5.4 They can tolerate complex manufacturing or premium pricing\nThis especially favors:\n- oncology,\n- not mass-market childhood vaccines in low-resource settings.\n\n---\n\n## 6) Key technical trends shaping what comes next\n\n## 6.1 Self-amplifying mRNA (sa-mRNA)\nsa-mRNA aims to get comparable or better responses at lower doses. Clinical and late-stage COVID-related sa-mRNA studies suggest this is a credible next-generation direction, though most evidence remains platform-building rather than disease-specific beyond COVID.  \nSources: Nature Medicine; PMC phase 3 sa-mRNA study  \nhttps://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-024-02955-2  \nhttps://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12396474\n\n## 6.2 Better delivery and safety engineering\nA major 2024 review emphasized that future gains depend heavily on reducing toxicity and improving tissue/cell targeting.  \nSource: Nature Reviews Drug Discovery  \nhttps://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-023-00859-3\n\n## 6.3 Thermostability and global access\nCold-chain demands still limit some use cases. Reviews of the global landscape emphasize that broader access will depend on improved formulation stability, manufacturing transfer, and regulatory standardization.  \nSources: global landscape review; CAS review  \nhttps://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12962614  \nhttps://www.cas.org/resources/cas-insights/future-mrna-vaccines\n\n---\n\n## 7) Ranked judgment: the most promising mRNA vaccine applications beyond COVID-19\n\n### Tier 1: strongest current prospects\n1. **Seasonal influenza**\n   - late-stage efficacy data,\n   - clear annual market,\n   - natural fit for rapid update.  \n   https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11970786\n\n2. **Pandemic/outbreak influenza**\n   - speed advantage is unusually valuable here.  \n   https://www.nihr.ac.uk/news/bird-flu-vaccine-trial-launches-prepare-potential-pandemic\n\n3. **Personalized cancer vaccines**\n   - strongest long-term upside,\n   - best fit for mRNA\u2019s programmability,\n   - already showing meaningful clinical signals in melanoma and mechanistic signals in pancreatic cancer.  \n   https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(23)02268-7/abstract  \n   https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06063-y\n\n### Tier 2: promising but less mature\n4. **Combination respiratory vaccines**\n   - commercially attractive,\n   - likely to build on flu and COVID platforms.  \n   https://www.modernatx.com/research/product-pipeline\n\n5. **Targeted emerging infections** such as Zika and chikungunya\n   - strong platform fit,\n   - but smaller or less predictable commercial markets.  \n   https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36682364  \n   https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37210308\n\n6. **HIV germline-targeting vaccine strategies**\n   - scientifically important,\n   - but still very early and high-risk.  \n   https://www.iavi.org/press-release/iavi-and-moderna-launch-trial-of-hiv-vaccine-antigens-delivered-through-mrna-technology\n\n### Tier 3: exciting but speculative\n7. **Autoimmune tolerizing mRNA**\n   - potentially paradigm-shifting,\n   - but not yet clinically validated in humans.  \n   https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33414215\n\n---\n\n## Conclusion\n\nThe current state of mRNA vaccine technology beyond COVID-19 is best described as **validated, expanding, but uneven**.\n\n- It is **validated** because RSV is now an approved non-COVID mRNA vaccine indication.  \n- It is **expanding** because flu, cancer, HIV, and multiple emerging infections are now active clinical targets.  \n- It is **uneven** because some late-stage bets, such as CMV, have failed, and the field still faces real constraints in delivery, tolerability, and durable efficacy.\n\nThe **most promising near-term applications** are **influenza** and broader **respiratory vaccination**, because the platform\u2019s speed, multivalency, and update flexibility match the biology and public-health need. The **most promising long-term application** is **personalized cancer vaccination**, where mRNA\u2019s programmability offers something traditional vaccine platforms largely cannot.\n\n**Short direct answer:** mRNA beyond COVID is already real in RSV, closest to major expansion in influenza, and most transformative in personalized cancer vaccines.",

        "report": "# Economic and Environmental Arguments For and Against Deep-Sea Mining\n\n## Executive summary\n\nDeep-sea mining (DSM) is proposed as a new source of metals such as nickel, cobalt, copper, and manganese from polymetallic nodules, seafloor massive sulfides, and cobalt-rich crusts on the ocean floor. Supporters argue that DSM could expand supply of critical minerals used in batteries, electrification, and renewable-energy infrastructure, reduce some harms associated with terrestrial mining, diversify supply chains, and generate revenues for states and the International Seabed Authority (ISA). Sources from the World Bank, RAND, the U.S. GAO, and industry-adjacent policy analyses all note these potential economic benefits.  \nSources: World Bank precautionary management report: https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/349631503675168052/pdf/119106-WP-PUBLIC-114p-PPDSMbackgroundfinal.pdf ; RAND: https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA3560-1.html ; GAO PDF: https://www.gao.gov/assets/720/718170.pdf ; WEF briefing paper: https://www3.weforum.org/docs/WEF_BP_Deep-Sea_Minerals_2020.pdf\n\nOpponents argue that the economic case remains highly uncertain and may be weakening. Academic and policy sources challenge the claim that DSM is necessary for the energy transition, pointing to changing battery chemistries, recycling, circular-economy strategies, and terrestrial supply expansion. They also emphasize potentially large unpriced environmental costs, governance uncertainty, liability risks, and possible effects on fisheries and other ocean-dependent industries.  \nSources: Frontiers review challenging need: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2021.706161/full ; UNEP finance briefing: https://www.unepfi.org/publications/harmful-marine-extractives-deep-sea-mining/ ; World Bank benefit-cost discussion: https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/bitstreams/50c5bdb0-e5f6-570b-baaa-a1276ee2c4c0/download ; npj Ocean Sustainability critique: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44183-025-00127-4\n\nEnvironmentally, the core concern is that DSM would damage extremely slow-growing and poorly understood deep-sea ecosystems. The scientific literature and UNEP warn of habitat destruction, biodiversity loss, sediment plumes, noise and light pollution, and uncertain but potentially important impacts on carbon cycling and ecosystem services. Many scientists therefore support a pause or moratorium until impacts are better understood.  \nSources: UNEP issue note: https://www.unep.org/resources/publication/deep-sea-mining ; Current Biology review: https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(26)00303-9 ; IUCN issues brief: https://iucn.org/resources/issues-brief/deep-sea-mining ; Science statement: https://seabedminingsciencestatement.org\n\nThe best-supported conclusion in current research is not that DSM is clearly good or clearly bad economically, but that it involves a sharp tradeoff: possible mineral-supply and geopolitical benefits versus potentially irreversible environmental damage and major uncertainty over whether the economic benefits would outweigh the full costs.\n\n---\n\n## 1. What deep-sea mining is\n\nDeep-sea mining refers to extracting mineral deposits from the seabed, usually at depths greater than 200 meters and often far deeper. The main target resources are:\n\n- **Polymetallic nodules** on abyssal plains, especially in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ)\n- **Seafloor massive sulfides** around hydrothermal vents\n- **Cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts** on seamounts\n\nThese resources contain metals including nickel, cobalt, copper, and manganese that are relevant to batteries, electrical infrastructure, and other industrial uses.  \nSources: GAO: https://www.gao.gov/assets/720/718170.pdf ; WRI overview: https://www.wri.org/insights/deep-sea-mining-explained ; ISA overview of environmental plans: https://isa.org.jm/protection-of-the-marine-environment/regional-environmental-management-plans\n\n---\n\n## 2. Economic arguments in favor of deep-sea mining\n\n## 2.1 Expanding supply of critical minerals\n\nThe strongest pro-DSM economic argument is that it could add a major new source of minerals needed for electrification and low-carbon technologies. The energy transition is expected to increase demand for minerals used in batteries, grids, and renewable infrastructure. Supporters argue that seabed resources could reduce future supply bottlenecks.  \nSources: WEF briefing: https://www3.weforum.org/docs/WEF_BP_Deep-Sea_Minerals_2020.pdf ; GAO: https://www.gao.gov/assets/720/718170.pdf ; RAND: https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA3560-1.html\n\nRAND\u2019s 2025 report frames seabed mining as potentially relevant to critical-mineral supply chains and geopolitics, especially if supply concentration or export controls worsen on land.  \nSource: https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA3560-1.html\n\n## 2.2 Diversifying and de-risking supply chains\n\nCritical-mineral markets are geographically concentrated. A few countries dominate mining, refining, or processing for several battery minerals. Proponents argue DSM could diversify supply and reduce vulnerability to geopolitical disruption, cartels, or trade restrictions.  \nSources: RAND: https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA3560-1.html ; Stimson geopolitical discussion: https://www.stimson.org/2026/current-geopolitics-shift-deep-sea-mining-debates\n\nThis argument is economic as well as strategic: diversification can reduce price volatility and supply risk for manufacturers.\n\n## 2.3 Possible reduction of some terrestrial mining harms\n\nSome pro-DSM analyses argue that collecting nodules from the seafloor may avoid certain harms associated with terrestrial mining, such as deforestation, displacement of communities, child labor risks in some mineral supply chains, and high freshwater use on land.  \nSources: WEF briefing: https://www3.weforum.org/docs/WEF_BP_Deep-Sea_Minerals_2020.pdf ; Practical Law PDF discussing drivers: https://marketingstorageragrs.blob.core.windows.net/webfiles/PracticalLaw_Jago_Lockwood_06102024.pdf\n\nThis is not an argument that DSM is impact-free; rather, it is a relative comparison claiming some impacts may be lower than those of poorly governed terrestrial mining.\n\n## 2.4 Potential public revenues and economic activity\n\nIf commercialized, DSM could generate:\n\n- royalty or fee revenues for sponsoring states and the ISA,\n- profits for operators and contractors,\n- jobs in engineering, shipping, processing, and monitoring,\n- industrial spillovers in robotics and offshore systems.\n\nThe World Bank\u2019s Pacific-focused work and other economic analyses note that governments are interested in whether seabed mining can support development or fiscal revenues.  \nSources: World Bank report: https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/349631503675168052/pdf/119106-WP-PUBLIC-114p-PPDSMbackgroundfinal.pdf ; Nicholas Institute chapter: https://nicholasinstitute.duke.edu/sites/default/files/publications/chapter_4_-_sustainable_economic_development_and_deep_sea_mining.pdf\n\n## 2.5 Potentially large resource base\n\nSome reviews note that the CCZ and other deep-sea regions contain very large quantities of target metals. This scale underpins the economic interest: if extraction becomes technically and legally viable, the resource base could be globally significant.  \nSources: Frontiers review: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2025.1598584/full ; GAO: https://www.gao.gov/assets/720/718170.pdf\n\n---\n\n## 3. Economic arguments against deep-sea mining\n\n## 3.1 The \u201cneed\u201d case is disputed\n\nA major counterargument is that DSM may not be necessary to meet mineral demand. A widely cited 2021 Frontiers article argues that the case for DSM is weakened by:\n\n- changing battery chemistry that can reduce cobalt and nickel demand,\n- increased mineral efficiency,\n- recycling and reuse,\n- circular-economy strategies,\n- improved terrestrial governance and innovation.  \nSource: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2021.706161/full\n\nThis matters economically because if DSM is not needed, its risk-adjusted business case weakens sharply.\n\n## 3.2 High uncertainty over commercial viability\n\nNo commercial-scale mining in international waters has yet been authorized. That means capital costs, operating costs, ore-processing performance, insurance, liability exposure, and regulatory delays remain highly uncertain. GAO notes that commercial mining had not yet begun, despite years of exploration and technology development.  \nSource: https://www.gao.gov/assets/720/718170.pdf\n\nAcademic critiques argue that DSM may be a risky and possibly unprofitable investment once technical, regulatory, and environmental costs are fully counted.  \nSource: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44183-025-00127-4\n\n## 3.3 Environmental damage may create large hidden or externalized costs\n\nA central economic objection is that project profitability may ignore costs imposed on others, including biodiversity loss, ecosystem-service damage, and possible impacts on fisheries or other ocean sectors. The World Bank\u2019s work on precaution in benefit-cost analysis emphasizes that DSM involves uncertainty, irreversibility, and valuation challenges that complicate standard cost-benefit analysis.  \nSource: https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/bitstreams/50c5bdb0-e5f6-570b-baaa-a1276ee2c4c0/download\n\nIf these external costs are large, then private profitability would overstate social benefit.\n\n## 3.4 Risk to other ocean-dependent industries\n\nSome critics argue DSM could conflict with fisheries, blue-economy development, and conservation-based tourism, especially in Pacific Island contexts. The concern is not only direct ecological impact but also economic opportunity cost: using the ocean for mining could undermine other, potentially more sustainable uses.  \nSources: ODI \u201cKeep the Ocean Blue\u201d: https://media.odi.org/documents/Kasanawaqa_Keep_the_Ocean_Blue.pdf ; Geneva Environment Network overview: https://www.genevaenvironmentnetwork.org/resources/updates/deep-sea-mining-and-the-role-of-geneva\n\n## 3.5 Regulatory and reputational risk\n\nFinancial institutions and civil-society analyses increasingly describe DSM as a sector with high governance and reputational risk. UNEP FI argues that financiers should focus on alternatives that reduce pressure for new extraction, especially where environmental risks remain unresolved.  \nSource: https://www.unepfi.org/publications/harmful-marine-extractives-deep-sea-mining/\n\nThis can raise the cost of capital and reduce investor appetite, which is directly relevant to economic viability.\n\n## 3.6 Benefit-sharing remains uncertain\n\nBecause seabed resources in \u201cthe Area\u201d are governed as the common heritage of humankind under UNCLOS, benefits are supposed to be shared broadly. Critics argue that the institutional design for fair benefit-sharing remains incomplete or contested, meaning economic gains may be unevenly distributed.  \nSources: Frontiers article: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2021.706161/full ; UNU brief: https://unu.edu/cpr/brief/deep-sea-mining\n\n---\n\n## 4. Environmental arguments in favor of deep-sea mining\n\nEnvironmental arguments for DSM are usually comparative rather than absolute.\n\n## 4.1 It may reduce pressure on some terrestrial ecosystems\n\nSupporters argue that, if seabed minerals substitute for some land-based mining, DSM could reduce deforestation, land clearance, toxic tailings on land, freshwater depletion, and some social harms associated with terrestrial extraction.  \nSources: WEF briefing: https://www3.weforum.org/docs/WEF_BP_Deep-Sea_Minerals_2020.pdf ; NOC overview: https://www.noc.ac.uk/our-work/sustainable-marine-economy/marine-economy-sectors/deep-sea-mining\n\nThis argument is strongest when comparing DSM with poorly regulated terrestrial mining, and weaker when terrestrial mining can be improved.\n\n## 4.2 It could support decarbonization if it supplies transition minerals\n\nAnother pro-DSM environmental argument is indirect: if DSM helps secure inputs for EVs, grids, and renewables, it could support faster decarbonization and lower greenhouse-gas emissions over time.  \nSources: WEF briefing: https://www3.weforum.org/docs/WEF_BP_Deep-Sea_Minerals_2020.pdf ; Carbon Brief overview of the debate: https://interactive.carbonbrief.org/deep-sea-mining/index.html\n\nThis is an enabling argument, not proof that DSM itself has low environmental impact.\n\n## 4.3 Some governance tools exist\n\nSupporters also note that the ISA has created environmental management approaches, including the CCZ environmental management plan and protected Areas of Particular Environmental Interest (APEIs).  \nSources: ISA REMP page: https://isa.org.jm/protection-of-the-marine-environment/regional-environmental-management-plans ; CCZ plan: https://isa.org.jm/protection-of-the-marine-environment/regional-environmental-management-plans/ccz\n\nThis supports the claim that environmental risks might be managed, though whether current tools are sufficient is contested.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Environmental arguments against deep-sea mining\n\n## 5.1 Habitat destruction and biodiversity loss\n\nThis is the most consistent finding across scientific and policy sources. Mining nodules, crusts, or sulfides would physically remove habitat and disturb seabed communities that often recover extremely slowly, if at all, because deep-sea ecosystems operate on geological and biological timescales much slower than many shallow-water systems.  \nSources: Current Biology review: https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(26)00303-9 ; IUCN issues brief: https://iucn.org/resources/issues-brief/deep-sea-mining ; UNEP issue note: https://www.unep.org/resources/publication/deep-sea-mining\n\nFor nodule fields specifically, removing nodules eliminates the hard substrate that many organisms rely on.\n\n## 5.2 Sediment plumes could spread impacts beyond the mine site\n\nMining is expected to generate plumes both at the seabed and potentially in the water column from dewatering discharges. These plumes may smother organisms, interfere with feeding, and affect ecosystems beyond the directly mined track.  \nSources: Current Biology review: https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(26)00303-9 ; NOC overview: https://www.noc.ac.uk/our-work/sustainable-marine-economy/marine-economy-sectors/deep-sea-mining\n\nPlume behavior and ecological effects remain uncertain, but uncertainty itself is part of the risk.\n\n## 5.3 Noise, vibration, and light pollution\n\nDeep-sea organisms evolved in dark, quiet, relatively stable conditions. Mining equipment and surface operations would add chronic noise, vibration, and artificial light, potentially affecting behavior, communication, and survival of deep-sea and pelagic species.  \nSources: Current Biology review: https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(26)00303-9 ; IUCN NL overview: https://www.iucn.nl/en/story/the-impact-of-deep-sea-mining-on-biodiversity-climate-and-human-cultures\n\n## 5.4 Irreversibility and poor scientific knowledge\n\nA recurring objection is that humanity still knows too little about deep-sea biodiversity and ecosystem functioning to confidently authorize industrial mining. UNEP and IUCN both emphasize large knowledge gaps.  \nSources: UNEP: https://www.unep.org/resources/publication/deep-sea-mining ; IUCN: https://iucn.org/resources/issues-brief/deep-sea-mining\n\nBecause some species are undescribed and ecosystem recovery may take centuries or longer, impacts could be effectively irreversible on human time horizons.\n\n## 5.5 Possible impacts on carbon cycling and climate-regulating functions\n\nThe deep ocean plays an important role in global carbon storage and biogeochemical cycling. Several sources warn that disturbing deep sediments and ecosystems could affect carbon sequestration or other climate-relevant functions, though the scale of these effects remains uncertain and is an active research question.  \nSources: IUCN NL: https://www.iucn.nl/en/story/the-impact-of-deep-sea-mining-on-biodiversity-climate-and-human-cultures ; Geneva Environment Network summary referencing UNEP: https://www.genevaenvironmentnetwork.org/resources/updates/deep-sea-mining-and-the-role-of-geneva\n\n## 5.6 Precautionary principle and calls for a moratorium\n\nGiven the scientific uncertainty and potential irreversibility, many researchers support a pause or moratorium. The Deep-Sea Mining Science Statement argues for pausing exploitation until robust scientific information is available to judge whether mining can occur without significant environmental damage.  \nSource: https://seabedminingsciencestatement.org\n\nIUCN members adopted a moratorium-oriented resolution in 2021, and multiple governments now support some form of pause, moratorium, or ban.  \nSources: IUCN: https://iucn.org/resources/issues-brief/deep-sea-mining ; DSCC tracking page: https://deep-sea-conservation.org/solutions/no-deep-sea-mining/momentum-for-a-moratorium\n\n---\n\n## 6. The central policy dispute: comparative harm under uncertainty\n\nThe real debate is not whether DSM has impacts. It clearly would. The dispute is whether:\n\n1. its harms are lower than the harms of additional terrestrial mining,\n2. it is actually needed for the energy transition,\n3. its environmental risks can be governed adequately,\n4. its economic benefits exceed its full social and environmental costs.\n\nCurrent research does not resolve these questions decisively. But it does show that **claims that DSM is necessary, low-impact, or obviously beneficial are not established facts**. Equally, it is also true that **DSM\u2019s supporters are not wrong to note real mineral-supply and geopolitical pressures**.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Bottom line\n\n### Best economic arguments for DSM\n- could expand supply of critical minerals,\n- diversify vulnerable supply chains,\n- reduce some terrestrial mining pressures,\n- create revenues and industrial activity.  \nSources: RAND: https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA3560-1.html ; GAO: https://www.gao.gov/assets/720/718170.pdf ; World Bank: https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/349631503675168052/pdf/119106-WP-PUBLIC-114p-PPDSMbackgroundfinal.pdf\n\n### Best economic arguments against DSM\n- commercial viability remains uncertain,\n- mineral \u201cneed\u201d may be overstated,\n- environmental externalities may be very large,\n- governance, legal, and financing risks are substantial,\n- opportunity costs to fisheries and sustainable ocean economies may be high.  \nSources: Frontiers: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2021.706161/full ; UNEP FI: https://www.unepfi.org/publications/harmful-marine-extractives-deep-sea-mining/ ; World Bank precaution analysis: https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/bitstreams/50c5bdb0-e5f6-570b-baaa-a1276ee2c4c0/download\n\n### Best environmental arguments for DSM\n- could, in principle, substitute for some land-based mining impacts,\n- could support decarbonization if it materially expands transition-mineral supply,\n- some environmental management frameworks exist.  \nSources: WEF: https://www3.weforum.org/docs/WEF_BP_Deep-Sea_Minerals_2020.pdf ; ISA: https://isa.org.jm/protection-of-the-marine-environment/regional-environmental-management-plans\n\n### Best environmental arguments against DSM\n- likely habitat destruction and biodiversity loss,\n- plume, noise, and light impacts beyond mine sites,\n- uncertain and potentially irreversible ecosystem damage,\n- insufficient scientific knowledge,\n- possible interference with ocean carbon and ecosystem services.  \nSources: Current Biology: https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(26)00303-9 ; UNEP: https://www.unep.org/resources/publication/deep-sea-mining ; IUCN: https://iucn.org/resources/issues-brief/deep-sea-mining\n\n## Direct answer\n\nThe main argument **for** deep-sea mining is that it could increase and diversify supplies of critical minerals for the energy transition and possibly reduce some harms of land-based mining. The main argument **against** it is that its economic necessity is unproven while its environmental risks\u2014especially potentially irreversible damage to poorly understood deep-sea ecosystems\u2014could be very large.",
