        "report": "# What are the economic and environmental arguments for and against deep-sea mining?\n\n## Executive summary\n\nDeep-sea mining (DSM) is proposed as a new source of nickel, cobalt, copper, and manganese from polymetallic nodules, seafloor massive sulfides, and cobalt-rich crusts in the deep ocean. The strongest **economic argument for** DSM is that it could diversify supply chains for critical minerals that are currently geographically concentrated, especially as clean-energy systems increase demand for some metals. The strongest **economic argument against** DSM is that its commercial case remains highly uncertain: mineral markets are changing, some battery chemistries are reducing nickel and cobalt intensity, recycling and substitution may reduce future demand pressure, and DSM still lacks a fully proven large-scale operating and regulatory model. Sources: IEA, World Bank, ISA ([IEA 2024](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2024), [World Bank](https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/extractiveindustries/brief/climate-smart-mining-minerals-for-climate-action), [ISA Mining Code](https://isa.org.jm/the-mining-code)).\n\nThe strongest **environmental argument against** DSM is that it would industrialize ecosystems that are poorly understood, slow to recover, and in some cases effectively irreplaceable on human timescales. Risks include direct habitat destruction, sediment plumes, impacts on midwater ecosystems, noise and light pollution, and uncertain effects on deep-ocean ecosystem functions. Long-term disturbance experiments show ecological effects can persist for decades. Sources: IUCN, PNAS, Scientific Reports, Frontiers, Nature Sustainability ([IUCN](https://iucn.org/resources/issues-brief/deep-sea-mining), [Drazen et al. 2020](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2011914117), [Simon-Lled\u00f3 et al. 2019](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-019-44492-w), [Niner et al. 2018](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2018.00053/full), [Levin et al. 2020](https://ideas.repec.org/a/nat/natsus/v3y2020i10d10.1038_s41893-020-0558-x.html)).\n\nThe main **environmental argument for** DSM is comparative: some supporters argue it could avoid certain harms associated with land mining, such as deforestation, large volumes of overburden, road building, freshwater use, and displacement of human communities. But that claim is conditional and disputed, because it depends on how marine impacts are valued and on whether deep-sea harms can be effectively limited or restored. Sources: IUCN, ISA, Miller et al. ([IUCN](https://iucn.org/resources/issues-brief/deep-sea-mining), [ISA](https://isa.org.jm/the-mining-code), [Miller et al. 2018](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fmars.2017.00418/full)).\n\n## 1. Background: what deep-sea mining is\n\nDeep-sea mining refers to extracting mineral deposits from the seabed, generally below 200 meters. In international waters, mining activities in \u201cthe Area\u201d are overseen by the International Seabed Authority (ISA), which has issued exploration contracts but is still developing the exploitation regime for commercial mining. The main target resources are polymetallic nodules, polymetallic sulfides, and cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts ([ISA exploration contracts](https://isa.org.jm/exploration-contracts), [ISA Mining Code](https://isa.org.jm/the-mining-code), [ISA draft exploitation regulations](https://isa.org.jm/the-mining-code/draft-exploitation-regulations-2)).\n\n## 2. Economic arguments in favor of deep-sea mining\n\n### 2.1 Supply diversification for critical minerals\n\nThe strongest pro-DSM economic case is supply security. The International Energy Agency has emphasized that critical mineral supply chains are highly concentrated, especially refining and processing. That concentration creates vulnerability to trade restrictions, geopolitical shocks, and investment bottlenecks. DSM advocates argue that seabed resources could provide an additional source of nickel, cobalt, copper, and manganese and therefore reduce overreliance on a few terrestrial suppliers ([IEA critical minerals topic](https://www.iea.org/topics/critical-minerals), [IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2024](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2024)).\n\n### 2.2 Rising demand from the energy transition\n\nThe World Bank\u2019s climate-smart mining work argues that clean-energy technologies are much more mineral-intensive than fossil-based energy systems, and that large increases in mineral production will be needed to support decarbonization. Proponents of DSM use this broader demand outlook to argue that ruling out a potentially large new mineral source could make the energy transition more supply-constrained or more expensive ([World Bank overview](https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/climate-smart-mining/overview), [World Bank report page](https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/4dd08d0c-ab51-4955-a464-35a95201a5eb)).\n\n### 2.3 Multi-metal deposits\n\nPolymetallic nodules contain several commercially interesting metals in one deposit. Supporters argue this could reduce the need for multiple separate mines on land and, in principle, create efficiencies if one extraction system produces several battery-relevant inputs at once. This is often presented as a comparative economic advantage over some lower-grade terrestrial ores ([Miller et al. 2018](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fmars.2017.00418/full)).\n\n### 2.4 Strategic option value\n\nEven if DSM is not immediately necessary, supporters argue it has strategic value as an \u201coption\u201d in case terrestrial supplies tighten, geopolitical tensions increase, or ore grades decline. This is less an argument that DSM is obviously cheapest today than an argument that it may be valuable to have it available as a future source of supply ([IEA 2024](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2024)).\n\n## 3. Economic arguments against deep-sea mining\n\n### 3.1 The \u201curgent need\u201d case is weaker than proponents suggest\n\nThe same IEA outlook that highlights long-term supply risks also reports that some critical mineral markets loosened after the severe tightness of 2021\u20132022, with price corrections and new supply entering the market. That weakens the claim that DSM is urgently required in the short term. A high-cost new mining industry is economically less compelling if terrestrial markets are already adjusting ([IEA 2024](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2024)).\n\n### 3.2 Demand uncertainty from technology shifts\n\nDSM\u2019s most cited metals are nickel and cobalt, but battery chemistry is evolving. The IEA notes growing use of lithium iron phosphate batteries, which reduce demand intensity for nickel and cobalt in part of the EV market. That does not eliminate demand, but it increases uncertainty about whether deep-sea nodules will be as economically indispensable as some early advocates claimed ([IEA 2024](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2024)).\n\n### 3.3 Competition from recycling, substitution, and better terrestrial governance\n\nA major anti-DSM economic argument is that supply problems need not be solved only by opening new frontiers. Recycling, substitution, material efficiency, and improved terrestrial mining and processing can also relieve pressure. The World Bank and IEA both discuss these levers as part of a broader critical-minerals strategy ([World Bank](https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/extractiveindustries/brief/climate-smart-mining-minerals-for-climate-action), [IEA 2024](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2024)).\n\n### 3.4 High commercial and regulatory uncertainty\n\nDSM has no mature, established commercial model in international waters. The ISA has exploration contracts in force, but exploitation regulations are still under negotiation. That means companies still face uncertainty about royalties, liability, environmental requirements, insurance, monitoring, and enforcement. Such uncertainty raises financing costs and makes investment risk unusually high ([ISA exploration contracts](https://isa.org.jm/exploration-contracts), [ISA Mining Code](https://isa.org.jm/the-mining-code), [ISA draft exploitation regulations](https://isa.org.jm/the-mining-code/draft-exploitation-regulations-2)).\n\n### 3.5 Environmental externalities may make private profits socially misleading\n\nEven if a DSM project appears privately profitable, that does not mean it is socially efficient. If biodiversity loss, ecosystem disruption, or long-tail liabilities are large and hard to price, conventional project economics may understate the true cost. This is both an environmental and an economic argument against DSM ([Levin et al. 2020](https://ideas.repec.org/a/nat/natsus/v3y2020i10d10.1038_s41893-020-0558-x.html), [Niner et al. 2018](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2018.00053/full)).\n\n## 4. Environmental arguments in favor of deep-sea mining\n\n### 4.1 Possible avoidance of some land-based impacts\n\nThe main environmental case for DSM is comparative. Some supporters argue that collecting nodules from abyssal plains could avoid some harms associated with land mining, such as deforestation, open pits, road construction, tailings dams, freshwater demand, and displacement of nearby communities. On this view, DSM does not have to be impact-free to be preferable; it only has to be less damaging than some terrestrial alternatives ([IUCN](https://iucn.org/resources/issues-brief/deep-sea-mining), [Miller et al. 2018](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fmars.2017.00418/full)).\n\n### 4.2 Potentially lower visible human conflict in remote areas\n\nSupporters sometimes argue that remote abyssal mining areas are far from population centers and therefore may avoid some direct land-rights conflicts and social disruption associated with terrestrial extraction. This is a real comparative consideration, though it does not address ecological harm to the marine environment itself ([ISA](https://isa.org.jm/the-mining-code), [Miller et al. 2018](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fmars.2017.00418/full)).\n\n### 4.3 Theoretically controllable through international regulation\n\nBecause mining in the Area falls under a treaty-based international regime, proponents argue that DSM could, in theory, be governed under uniform environmental standards, mandatory baseline studies, and shared monitoring rules rather than under uneven national systems. This is a governance argument for proceeding carefully rather than rejecting the industry outright ([ISA Mining Code](https://isa.org.jm/the-mining-code)).\n\n## 5. Environmental arguments against deep-sea mining\n\n### 5.1 Direct habitat destruction in ecosystems that recover very slowly\n\nThe strongest environmental objection is that DSM would remove or heavily disrupt habitats that formed over geological timescales. In nodule fields, the nodules themselves are habitat for sessile organisms. Removing them is not like temporary disturbance on a fast-recovering surface ecosystem. IUCN states that deep-sea mining could severely harm marine biodiversity and that we still lack the knowledge and means to protect these ecosystems adequately ([IUCN brief](https://iucn.org/resources/issues-brief/deep-sea-mining)).\n\n### 5.2 Long-term evidence suggests impacts can persist for decades\n\nLong-running disturbance studies are among the most important pieces of evidence in this debate. Simon-Lled\u00f3 and colleagues found that the physical and biological effects of simulated deep-sea mining were still evident after 26 years, indicating very slow recovery ([Simon-Lled\u00f3 et al. 2019](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-019-44492-w)). That finding strongly supports the argument that DSM damage may be effectively irreversible on policy-relevant timescales.\n\n### 5.3 Sediment plumes and water-column impacts\n\nMining is expected to create sediment plumes both at the seabed and in the water column. Drazen and colleagues argue that these plumes, along with mining noise, may create substantial risks not just for benthic communities but also for midwater ecosystems. This matters because early DSM debates often focused too narrowly on the seafloor itself ([Drazen et al. 2020](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2011914117)).\n\n### 5.4 Noise and light pollution\n\nThe deep ocean is naturally dark and relatively quiet. Industrial mining would introduce continuous noise, vibration, and artificial light into environments where many organisms are adapted to stable sensory conditions. The science is still developing, but this is widely recognized as a plausible and important impact pathway ([Miller et al. 2018](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fmars.2017.00418/full), [Drazen et al. 2020](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2011914117)).\n\n### 5.5 Weak prospects for restoration or biodiversity offsets\n\nNiner and colleagues argue that \u201cno net loss\u201d of biodiversity is effectively an impossible aim for deep-sea mining under current knowledge and management tools. This undermines one of the standard approaches used in other extractive industries: offset the damage elsewhere or restore the site later. In the deep sea, that may not be realistic ([Niner et al. 2018](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2018.00053/full)).\n\n### 5.6 Governance is not yet commensurate with the risks\n\nLevin and colleagues argue that major sustainability challenges remain unresolved, including thresholds for serious harm, cumulative impacts, monitoring, and benefit-sharing. Critics therefore argue that proceeding before the science and regulatory regime are clearly adequate would be premature ([Levin et al. 2020](https://ideas.repec.org/a/nat/natsus/v3y2020i10d10.1038_s41893-020-0558-x.html), [ISA draft exploitation regulations](https://isa.org.jm/the-mining-code/draft-exploitation-regulations-2)).\n\n## 6. The core trade-off\n\nThe debate is not simply \u201cminerals versus environment.\u201d It is a choice between:\n\n1. **Opening a new mineral frontier** that may diversify supply and reduce some terrestrial impacts, but whose economics remain uncertain; and  \n2. **Avoiding industrialization of deep-ocean ecosystems** that are poorly understood, slow to recover, and likely difficult or impossible to restore if damaged.\n\nThe balance of current evidence supports a cautious conclusion: the case **for** DSM is strongest on strategic supply diversification and comparative arguments against some land-mining harms; the case **against** DSM is strongest on ecological uncertainty, irreversibility, and unresolved governance and commercial risk.\n\n## 7. Conclusion\n\nEconomically, deep-sea mining\u2019s best argument is that it could provide an additional source of critical minerals in a world worried about concentrated supply chains. Its weakest point is that it may arrive into markets that are changing quickly, while carrying unusually high technical, financial, and regulatory risk.\n\nEnvironmentally, deep-sea mining\u2019s best argument is only relative: it may avoid some harms of land mining. Its weakest point is also its most serious one: the deep sea is not empty, recovery is slow, and the evidence suggests that mining could cause long-lasting or irreversible damage in ecosystems that are not yet well understood.\n\n**Short answer:** The main argument for deep-sea mining is critical-mineral supply diversification; the main argument against it is potentially irreversible environmental harm combined with high economic and regulatory uncertainty.",

        "report": "# How Precision Agriculture Is Changing Farming, and What Evidence Exists for Its Impact on Yields and Sustainability\n\n## Executive summary\n\nPrecision agriculture is changing farming by shifting decisions from field-average management to site-specific, data-driven management. In practice, that means using technologies such as GPS guidance, yield monitors, soil and crop sensors, remote sensing, variable-rate application, connected machinery, and decision-support software to adjust seeds, fertilizer, pesticides, irrigation, and field operations to local conditions instead of treating every acre the same. FAO defines precision agriculture as \u201ca management strategy that gathers, processes and analyses temporal, spatial and individual data and combines it with other information to support management decisions according to estimated variability for improved resource use efficiency, productivity, quality, profitability and sustainability.\u201d  \nSource: FAO AGROVOC, https://www.fao.org/agrovoc/news/agrovoc-concept-week-precision-agriculture\n\nThe strongest evidence suggests three broad conclusions:\n\n1. **Precision agriculture can improve yields, but effects are variable rather than universal.** Yield gains are often largest where fields are heterogeneous, management is already input-intensive, or technologies are bundled effectively. Evidence from reviews and case studies generally finds positive but context-dependent yield effects rather than guaranteed large gains everywhere.  \n   Sources: USDA ERS, https://www.ers.usda.gov/media/8791/err-217.pdf?v=90122 ; PMC systematic review, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11483651\n\n2. **The clearest and most consistent benefits are on input efficiency and environmental performance.** Across the literature, the most repeated findings are reductions in over-application of fertilizer, pesticides, fuel, and irrigation water, along with lower runoff risk and, in some cases, lower greenhouse-gas emissions.  \n   Sources: Nature review summary page, https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x ; USDA ERS digital era report, https://ers.usda.gov/sites/default/files/_laserfiche/publications/105894/EIB-248.pdf\n\n3. **Adoption is growing, but uneven.** Easier-to-use technologies such as guidance systems and yield monitors have diffused faster than more management-intensive tools like variable-rate application and integrated analytics. Cost, interoperability, broadband/connectivity, data skills, and uncertainty about returns remain major constraints.  \n   Sources: USDA ERS, https://www.ers.usda.gov/publications/105893 ; GAO, https://www.gao.gov/assets/d24105962.pdf\n\n## 1) What precision agriculture is changing in farming\n\nPrecision agriculture changes farming in two main ways.\n\n### A. It changes how farmers observe fields\nInstead of relying mainly on whole-field averages and experience alone, farmers can now collect fine-grained data on:\n- yield variation within fields,\n- soil properties,\n- moisture and nutrient status,\n- weed, pest, and disease pressure,\n- weather and microclimate,\n- machinery performance and application accuracy.\n\nUSDA describes core precision technologies as yield monitors and mapping, GPS guidance, and variable-rate technologies, with newer systems extending into automatic section control, telematics, remote sensing, sensors, and decision support.  \nSource: USDA ERS, *Precision Agriculture in the Digital Era: Recent Adoption on U.S. Farms*, https://ers.usda.gov/sites/default/files/_laserfiche/publications/105894/EIB-248.pdf\n\n### B. It changes how farmers act on that information\nThe practical shift is from \u201cuniform application\u201d to \u201ctargeted application.\u201d Farmers can:\n- plant at different seeding rates in different parts of a field,\n- vary fertilizer and lime by soil need,\n- apply pesticides only where pressure is detected,\n- use auto-guidance and section control to reduce overlap,\n- schedule irrigation using sensor or imagery data,\n- identify unprofitable field zones for alternative management.\n\nFAO and USDA both frame precision agriculture around improved resource-use efficiency and site-specific management rather than simply adding gadgets to existing farming.  \nSources:  \nFAO, https://www.fao.org/agrovoc/news/agrovoc-concept-week-precision-agriculture  \nUSDA ERS, https://ers.usda.gov/sites/default/files/_laserfiche/publications/105894/EIB-248.pdf\n\n## 2) How far adoption has progressed\n\nAdoption has been substantial, especially on major row crops in the United States, but it varies strongly by technology and crop.\n\nUSDA ERS reports that adoption of yield maps, soil maps, and variable-rate technologies has been substantial on corn and soybean acreage for many years, while adoption on crops such as winter wheat, cotton, sorghum, and rice has generally been lower. It also notes that variable-rate technology use rose over time; for example, VRT adoption on U.S. corn acreage reached 37.4% in 2016, up from 11.5% in 2005.  \nSources:  \nUSDA ERS publication page, https://www.ers.usda.gov/publications/105893  \nUSDA ERS chart note, https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/charts-of-note/107116\n\nEarlier USDA work found that yield monitors were among the most widely adopted precision tools on corn and soybean farms, while mapping and VRT lagged behind guidance systems.  \nSource: USDA ERS Amber Waves, http://www.ers.usda.gov/amber-waves/2016/december/precision-agriculture-technologies-and-factors-affecting-their-adoption\n\nThe pattern matters because it helps explain why measured impacts vary: some technologies reduce waste directly and immediately, while others require better data interpretation and management changes before benefits show up.\n\n## 3) Evidence on yields: what the research actually shows\n\n## A. Precision agriculture often raises yields, but not always by a lot\n\nA 2024 systematic review in *Sustainability* concluded that precision agriculture technologies generally enhance productivity and environmental sustainability, with variable-rate technology, sensors, and remote sensing often improving crop management and yield outcomes.  \nSource: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11483651\n\nThat finding fits the broader logic of precision agriculture: yields can improve when limiting factors are identified earlier, inputs are matched better to crop needs, and stress is managed more precisely. But the review also indicates that outcomes depend on crop, region, technology, and management quality.\n\nA separate study on U.S. corn farms from USDA ERS found that the impact of precision-agriculture adoption on profits was \u201cpositive, but small.\u201d That is not a direct yield estimate, but it is important evidence that even where agronomic benefits exist, farm-level economic gains may be modest once equipment, software, and management costs are considered.  \nSource: USDA ERS, *Farm Profits and Adoption of Precision Agriculture*, https://www.ers.usda.gov/media/8791/err-217.pdf?v=90122\n\n## B. The most credible interpretation is \u201ccontext-dependent improvement\u201d\nThe best-supported interpretation is not that precision agriculture automatically boosts yields everywhere. Instead:\n- **Yield gains are more likely** where soil and yield variability within fields is large.\n- **Benefits increase** when technologies are combined, such as maps + VRT + decision support.\n- **Returns can be small or delayed** if farms lack the data skills, scale, connectivity, or agronomic support needed to turn data into better decisions.\n\nUSDA\u2019s cost-savings analysis for corn farms found that combinations of technologies can matter: VRT paired with yield mapping was associated with slightly higher per-acre savings than VRT with soil mapping alone.  \nSource: USDA ERS Amber Waves, http://www.ers.usda.gov/amber-waves/2016/may/cost-savings-from-precision-agriculture-technologies-on-u-s-corn-farms\n\nIn short, the evidence supports **selective yield improvement and better consistency of management**, not a simple universal yield revolution.\n\n## 4) Evidence on sustainability: where the case is strongest\n\nThis is where the evidence is most persuasive.\n\n## A. Fertilizer efficiency and nutrient losses\n\nA recent review of evidence on precision agriculture and environmental sustainability found that among 54 field-trial or modeling papers identified, 45 showed environmental benefits. The strongest evidence was for variable-rate technologies in grain farming, especially **reduced fertilizer use** relative to uniform application.  \nSource: Nature review summary, https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x\n\nThat matters because fertilizer misuse is a major source of:\n- nitrate leaching,\n- phosphorus runoff,\n- eutrophication,\n- nitrous oxide emissions.\n\nPrecision application does not eliminate these risks, but the literature supports the conclusion that it can reduce excess application and improve nutrient-use efficiency when implemented well.\n\nThe International Fertilizer Association similarly describes precision agriculture as improving nutrient-use efficiency by enabling more accurate monitoring and application of plant nutrients.  \nSource: https://www.fertilizer.org/science/emerging-products-and-services/precision-agriculture\n\n## B. Pesticide use and crop protection\n\nThe same Nature review found evidence of **reduced herbicide or pesticide use** in many studies.  \nSource: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x\n\nA meta-analysis on precision farming technologies for crop protection also concluded that precision approaches can optimize input use and support lower-cost, more targeted protection strategies.  \nSource: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2772375523001521\n\nThe mechanism is straightforward: sensing, mapping, and spot-treatment allow farmers to spray where pressure exists instead of blanket-treating whole fields. In sustainability terms, that can reduce chemical load, drift risk, and non-target exposure.\n\n## C. Water use and irrigation\n\nPrecision irrigation tools use soil-moisture sensors, weather data, and remote sensing to better align irrigation timing and amount with crop need. The evidence base is weaker and more region-specific than for fertilizer management, but reviews generally report **reduced water use or reduced water contamination risk** in a significant share of studies.  \nSources:  \nNature review summary, https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x  \nReview on precision agriculture and water conservation, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11598231\n\nThis is especially relevant in arid and water-stressed regions, where small improvements in irrigation timing can materially improve water productivity.\n\n## D. Fuel use, overlap reduction, and greenhouse gases\n\nGPS guidance and automatic section control can reduce overlap in passes for seeding, spraying, and fertilizer spreading. That lowers:\n- fuel use,\n- machine hours,\n- operator fatigue,\n- unnecessary input use.\n\nUSDA ARS highlights reduced overlap from tractor guidance as a core benefit of precision agriculture systems.  \nSource: https://www.ars.usda.gov/oc/utm/benefits-and-evolution-of-precision-agriculture\n\nThe evidence review in Nature also found studies showing **reduced GHG emissions or fuel consumption**.  \nSource: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x\n\nA 2024 review of life-cycle impacts and costs of precision agriculture concluded that research increasingly points to environmental benefits, but also that the evidence remains uneven and sometimes difficult to compare across technologies and production systems.  \nSource: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352550924003221\n\n## E. Soil and land stewardship\n\nPrecision agriculture can also improve sustainability by identifying low-performing or environmentally sensitive zones within fields. That enables:\n- differential management,\n- reduced intensity in marginal areas,\n- targeted conservation,\n- better matching of land use to profitability and risk.\n\nResearch on \u201cprecision conservation\u201d uses spatial yield and profit data to identify areas that could be managed differently or removed from intensive production.  \nSource: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0308521X18305584\n\nThis does not mean all precision agriculture leads automatically to conservation, but it expands the information base for such decisions.\n\n## 5) What the evidence does and does not prove\n\n## What is well supported\nThe strongest evidence supports these claims:\n- precision agriculture improves **information quality** and **site-specific decision-making**;\n- it often improves **input-use efficiency**;\n- it frequently reduces **over-application** of fertilizer, pesticides, water, and fuel;\n- it can improve **yields and profitability**, especially in the right contexts.\n\nSources:  \nFAO, https://www.fao.org/agrovoc/news/agrovoc-concept-week-precision-agriculture  \nUSDA ERS, https://ers.usda.gov/sites/default/files/_laserfiche/publications/105894/EIB-248.pdf  \nUSDA ERS, https://www.ers.usda.gov/media/8791/err-217.pdf?v=90122  \nNature review summary, https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x\n\n## What remains uncertain\nThe evidence is less definitive on:\n- the **average size** of yield gains across all crops and regions,\n- whether benefits justify costs for all farm sizes,\n- long-term whole-farm emissions effects,\n- adoption impacts in low-connectivity or low-capital settings,\n- whether one technology alone performs as well as a well-integrated package.\n\nGAO noted that interoperability problems, lack of standards, and other barriers can limit adoption and benefits.  \nSource: https://www.gao.gov/assets/d24105962.pdf\n\nUSDA ARS and other sources also point to training, technical support, and data-management challenges as important constraints.  \nSource: USDA ARS educational needs paper, https://www.ars.usda.gov/ARSUserFiles/50701000/cswq-0196-114689.pdf\n\n## 6) Why results vary so much\n\nPrecision agriculture is not one thing. It is a stack of tools and decisions. That helps explain mixed evidence.\n\n### Factors that increase impact\n- strong field variability,\n- high-value crops or large input bills,\n- good quality data,\n- agronomic interpretation capacity,\n- integrated technology use,\n- reliable connectivity and service support.\n\n### Factors that reduce impact\n- small or relatively uniform fields,\n- weak data interpretation,\n- incompatible software/equipment,\n- high upfront costs,\n- insufficient broadband,\n- limited operator training,\n- uncertainty about ownership and value of farm data.\n\nA review of barriers to IoT-based precision agriculture identifies cost, power requirements, communication range, latency, scalability, storage, processing, and interoperability as recurring obstacles.  \nSource: https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0472/13/1/163\n\nGAO also identifies lack of uniform standards and interoperability as a barrier to effective use.  \nSource: https://www.gao.gov/assets/d24105962.pdf\n\n## 7) Overall assessment\n\nPrecision agriculture is changing farming less by replacing farmers than by changing how they allocate attention, inputs, and risk. The clearest transformation is from uniform management toward **spatially and temporally targeted management** supported by digital data.\n\nOn impact:\n- **Yields:** evidence is positive but mixed in magnitude; gains are real in many settings, but not guaranteed and often modest when averaged broadly.\n- **Sustainability:** evidence is stronger and more consistent for improved efficiency and reduced environmental pressure, especially through more precise use of fertilizer, pesticides, water, and fuel.\n- **Economics:** profitability can improve, but returns depend heavily on scale, crop type, management capability, and whether technologies are used as part of a coherent system rather than as isolated add-ons.\n\nThe most defensible conclusion from current research is that precision agriculture is a meaningful tool for **sustainable intensification**, but not a standalone solution. Its biggest proven value is making farming more precise, less wasteful, and in many cases more resilient.\n\n## Selected sources\n\n- FAO AGROVOC definition of precision agriculture: https://www.fao.org/agrovoc/news/agrovoc-concept-week-precision-agriculture  \n- USDA ERS, *Precision Agriculture in the Digital Era: Recent Adoption on U.S. Farms*: https://www.ers.usda.gov/publications/105893  \n- USDA ERS PDF of same report: https://ers.usda.gov/sites/default/files/_laserfiche/publications/105894/EIB-248.pdf  \n- USDA ERS, *Farm Profits and Adoption of Precision Agriculture*: https://www.ers.usda.gov/media/8791/err-217.pdf?v=90122  \n- USDA ERS chart note on VRT adoption: https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/charts-of-note/107116  \n- USDA ARS, *Benefits and Evolution of Precision Agriculture*: https://www.ars.usda.gov/oc/utm/benefits-and-evolution-of-precision-agriculture  \n- Systematic review on sustainable crop production and environmental sustainability: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11483651  \n- Review summary on precision agriculture and environmental sustainability: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x  \n- Review of life-cycle impacts and costs: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352550924003221  \n- Meta-analysis on crop protection technologies: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2772375523001521  \n- GAO report on precision agriculture challenges and policy options: https://www.gao.gov/assets/d24105962.pdf  \n- Review of IoT adoption barriers in precision agriculture: https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0472/13/1/163  \n\nDirect answer: Precision agriculture is changing farming by enabling site-specific, data-driven management of seeds, fertilizer, pesticides, water, and machinery; the best evidence shows modest-to-positive but variable yield gains, and stronger, more consistent improvements in input efficiency and sustainability.",

        "report": "# How precision agriculture is changing farming, and what evidence exists for its impact on yields and sustainability\n\n## Executive summary\n\nPrecision agriculture is changing farming by shifting decisions from uniform, field-wide management to site-specific, data-driven management. Instead of applying the same amount of seed, fertilizer, pesticide, or water everywhere, farmers use tools such as GPS guidance, yield monitors, soil and crop sensors, remote sensing, variable-rate technology (VRT), and decision-support software to manage variability within fields and over time. Authoritative definitions from FAO and USDA describe it as a strategy for using spatial, temporal, and individual data to improve resource-use efficiency, productivity, profitability, and sustainability.  \nSources: FAO AGROVOC definition: https://www.fao.org/agrovoc/news/agrovoc-concept-week-precision-agriculture ; USDA ERS overview: https://www.ers.usda.gov/publications/105893\n\nThe evidence suggests three main conclusions:\n\n1. **Precision agriculture clearly changes farm operations** by making them more data-intensive and more targeted in how inputs are applied. Adoption has been substantial for some technologies, especially guidance/autosteer and yield monitors, though more advanced tools such as variable-rate application remain less universal and vary by crop and farm size.  \n   Sources: USDA ERS adoption reports:  \n   https://www.ers.usda.gov/publications/105893  \n   http://www.ers.usda.gov/amber-waves/2016/december/precision-agriculture-technologies-and-factors-affecting-their-adoption\n\n2. **Evidence on yields is positive but not uniform.** Reviews and systematic assessments generally find that precision agriculture can increase yields and profitability, especially when technologies are used to manage nutrients, water, and pests more precisely. But the size of the benefit varies widely by crop, farm, management quality, and technology bundle. Some USDA evidence finds positive but small profit effects in U.S. corn, which is a reminder that yield gains do not automatically translate into large whole-farm gains in every setting.  \n   Sources:  \n   USDA ERS profit study: https://www.ers.usda.gov/media/8791/err-217.pdf?v=90122  \n   Systematic review: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11483651  \n   Fertilizer-focused review: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/agronomy/articles/10.3389/fagro.2025.1665444/full\n\n3. **Evidence on sustainability is stronger for input efficiency than for broad environmental transformation.** The best-supported environmental impacts are reduced fertilizer, pesticide, water, and fuel use where technology is properly implemented. A recent Nature review found that most field-trial or modeling studies it identified reported environmental benefits, especially from variable-rate technologies in grain farming. However, evidence is still uneven across crops, regions, and outcomes, and not every study shows benefits.  \n   Source: Nature review: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x\n\n---\n\n## 1) What precision agriculture is\n\nFAO defines precision agriculture as a management strategy that \u201cgathers, processes and analyses temporal, spatial and individual data\u201d to support decisions that improve resource-use efficiency, productivity, quality, profitability, and sustainability.  \nSource: https://www.fao.org/agrovoc/news/agrovoc-concept-week-precision-agriculture\n\nUSDA ERS describes precision agriculture as a suite of technologies such as GPS soil and yield mapping, GPS tractor guidance, and variable-rate input application that allow farm operators to fine-tune production practices.  \nSource: https://www.ers.usda.gov/media/8791/err-217.pdf?v=90122\n\nIn practice, this means farming is moving from:\n- **uniform treatment of whole fields**\nto\n- **targeted management of smaller zones or even individual plants**\n\nKey technologies include:\n- GPS guidance/autosteer\n- yield monitors and yield maps\n- soil maps and grid/zone sampling\n- variable-rate application of seed, fertilizer, lime, pesticides, and irrigation\n- remote sensing from satellites, aircraft, or drones\n- in-field sensors\n- farm management and decision-support software  \nSource: USDA ERS digital era report: https://ers.usda.gov/sites/default/files/_laserfiche/publications/105894/EIB-248.pdf\n\n---\n\n## 2) How it is changing farming\n\n### A. It makes farming more data-driven\nPrecision agriculture converts field conditions into digital information: yield maps, soil maps, weather data, imagery, and sensor readings. These data feed decisions about where and when to plant, irrigate, fertilize, spray, and harvest.  \nSource: USDA ERS digital era report: https://ers.usda.gov/sites/default/files/_laserfiche/publications/105894/EIB-248.pdf\n\n### B. It changes machinery from passive equipment into decision-executing systems\nGuidance systems reduce overlap and improve traffic patterns. Variable-rate systems let equipment adjust input rates as it moves across the field. This changes the role of machinery from simply applying inputs to applying them selectively.  \nSources:  \nUSDA ERS adoption article: http://www.ers.usda.gov/amber-waves/2016/december/precision-agriculture-technologies-and-factors-affecting-their-adoption  \nUSDA ARS discussion: https://www.ars.usda.gov/oc/utm/benefits-and-evolution-of-precision-agriculture\n\n### C. It shifts management toward within-field variability\nTraditional management often assumes the field is fairly uniform. Precision agriculture starts from the opposite assumption: soils, moisture, pest pressure, and yield potential vary materially within fields, so management should vary too.  \nSource: FAO definition and discussion: https://www.fao.org/agrovoc/news/agrovoc-concept-week-precision-agriculture\n\n### D. Adoption is real, but uneven\nUSDA data show that adoption has grown substantially, especially for guidance systems and yield monitoring. Yet adoption differs across technologies and crops. In earlier USDA data, guidance systems were used on about half of planted acres for some crops, while GPS soil mapping and VRT were below 25 percent. USDA\u2019s 2023 report shows that yield maps, soil maps, and VRT are substantial in corn and soybean systems but still much less common in crops such as winter wheat, cotton, sorghum, and rice. Larger farms tend to adopt more.  \nSources:  \nhttp://www.ers.usda.gov/amber-waves/2016/december/precision-agriculture-technologies-and-factors-affecting-their-adoption  \nhttps://www.ers.usda.gov/publications/105893  \nhttps://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/charts-of-note/107116\n\n---\n\n## 3) Evidence for impact on yields\n\n## Overall finding\nThe balance of the literature supports the claim that precision agriculture **can improve yields**, but the effect is heterogeneous rather than universal.\n\n### A. Reviews generally find yield gains\nA systematic review on precision agriculture technologies for sustainable crop production concludes that these technologies enhance productivity alongside environmental sustainability. It identifies VRT, remote sensing, sensors, robotics, UAVs, and AI-assisted systems as tools that can boost yields and profitability when aligned with local conditions.  \nSource: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11483651\n\nA Frontiers systematic review focused on precision agriculture for fertilizer optimization similarly concludes that PA significantly improves nutrient use efficiency and crop yields.  \nSource: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/agronomy/articles/10.3389/fagro.2025.1665444/full\n\n### B. U.S. farm-level evidence is more cautious\nUSDA ERS\u2019s report **Farm Profits and Adoption of Precision Agriculture** found that the impact of key precision technologies on U.S. corn profits was **positive, but small**. This matters because if yield gains exist but are modest, or if costs of equipment/data/services are high, net gains may be limited.  \nSource: https://www.ers.usda.gov/media/8791/err-217.pdf?v=90122\n\nUSDA also reported cost savings from precision technologies on U.S. corn farms, with estimated per-acre savings associated with VRT combined with mapping. This does not prove large yield increases by itself, but it supports the broader claim that more precise management can improve production efficiency.  \nSource: http://www.ers.usda.gov/amber-waves/2016/may/cost-savings-from-precision-agriculture-technologies-on-u-s-corn-farms\n\n### C. Why yield effects vary\nThe evidence points to several reasons results differ:\n- crop type\n- climate and soil variability\n- whether the limiting factor is nutrients, water, weeds, or disease\n- whether the technology is stand-alone or part of a broader management system\n- operator skill and data interpretation\n- farm size and ability to spread fixed technology costs\n\nThese patterns are discussed in USDA adoption/profit studies and in recent reviews.  \nSources:  \nhttps://www.ers.usda.gov/media/8791/err-217.pdf?v=90122  \nhttps://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11483651\n\n### Bottom line on yields\nThe strongest defensible claim is: **precision agriculture often improves yields, especially by better matching inputs to crop needs, but the magnitude is context-dependent and not always large enough to transform profits on its own.**\n\n---\n\n## 4) Evidence for impact on sustainability\n\n## Overall finding\nEvidence is strongest that precision agriculture improves **input efficiency** and can reduce some environmental harms. Evidence is weaker, though still promising, on broader outcomes such as total greenhouse-gas reduction or long-term soil regeneration at scale.\n\n### A. Fertilizer use and nutrient efficiency\nThis is one of the most consistently supported sustainability benefits.\n\nA 2026 Nature review of 444 academic publications on precision agriculture and sustainability found 54 studies with field-trial or modeling evidence, of which **45 reported environmental benefits**. The strongest body of evidence was for **variable-rate technologies in grain farming**, especially for **decreased fertilizer use** relative to uniform applications.  \nSource: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x\n\nThe Frontiers review on fertilizer optimization found that precision agriculture significantly improves nutrient use efficiency and supports yield gains, reinforcing the idea that better targeting of fertilizer is one of PA\u2019s clearest benefits.  \nSource: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/agronomy/articles/10.3389/fagro.2025.1665444/full\n\n### B. Pesticide use\nThe same Nature review found evidence of reduced herbicide or pesticide use in many studies. This fits the logic of spot treatment, guided scouting, and sensor-based detection, though the evidence base is still more mixed than for fertilizer.  \nSource: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x\n\nThe broader systematic review of precision agriculture technologies also reports that more precise application can reduce environmental impact while supporting productivity.  \nSource: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11483651\n\n### C. Water use and irrigation\nPrecision irrigation, soil-moisture sensing, and data-driven scheduling can reduce overwatering and improve water-use efficiency. The Nature review identified studies reporting reduced water use or reduced water contamination/runoff.  \nSource: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x\n\nThe broader systematic review also identifies precision irrigation and sensing among the main pathways through which PA contributes to more sustainable crop production.  \nSource: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11483651\n\n### D. Fuel use and field operations\nGuidance/autosteer systems can reduce overlap in planting, fertilizing, and spraying, which lowers fuel use and sometimes labor use. USDA and USDA ARS materials emphasize this operational efficiency channel.  \nSources:  \nhttp://www.ers.usda.gov/amber-waves/2016/december/precision-agriculture-technologies-and-factors-affecting-their-adoption  \nhttps://www.ars.usda.gov/oc/utm/benefits-and-evolution-of-precision-agriculture\n\n### E. Greenhouse gas emissions\nThe environmental case is plausible and increasingly supported, especially through:\n- lower nitrogen fertilizer use\n- less fuel use\n- lower nitrous oxide risk from overapplication\n\nBut the evidence is less standardized than for input reduction, and whole-system GHG outcomes depend on how technologies are used. The Nature review includes studies reporting reduced GHG emissions or fuel consumption, but does not support a simple universal claim that precision agriculture always materially lowers emissions.  \nSource: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x\n\n### F. Soil quality\nSome studies in the Nature review reported improved soil quality, but this appears to be a smaller and less uniform evidence category than fertilizer savings. Precision agriculture can help avoid overapplication and compaction and can support more site-specific soil management, but long-term soil outcomes depend on complementary practices such as cover crops, reduced tillage, and rotation.  \nSource: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x\n\n### Bottom line on sustainability\nThe strongest defensible claim is: **precision agriculture most consistently improves sustainability by reducing unnecessary input use and making management more targeted; its broader environmental effects are promising but vary by technology and context.**\n\n---\n\n## 5) What the evidence does not support clearly\n\nA careful reading of the research suggests some claims should be qualified.\n\n### Not every precision tool delivers the same value\nAutosteer, yield mapping, VRT, irrigation controls, sensors, and drones are often grouped together, but they do different things and have different evidence bases. A farmer may adopt guidance because it is easy and operationally useful, while the benefits from data-heavy tools depend more on management skill.  \nSources:  \nhttp://www.ers.usda.gov/amber-waves/2016/december/precision-agriculture-technologies-and-factors-affecting-their-adoption  \nhttps://www.ers.usda.gov/publications/105893\n\n### Profit gains are not always large\nUSDA\u2019s farm-level evidence on U.S. corn found positive but small impacts on profits. That means technology can improve efficiency without revolutionizing margins, especially after accounting for capital costs, subscriptions, training, and time.  \nSource: https://www.ers.usda.gov/media/8791/err-217.pdf?v=90122\n\n### Environmental benefits are real but uneven\nThe evidence is strongest for reduced fertilizer use and other input savings, not for every sustainability metric in every crop.  \nSource: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00128-x\n\n---\n\n## 6) Why precision agriculture matters strategically\n\nEven with mixed magnitudes, precision agriculture matters because it changes the production model itself.\n\nIt helps farmers:\n- monitor fields continuously rather than episodically\n- treat variability as manageable rather than unavoidable\n- reduce waste from blanket applications\n- improve resilience under tighter environmental constraints and higher input costs\n\nThat is especially important where fertilizer, water, labor, fuel, and compliance pressures are rising. Precision agriculture is therefore not just a set of gadgets; it is a transition toward more information-intensive farming.  \nSources:  \nFAO: https://www.fao.org/agrovoc/news/agrovoc-concept-week-precision-agriculture  \nUSDA ERS: https://www.ers.usda.gov/publications/105893\n\n---\n\n## Conclusion\n\nPrecision agriculture is changing farming by replacing uniform, intuition-heavy management with site-specific, data-driven management. The clearest operational shift is that farmers can now measure variation within fields and respond with more precise applications of seed, fertilizer, chemicals, and water.\n\nThe evidence for impact is meaningful but nuanced. On **yields**, research generally points to improvements, especially when precision tools address real agronomic variability and are integrated into management, though farm-level gains can be modest and uneven. On **sustainability**, the evidence is strongest for reduced input use and greater resource efficiency, especially for fertilizer, pesticides, water, and fuel. The best-supported overall conclusion is that precision agriculture improves efficiency and often improves both yields and environmental performance, but the scale of benefit depends heavily on crop, geography, management quality, and the specific technologies used.\n\n**Short answer:** Precision agriculture is making farming more data-driven and site-specific; the best evidence shows it often raises yields modestly and more consistently improves sustainability by reducing unnecessary inputs such as fertilizer, pesticides, water, and fuel.",

// Define commands

    {
        name: 'ping',
        description: 'Replies with Pong!',
    },

        name: 'ask',
        description: 'Ask a question to the bot',
    },
];

    try {
        console.log('Started refreshing application (/) commands.');

        await rest.put(Routes.applicationCommands(process.env.DISCORD_CLIENT_ID), {
            body: commands,
        });

        console.log('Successfully reloaded application (/) commands.');
    } catch (error) {
        console.error(error);
    }
})();

FILE: docs/discord-bot/gptr-webhook.js

// gptr-webhook.js
const WebSocket = require('ws');

let socket = null;
const responseCallbacks = new Map(); // Using Map for multiple callbacks

async function initializeWebSocket() {
  if (!socket) {
    const host = 'gpt-researcher:8000';
    const ws_uri = `ws://${host}/ws`;

    socket = new WebSocket(ws_uri);

    socket.onopen = () => {
      console.log('WebSocket connection established');
    };

    socket.onmessage = (event) => {
      const data = JSON.parse(event.data);
      console.log('WebSocket data received:', data);

      // Get the callback for this request
      const callback = responseCallbacks.get('current');
      
      if (data.type === 'report') {
        // Send progress updates
        if (callback && callback.onProgress) {
          callback.onProgress(data.output);
        }
      } else if (data.content === 'dev_team_result') {
        // Send final result
        if (callback && callback.onComplete) {
          callback.onComplete(data.output);
          responseCallbacks.delete('current'); // Clean up after completion
        }
      }
    };

    socket.onclose = () => {
      console.log('WebSocket connection closed');
      socket = null;
    };

    socket.onerror = (error) => {
      console.error('WebSocket error:', error);
    };
  }
}

async function sendWebhookMessage({query, moreContext}) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    if (!socket || socket.readyState !== WebSocket.OPEN) {
      initializeWebSocket();
    }

    const data = {
      task: `${query}. Additional context: ${moreContext}`,
      report_type: 'research_report',
      report_source: 'web',
      tone: 'Objective',
      headers: {},
      repo_name: typeof repoName === 'undefined' || repoName === '' ? 'assafelovic/gpt-researcher' : repoName,
      branch_name: typeof branchName === 'undefined' || branchName === '' ? 'master' : branchName
    };

    const payload = "start " + JSON.stringify(data);

    // Store both progress and completion callbacks
    responseCallbacks.set('current', {
      onProgress: (progressData) => {
        resolve({ type: 'progress', data: progressData });
      },
      onComplete: (finalData) => {
        resolve({ type: 'complete', data: finalData });
      }
    });

    if (socket.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN) {
      socket.send(payload);
      console.log('Message sent:', payload);
    } else {
      socket.onopen = () => {
        socket.send(payload);
        console.log('Message sent after connection:', payload);
      };
    }
  });
}

module.exports = {
  sendWebhookMessage
};

FILE: docs/discord-bot/index.js

require('dotenv').config();
const { Client, GatewayIntentBits, ActionRowBuilder, Events, ModalBuilder, TextInputBuilder, TextInputStyle, ChannelType } = require('discord.js');
const keepAlive = require('./server');
const { sendWebhookMessage } = require('./gptr-webhook');
const { jsonrepair } = require('jsonrepair');
const { EmbedBuilder } = require('discord.js');

const client = new Client({
  intents: [
    GatewayIntentBits.Guilds,
    GatewayIntentBits.GuildMessages,
    GatewayIntentBits.MessageContent,
    GatewayIntentBits.DirectMessages
  ],
});

function splitMessage(message, chunkSize = 1500) {
  const chunks = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < message.length; i += chunkSize) {
    chunks.push(message.slice(i, i + chunkSize));
  }
  return chunks;
}

client.on('ready', () => {
  console.log(`Logged in as ${client.user.tag}!`);
});

// Cooldown object to store the last message time for each channel
const cooldowns = {};

client.on('messageCreate', async message => {
  if (message.author.bot) return;
  // only share the /ask guide when a new message is posted in the help forum -  limit to every 30 minutes per post
  console.log(`Channel Data: ${message.channel.id}`);
  console.log(`Message Channel Data: ${console.log(JSON.stringify(message.channel, null, 2))}`);
  
  const channelId = message.channel.id;
  const channelParentId = message.channel.parentId;
  //return if its not posted in the help forum
  if(channelParentId != '1129339320562626580') return
  
  const now = Date.now();
  const cooldownAmount = 30 * 60 * 1000; // 30 minutes in milliseconds

  if (!cooldowns[channelId] || (now - cooldowns[channelId]) > cooldownAmount) {
    // await message.reply('please use the /ask command to launch a report by typing `/ask` into the chatbox & hitting ENTER.');

    const exampleEmbed = new EmbedBuilder()
      .setTitle('please use the /ask command to launch a report by typing `/ask` into the chatbox & hitting ENTER.')
      .setImage('https://media.discordapp.net/attachments/1127851779573420053/1285577932353568902/ask.webp?ex=66eb6fff&is=66ea1e7f&hm=32bc8335ed4c09c15a8541c058bbd513cf2ce757221a116d9c248c39a12d75df&=&format=webp&width=1740&height=704');
    
    message.channel.send({ embeds: [exampleEmbed] });
    cooldowns[channelId] = now;
  }
});


client.on(Events.InteractionCreate, async interaction => {
  if (interaction.isChatInputCommand()) {
    if (interaction.commandName === 'ask') {
      const modal = new ModalBuilder()
        .setCustomId('myModal')
        .setTitle('Ask the AI Researcher');

      const queryInput = new TextInputBuilder()
        .setCustomId('queryInput')
        .setLabel('Your question')
        .setStyle(TextInputStyle.Paragraph)
        .setPlaceholder('What are you exploring today / what tickles your mind?');

      const moreContextInput = new TextInputBuilder()
        .setCustomId('moreContextInput')
        .setLabel('Additional context (optional)')
        .setStyle(TextInputStyle.Paragraph)
        .setPlaceholder('Any additional context or details that would help us understand your question better?')
        .setRequired(false);

      const firstActionRow = new ActionRowBuilder().addComponents(queryInput);
      const secondActionRow = new ActionRowBuilder().addComponents(moreContextInput);

      modal.addComponents(firstActionRow, secondActionRow);

      await interaction.showModal(modal);
    }
  } else if (interaction.isModalSubmit()) {
    if (interaction.customId === 'myModal') {
      const query = interaction.fields.getTextInputValue('queryInput');
      const moreContext = interaction.fields.getTextInputValue('moreContextInput');

      let thread;
      if (interaction?.channel?.type === ChannelType.GuildText) {
        thread = await interaction.channel.threads.create({
          name: `Discussion: ${query.slice(0, 30)}...`,
          autoArchiveDuration: 60,
          reason: 'Discussion thread for the query',
        });
      }

      await interaction.deferUpdate();

      runDevTeam({ interaction, query, moreContext, thread })
        .catch(console.error);
    }
  }
});

async function runDevTeam({ interaction, query, moreContext, thread }) {
  const queryToDisplay = `**user query**: ${query}. 
                          ${moreContext ? '\n**more context**: ' + moreContext : ''} 
                          \nBrowsing the web to investigate your query... give me a minute or so`;

  if (!thread) {
    await interaction.followUp({ content: queryToDisplay });
  } else {
    await thread.send(queryToDisplay);
  }

  try {
    while (true) {
      const response = await sendWebhookMessage({ query, moreContext });
      
      if (response.type === 'progress') {
        // Handle progress updates
        const progressChunks = splitMessage(response.data);
        for (const chunk of progressChunks) {
          if (!thread) {
            await interaction.followUp({ content: chunk });
          } else {
            await thread.send(chunk);
          }
        }
      } else if (response.type === 'complete') {
        // Handle final result
        if (response.data && response.data.rubber_ducker_thoughts) {
          let rubberDuckerChunks = '';
          let theGuidance = response.data.rubber_ducker_thoughts;

          try {
            rubberDuckerChunks = splitMessage(theGuidance);
          } catch (error) {
            console.error('Error splitting messages:', error);
            rubberDuckerChunks = splitMessage(typeof theGuidance === 'object' ? JSON.stringify(theGuidance) : theGuidance);
          }

          for (const chunk of rubberDuckerChunks) {
            if (!thread) {
              await interaction.followUp({ content: chunk });
            } else {
              await thread.send(chunk);
            }
          }
        }
        break; // Exit the loop when we get the final result
      }
    }

    return true;
  } catch (error) {
    console.error({ content: 'Error handling message:', error });
    if (!thread) {
      return await interaction.followUp({ content: 'There was an error processing your request.' });
    } else {
      return await thread.send('There was an error processing your request.');
    }
  }
}

keepAlive();
client.login(process.env.DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN);

const express = require("express")

const server = express()

server.all("/", (req, res) => {
  res.send("Bot is running!")
})

function keepAlive() {
  server.listen(5000, () => {
    console.log("Server is ready.")
  })

  // Handle uncaught exceptions
  process.on("uncaughtException", (err) => {
    console.error("Uncaught Exception:", err);
    // Graceful shutdown logic
    // process.exit(1); // Exit process to trigger Docker's restart policy
  });

  // Handle unhandled promise rejections
  process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason, promise) => {
    console.error("Unhandled Rejection at:", promise, "reason:", reason);
    // Graceful shutdown logic
    // process.exit(1); // Exit process to trigger Docker's restart policy
  });
}

"""
Custom Prompt Example for GPT Researcher

This example demonstrates how to use the custom_prompt parameter to customize report generation
based on specific formatting requirements or content needs.
"""

import asyncio
import nest_asyncio  # Required for notebooks/interactive environments

# Apply nest_asyncio to allow for nested event loops (needed in notebooks)
nest_asyncio.apply()

from gpt_researcher import GPTResearcher


async def custom_report_example():
    """Demonstrate various custom prompt examples with GPT Researcher."""
    
    # Define your research query
    query = "What are the latest advancements in renewable energy?"
    report_type = "research_report"
    
    # Initialize the researcher
    researcher = GPTResearcher(
        query=query,
        report_type=report_type,
        verbose=True  # Set to True to see detailed logs
    )
    
    # Conduct the research (this step is the same regardless of custom prompts)
    print("🔍 Conducting research...")
    await researcher.conduct_research()
    print("✅ Research completed!\n")
    
    # Example 1: Standard report (no custom prompt)
    print("\n📝 EXAMPLE 1: STANDARD REPORT\n" + "="*40)
    standard_report = await researcher.write_report()
    print(f"Standard Report Length: {len(standard_report.split())} words\n")
    print(standard_report[:500] + "...\n")  # Print first 500 chars
    
    # Example 2: Short summary with custom prompt
    print("\n📝 EXAMPLE 2: SHORT SUMMARY\n" + "="*40)
    short_prompt = "Provide a brief summary of the research findings in 2-3 paragraphs without citations."
    short_report = await researcher.write_report(custom_prompt=short_prompt)
    print(f"Short Report Length: {len(short_report.split())} words\n")
    print(short_report + "\n")
    
    # Example 3: Bullet point format
    print("\n📝 EXAMPLE 3: BULLET POINT FORMAT\n" + "="*40)
    bullet_prompt = "List the top 5 advancements in renewable energy as bullet points with a brief explanation for each."
    bullet_report = await researcher.write_report(custom_prompt=bullet_prompt)
    print(bullet_report + "\n")
    
    # Example 4: Question and answer format
    print("\n📝 EXAMPLE 4: Q&A FORMAT\n" + "="*40)
    qa_prompt = "Present the research as a Q&A session with 5 important questions and detailed answers about renewable energy advancements."
    qa_report = await researcher.write_report(custom_prompt=qa_prompt)
    print(qa_report[:500] + "...\n")  # Print first 500 chars
    
    # Example 5: Technical audience
    print("\n📝 EXAMPLE 5: TECHNICAL AUDIENCE\n" + "="*40)
    technical_prompt = "Create a technical summary focusing on engineering challenges and solutions in renewable energy. Use appropriate technical terminology."
    technical_report = await researcher.write_report(custom_prompt=technical_prompt)
    print(technical_report[:500] + "...\n")  # Print first 500 chars
    
    # Show research costs
    print("\n💰 RESEARCH COSTS")
    print(f"Total tokens used: {researcher.get_costs()}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(custom_report_example())

// index.js
const WebSocket = require('ws');

class GPTResearcher {
  constructor(options = {}) {
    this.host = options.host || 'http://localhost:8000';
    this.socket = null;
    this.responseCallbacks = new Map();
    this.logListener = options.logListener;
    this.tone = options.tone || 'Reflective';
  }

  async initializeWebSocket() {
    if (!this.socket) {      
      const protocol = this.host.includes('https') ? 'wss:' : 'ws:';
      const cleanHost = this.host.replace('http://', '').replace('https://', '');
      const ws_uri = `${protocol}//${cleanHost}/ws`;

      this.socket = new WebSocket(ws_uri);

      this.socket.onopen = () => {
        console.log('WebSocket connection established');
      };

      this.socket.onmessage = (event) => {
        const data = JSON.parse(event.data);
        
        // Handle logs with custom listener if provided
        if (this.logListener) {
          this.logListener(data);
        } else {
          console.log('WebSocket data received:', data);
        }

        const callback = this.responseCallbacks.get('current');
        
      };

      this.socket.onclose = () => {
        console.log('WebSocket connection closed');
        this.socket = null;
      };

      this.socket.onerror = (error) => {
        console.error('WebSocket error:', error);
      };
    }
  }

  async sendMessage({
    task,
    useHTTP = false,
    reportType = 'research_report',
    reportSource = 'web', 
    queryDomains = [],
    tone = 'Reflective',
    query,
    moreContext
  }) {
    const data = {
      task: query ? `${query}. Additional context: ${moreContext}` : task,
      report_type: reportType,
      report_source: reportSource,
      headers: {},
      tone: tone,
      query_domains: queryDomains
    };

    if (useHTTP) {
      return this.sendHttpRequest(data);
    }

    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      if (!this.socket || this.socket.readyState !== WebSocket.OPEN) {
        this.initializeWebSocket();
      }


      const payload = "start " + JSON.stringify(data);

      this.responseCallbacks.set('current', {
        onProgress: (progressData) => {
          resolve({ type: 'progress', data: progressData });
        },
        onComplete: (finalData) => {
          resolve({ type: 'complete', data: finalData });
        }
      });

      if (this.socket.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN) {
        this.socket.send(payload);
        console.log('Message sent:', payload);
      } else {
        this.socket.onopen = () => {
          this.socket.send(payload);
          console.log('Message sent after connection:', payload);
        };
      }
    });
  }

  async sendHttpRequest(data) {
    try {
      const response = await axios.post(`${this.host}/report/`, data);
      return { message: 'success', data: response.data };
    } catch (error) {
      console.error('HTTP request error:', error);
      return { message: 'error', error: error.message };
    }
  }

  async getReport(reportId) {
    try {
      const response = await axios.get(`${this.host}/report/${reportId}`);
      return response;
    } catch (error) {
      console.error('HTTP request error:', error);
      return { message: 'error', error: error.message };
    }
  }
}

module.exports = GPTResearcher;

function CopyInstall() {
  const [copied, setCopied] = useState(false);
  const copy = async () => {
    try {
      await navigator.clipboard.writeText(INSTALL);
      setCopied(true);
      setTimeout(() => setCopied(false), 1600);
    } catch (e) {
      /* clipboard unavailable: the command stays visible to select */
    }
  };
  return (
    <button type="button" className={styles.install} onClick={copy} aria-label="Copy install command">
      <span className={styles.prompt}>$</span>
      <code>{INSTALL}</code>
      <span className={styles.copy}>{copied ? 'Copied' : 'Copy'}</span>
    </button>
  );
}

      </code></pre>

  );

================================================================================
FILE: evals/context_filter/collect.py
================================================================================

"""Step 1: run each query once and record what reached the context filter.

Every scraped page reaches the report through
``ContextManager.get_similar_content_by_query(query, pages)``. This records
each call's inputs, so ``replay.py`` can rebuild the context from the exact
same pages with every strategy. Only the filter varies; search results and
scraping, the noisiest parts of a run, are held fixed.

    python -m evals.context_filter.collect --out runs/ --concurrency 4
"""

import argparse
import asyncio
import json
import time
from pathlib import Path

from gpt_researcher import GPTResearcher
from gpt_researcher.skills.context_manager import ContextManager

HERE = Path(__file__).parent

# researcher -> recorded calls. Patched once for the whole process, because
# runs execute concurrently and per-run patch/restore would race.
_RECORDINGS: dict[int, list] = {}
_original = ContextManager.get_similar_content_by_query


async def _recording(self, query, pages):
    calls = _RECORDINGS.get(id(self.researcher))
    if calls is not None:
        calls.append({"query": query, "pages": [
            {"url": p.get("url"), "title": p.get("title"), "raw_content": p.get("raw_content")}
            for p in pages
        ]})
    return await _original(self, query, pages)


ContextManager.get_similar_content_by_query = _recording


async def collect_one(item: dict, out: Path, sem: asyncio.Semaphore) -> None:
    path = out / f"{item['id']}.json"
    if path.exists():
        return
    async with sem:
        researcher = GPTResearcher(query=item["query"], report_type="research_report")
        calls = _RECORDINGS[id(researcher)] = []
        start = time.perf_counter()
        try:
            await researcher.conduct_research()
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"{item['id']}: FAILED {e}")
            return
        finally:
            _RECORDINGS.pop(id(researcher), None)
        path.write_text(json.dumps({
            **item,
            "research_seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - start, 1),
            "research_cost": researcher.get_costs(),
            "calls": calls,
        }))
        print(f"{item['id']}: {len(calls)} filter calls, "
              f"{sum(len(c['pages']) for c in calls)} pages, {time.perf_counter() - start:.0f}s", flush=True)


async def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--out", type=Path, default=HERE / "runs")
    parser.add_argument("--concurrency", type=int, default=4)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    args.out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    items = json.loads((HERE / "queries.json").read_text())
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(args.concurrency)
    await asyncio.gather(*[collect_one(item, args.out, sem) for item in items])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())



================================================================================
FILE: evals/context_filter/judge.py
================================================================================

"""Step 3: score the replayed reports and summarise.

Quality signals, from most to least objective:

  accuracy    SimpleQA questions have a known answer; each report is graded
              with the repo's SimpleQA grader (CORRECT / INCORRECT /
              NOT_ATTEMPTED).
  precision   Share of the context's chunks an independent judge model rates
              relevant to the research question. Measures the filter itself.
              Not defined for ``none``, which applies no filter.
  pairwise    Blind head-to-head against ``embeddings``, run in both orders
              to cancel position bias; a pair counts as a win only if the
              strategy wins both orders.

    python -m evals.context_filter.judge --results results/ --judge-model gpt-5.4
    python -m evals.context_filter.judge --results results/ --baseline none --only jev jev_wide
"""

import argparse
import asyncio
import json
import re
import statistics
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

from openai import AsyncOpenAI

from evals.simple_evals.simpleqa_eval import GRADER_TEMPLATE

client = AsyncOpenAI(max_retries=6, timeout=300)
SEM = asyncio.Semaphore(8)


async def ask(model: str, prompt: str) -> str:
    async with SEM:
        response = await client.chat.completions.create(
            model=model, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()


async def grade_simpleqa(model: str, r: dict) -> str:
    text = await ask(model, GRADER_TEMPLATE.format(
        question=r["query"], target=r["answer"], predicted_answer=r["report"] or "(no report)"))
    return {"A": "CORRECT", "B": "INCORRECT", "C": "NOT_ATTEMPTED"}.get(text[:1], "NOT_ATTEMPTED")


def split_chunks(context: str) -> list[str]:
    return [c.strip() for c in re.split(r"\n(?=Source: )", "\n" + context) if c.strip()]


async def context_precision(model: str, r: dict) -> float | None:
    if r["strategy"] == "none":
        return None
    chunks = split_chunks(r["context"])
    if not chunks:
        return 0.0
    listing = "\n\n".join(f"[{i}] {c[:1500]}" for i, c in enumerate(chunks))
    text = await ask(model, (
        f"Research question: {r['query']}\n\n"
        f"Below are {len(chunks)} numbered passages. A passage is RELEVANT if it contains information "
        "that would help write an accurate answer to the research question; passages that are only "
        "on the same general topic, navigation, boilerplate or unrelated are NOT relevant.\n\n"
        f"{listing}\n\nReply with only a JSON list of the numbers of the RELEVANT passages, e.g. [0, 3]."))
    try:
        relevant = {int(i) for i in json.loads(re.search(r"\[.*?\]", text, re.S).group(0))}
    except (AttributeError, ValueError):
        return None
    return len(relevant & set(range(len(chunks)))) / len(chunks)


PAIRWISE = """You are comparing two research reports that answer the same question.

Question: {query}

=== Report 1 ===
{a}

=== Report 2 ===
{b}

Judge which report better answers the question: factual accuracy and specificity first, then
relevance (no padding or off-topic material), then completeness. Length alone is not a merit.
Reply with exactly one of: "1", "2", or "tie"."""


async def pairwise(model: str, r: dict, base: dict) -> str:
    """'win', 'loss' or 'tie' for r against base, requiring agreement across both orders."""
    first = await ask(model, PAIRWISE.format(query=r["query"], a=r["report"], b=base["report"]))
    second = await ask(model, PAIRWISE.format(query=r["query"], a=base["report"], b=r["report"]))
    first, second = first.strip('"').lower(), second.strip('"').lower()
    if first.startswith("1") and second.startswith("2"):
        return "win"
    if first.startswith("2") and second.startswith("1"):
        return "loss"
    return "tie"


async def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--results", type=Path, required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--judge-model", default="gpt-5.4")
    parser.add_argument("--precision-model", default="gpt-5.4-mini")
    parser.add_argument("--baseline", default="embeddings", help="strategy the pairwise judge compares against")
    parser.add_argument("--only", nargs="*", help="score only these strategies (the baseline is still loaded)")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    BASELINE = args.baseline

    by_strategy = defaultdict(dict)
    for path in args.results.glob("*/*.json"):
        r = json.loads(path.read_text())
        by_strategy[r["strategy"]][r["id"]] = r
    strategies = sorted(by_strategy, key=lambda s: (s != BASELINE, s))
    if args.only:
        strategies = [s for s in strategies if s in args.only]
    tag = f"_vs_{BASELINE}" + (f"_{'_'.join(args.only)}" if args.only else "")

    async def score(r: dict) -> dict:
        tasks = {"precision": context_precision(args.precision_model, r)}
        if r["kind"] == "simpleqa":
            tasks["grade"] = grade_simpleqa(args.judge_model, r)
        base = by_strategy[BASELINE].get(r["id"])
        if r["strategy"] != BASELINE and base and r["report"] and base["report"]:
            tasks["pairwise"] = pairwise(args.judge_model, r, base)
        values = await asyncio.gather(*tasks.values())
        return {**r, **dict(zip(tasks, values))}

    scored = await asyncio.gather(*[score(r) for s in strategies for r in by_strategy[s].values()])
    (args.results / f"scored{tag}.json").write_text(json.dumps(
        [{k: v for k, v in r.items() if k not in ("report", "context")} for r in scored], indent=1))

    rows = []
    for s in strategies:
        rs = [r for r in scored if r["strategy"] == s]
        sqa = [r for r in rs if r["kind"] == "simpleqa"]
        pw = [r["pairwise"] for r in rs if r.get("pairwise")]
        prec = [r["precision"] for r in rs if r.get("precision") is not None]
        med = lambda k: statistics.median(r[k] for r in rs)
        rows.append({
            "strategy": s,
            "runs": len(rs),
            "errors": sum(1 for r in rs if r["error"]),
            "simpleqa_correct": sum(r["grade"] == "CORRECT" for r in sqa),
            "simpleqa_incorrect": sum(r["grade"] == "INCORRECT" for r in sqa),
            "simpleqa_not_attempted": sum(r["grade"] == "NOT_ATTEMPTED" for r in sqa),
            "simpleqa_n": len(sqa),
            "precision": round(statistics.mean(prec), 3) if prec else None,
            f"pairwise_vs_{BASELINE}": {k: pw.count(k) for k in ("win", "tie", "loss")} if pw else None,
            "median_filter_seconds": med("filter_seconds"),
            "median_context_tokens": med("context_tokens"),
            "median_write_seconds": med("write_seconds"),
            "mean_filter_cost": round(statistics.mean(r["filter_cost"] for r in rs), 5),
            "mean_write_cost": round(statistics.mean(r["write_cost"] for r in rs), 4),
        })
    (args.results / f"summary{tag}.json").write_text(json.dumps(rows, indent=1))
    print(json.dumps(rows, indent=1))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

FILE: evals/context_filter/replay.py
